title: II. Subsidies and Countervailing Measures
subject: PART THREE – TRADE REMEDY MEASURES

paragraphs.text:
What is a subsidy and countervailing measure?

Subsidies and countervailing measure is a trade counter-measure adopted by government to offset any specific subsidy given to exporters or manufacturers of the subsidized product, and the importation of such subsidized product is causing or is threatening to cause material injury to a domestic industry, or is materially retarding the growth or preventing the establishment of a domestic industry.

What is a subsidy?

A subsidy refers to any specific assistance (e.g., financial contribution, income or price support schemes) provided directly or indirectly by the government of the country of export or origin in respect of the product imported into the Philippines, which confers a benefit to the foreign exporter or producer of said product. Examples of financial contributions are grants, soft loans, guarantees and certain equity infusions, tax credits, and goods and services provided by governments.

What are non-actionable subsidies?

Non-actionable subsidies or “green” subsidies refer to subsidies protected from countervailing action either because they are considered to be of particular value and not to be discouraged, or because they are considered to have no, or at most minimal, trade-distorting effects or production effects.

The following categories of subsidies shall be non-actionable:
• Assistance for research activities conducted by foreign firms or by higher education or research establishments on a contract basis with such foreign firms if the assistance covers not more than seventy-five per cent (75%) of the costs of industrial research or fifty per cent (50%) of the costs of pre-competitive development activity, and that such assistance is limited exclusively to: a. costs of personnel (researchers, technicians and other supporting staff employed exclusively in the research activity); b. costs of instruments, equipment, land, and buildings used exclusively and permanently (except when disposed of on a commercial basis) for the research activity; c. costs of consultancy and equivalent services used exclusively for the research activity, including bought-in research, technical knowledge, patents, etc.; d. additional overhead costs incurred directly because of the research activity; and e. other running costs (such as those of materials, supplies and the like), incurred directly because of the research activity.
• Assistance to disadvantaged regions within the territory of a country of export or origin pursuant to a general framework of regional development and non-specific within the meaning of Section 12 within an eligible region provided that: a. each disadvantaged region must be a clearly designated contiguous geographical area with a definable economic and administrative identity; b. the region is considered as disadvantaged on the basis of neutral and objective criteria, indicating that the region’s difficulties arise out of more than temporary circumstances; such criteria must be clearly spelled out in law, regulation, or other official document, so as to be capable of verification; c. the criteria shall include a measurement of economic development which shall be based on at least one of the following factors: one of either income per capita or household income per capita, or Gross Domestic Product per capita, which must not be above eighty-five per cent (85%) of the average for the territory concerned; unemployment rate, which must be at least one hundred ten per cent (110%) of the average for the territory concerned; as measured over a three-year period; such measurement, however, may be a composite one and may include other factors.
• Assistance to promote adaptation of existing facilities to new environmental requirements imposed by law and/or regulations which result in greater constraints and financial burden on foreign firms, provided that the assistance: a. is a one-time non-recurring measure; and b. is limited to twenty per cent (20%) of the cost of adaptation; and c. does not cover the cost of replacing and operating the assisted investment, which must be fully borne by the foreign firms; and d. is directly linked to and proportionate to a foreign firm’s planned reduction of nuisance and pollution, and does not cover any manufacturing cost savings which may be achieved; and e. is available to all foreign firms which can adopt the new equipment and/or production processes.
• Likewise, the following categories of domestic support measures that are exempt from reduction commitments under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture shall be non-actionable: Provided, however, that: a. they have no, or at most minimal, trade-distorting effects or effects on production; b. they are provided through a publicly funded government program not involving transfers from consumers; and c. they do not have the effect of providing price support to foreign producers.

What is a specific subsidy?

A specific subsidy refers to the subsidy limited to an enterprise or industry, or to a group of enterprises or industries. A subsidy can be limited to certain enterprises or industries by being available only in particular regions of a country. All export related subsidies and subsidies related to the use of domestic over imported goods are specific. Subsidies can also be specific if they are provided in practice to only certain enterprises or industries even though the law may not explicitly limit their application in such a manner.

What are actionable subsidies?

Actionable subsidies or “yellow” subsidies are those falling under the definition of subsidy described above.

What is a subsidized import/product?

A subsidized import/product refers to any product which is granted, directly or indirectly by the government in the country of export or origin, any kind or form of specific subsidy upon the exportation or manufacture of such product, and which is causing or is threatening to cause material injury to a domestic industry, or is materially retarding the growth or preventing the establishment of a domestic industry producing the like product.

What is the Philippine legislation on subsidies?

RA No. 8751, otherwise known as “An Act Strengthening the Mechanisms for the Imposition of Countervailing Duties on imported Subsidized Products, Commodities or Articles of Commerce in Order to Protect Domestic Industries from Unfair Trade Competition, Amending for the Purpose Section 302, Part 2, Title II, Book I of Presidential Decree No. 1464”, was signed on 07 August 1999 and took effect on 31 August 1999. The provisions of RA No. 8751, which provide protection to a domestic industry which is being injured, or is likely to be injured, by subsidized products imported into or sold in the Philippines, were adopted in Section 713 of the CMTA.

The IRR of RA No. 8751 (Joint Administrative Order No. 02, series of 2000) took effect on 25 September 2000.

What was the rationale for the passage of RA No. 8751?

i. To transform the domestic countervailing duty law into a more workable and simpler piece of legislation providing safety nets against the inflow of cheap subsidized imports
ii. To strengthen the rules governing the investigation of countervailing cases
iii. To align the domestic law with the WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (Article XVI of GATT 1994).

Which government agencies administer the countervailing legislation?

a. DA or DTI-BIS – receives the properly documented application (DTI for industrial goods and DA for agricultural products); determines whether or not a prima facie case exists to warrant initiation of investigation; and conducts preliminary investigation for purposes of determining whether or not provisional measures may be imposed. When implementing countervailing measures pursuant to the results of the preliminary investigation (by the concerned Department) and formal investigation (by the Tariff Commission), the Secretary issues the written instructions and Department Order, respectively.
b. Tariff Commission – conducts formal investigation and makes the final determination for purposes of the imposition of the definitive countervailing duty; conducts the review of countervailing duty (i.e., interim or changed circumstances review and sunset or expiry review)
c. BOC – collects the countervailing duties

What is the coverage of a countervailing duty protest?

A countervailing duty protest shall apply to any product which is granted, directly or indirectly, by the government in the country of export or origin, any kind or form of specific subsidy upon the exportation or manufacture of such product, and the importation of such subsidized product is causing or threatening to cause material injury to a domestic industry, or is materially retarding the growth or preventing the establishment of a domestic industry.

What is a country of export?

A country of export is the country from where the allegedly subsidized product was shipped to the Philippines, regardless of the location of the seller. The country of export and the country of origin may be the same, but not in all instances.

What is a country of origin?

A country of origin is where the allegedly subsidized product was either wholly obtained or where the last substantial transformation took place. The country of origin and the country of export may be the same, but not in all instances. In case of transshipment, where a product is shipped from a third country that is not the country where the product was manufactured or processed, the country of origin would be different from the country of export.

What are the types of products that may be subsidized?

An agricultural product refers to a product classified under Chapters 1 to 24 of the HS, including those under the specific tariff lines listed in Annex A (Other Agricultural Products Not Falling Under Chapters 1 to 24 of the TCCP of Joint Administrative Order No. 02 Series of 2000) of the IRR of RA No. 8751.

Non-agricultural or industrial goods refer to products classified under Chapters 25 to 97 of the HS and excluded from Annex A.

Are there any importations exempted from countervailing action?

Yes. The following shipments and/or consignments shall not be subject to countervailing duty protest:
• articles imported by, or consigned to, government agencies not organized for profit and particularly designated by law or proper authorities to import, directly or through awardees, such commodities as would stabilize and/or supplement shortages; and
• conditionally duty-free importations allowable under Section 800 of the CMTA.

Who may file a petition for countervailing action?

Any person, whether natural or juridical, belonging to or representing a domestic industry may file with the Secretary of Agriculture, for agricultural products, or with the Secretary of Trade and Industry, for industrial goods, a verified petition requesting the imposition of a countervailing duty to counteract a subsidization which is causing or threatening to cause material injury to a domestic industry. Upon affirmative preliminary findings by the Secretary, the case is endorsed to the Tariff Commission for formal investigation.

What is a domestic industry?

The term “domestic industry” refers to the domestic producers as a whole of the like product, commodity or article or to those of them whose collective output of the product, commodity or article constitutes a major proportion of the total domestic production of that product, commodity or article, except that when producers are related to the exporters or importers or are themselves importers of the allegedly subsidized product or a like product from other countries, the term “domestic industry” may be interpreted as referring to the rest of the producers.

What is the threshold of support by producers for the petition to be accepted?

The thresholds of support by producers for the petition to be accepted are:
i. Support by domestic producers whose collective output constitutes more than fifty percent (50%) of the total production of the like product produced by that portion of the domestic industry expressing either support for, or opposition to, the application; and
ii. Support by producers accounting for at least twenty-five percent (25%) of the total production of the like product produced by the domestic industry.

Under what conditions can a countervailing investigation be initiated without a written application from the domestic industry?

In special circumstances, the DA or DTI may, on its own motion, initiate a countervailing action even without a written application from the domestic industry. The concerned authorities should have sufficient evidence of subsidy, injury, and causal link to justify the initiation of the investigation.

What relevant evidences and information reasonably available to the applicant (protestor) shall a properly documented application contain?

A properly documented application shall contain relevant evidences and information reasonably available to the applicant on the following: i. Identity of the applicant and a description of the volume and the value of his domestic production of the like product; ii. A list of all known domestic producers of the like product and, if possible, a description of the volume and value of domestic production of the like product accounted for by such producers, if the application is made on behalf of the domestic industry; iii. Complete description of the allegedly subsidized product; iv. Name of the country of export or origin of the allegedly subsidized product; v. Identity of each known foreign exporter or producer of the allegedly subsidized product, or their duly authorized representative organizations; vi. List of known persons importing the allegedly subsidized product with their last known address; vii. Estimated aggregate quantity, the port and the date of arrival, and the import entry declaration of the allegedly subsidized product; viii. The nature, extent, and estimated amount of the subsidy in question; ix. Number of persons employed by the affected domestic industry; x. Total capital invested, production and sales volume, and aggregate production capacity of the domestic industry; xi. Effect of the price of the allegedly subsidized products on the price of the like product in the domestic market; xii. Consequent impact of the importation of the allegedly subsidized products on the domestic industry demonstrated by relevant factors and indices having a bearing on the state of the domestic industry.

What are the stages of a countervailing investigation?

i. Prima Facie Determination. The DA or DTI-BIS has ten (10) days from receipt of the properly documented petition to examine the accuracy and adequacy of the evidence provided in the petition and determine whether there is sufficient evidence to justify the initiation of an investigation.
ii. Preliminary Determination. Once a prima facie case has been established, the DA or DTI initiates the investigation and makes a preliminary determination on whether or not a provisional measure may be imposed within twenty (20) days from receipt of the answers to the questionnaire from respondents and other interested parties.
iii. Final Determination. The Tariff Commission conducts the formal investigation during which it notifies all interested parties; receives representations and/or other submissions; holds preliminary conference and public consultations; and conducts on-site investigation/data verification (for both foreign and domestic parties). The Commission has 120 days from receipt of the advice from either the DA or DTI Secretary to complete its investigation and submit its report of findings to the Secretary.
iv. Issuance of Department Order. Within ten (10) days from receipt of the affirmative final determination by the Tariff Commission, the DA or DTI Secretary shall issue a Department Order for the imposition of a definitive countervailing duty, unless the Secretary has earlier accepted a price undertaking from the foreign exporter, producer or government of the country of export or origin.

In case of a negative determination, the Secretary shall issue, through the Secretary of Finance, after the lapse of the period for the petitioner to appeal to the Court of Tax Appeals, an Order for the Commissioner of Customs to immediately release the cash bond to the importer.

ai.title: What are the stages of a countervailing investigation?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Mas maikli ang timeline sa countervailing: 10 araw para sa prima facie at 20 araw para sa preliminary.

🔍 Breakdown
• Prima facie: 10 araw mula pagtanggap ng petition
• Preliminary: 20 araw mula pagtanggap ng sagot sa questionnaire
• Final (Commission): 120 araw
• Department Order: 10 araw mula affirmative final determination

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parehong proseso sa AD, pero mas maikli ang unang dalawang yugto.

📦 Halimbawa
Pagkatapos ng 10 araw, malalaman kung may sapat na ebidensya ng subsidy.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Ang pagkakaiba sa AD ang madalas itanong.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Provisional: security na katumbas ng calculated subsidy; hindi bababa sa 60 araw mula initiation

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Pagkumparahin: AD (5 working days at 30 working days) vs CVD (10 days at 20 days).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Sino ang final determiner?
Sagot: Tariff Commission.

🔗 Related Topics
RA 8751; Sec. 713; countervailing investigations

Give the meaning, a breakdown, a practical customs example, why it matters, key numbers and deadlines to remember, a board-exam tip, common confusions, and related CMTA sections, CAO/CMO issuances.

paragraphs.text:
What documents are required in the conduct of formal investigation for the imposition of countervailing duty?

Table 3.3 Formal Investigation for Subsidies and Countervailing Measure: Checklist of Requirements – (1) Official request for the conduct of formal investigation to determine the merit for the imposition of definitive countervailing duty (1 original copy or electronic copy) – DA Office of the Secretary (agricultural products) / DTI Office of the Secretary (industrial products); (2) Complete records of the case to include responses to questionnaires, position papers and documentary evidence (1 original set or electronic copy); (3) Product description, product specifications, product sample, manufacturing process, production data, trade data, financial data, and market data (3 copies: 1 original, 2 photocopy, and/or 1 electronic copy) – domestic producer/s and relevant government agencies; (4) Proof of payment to the publisher of the cost of publication of notices (1 certified true copy, original or electronic copy) – Publisher, two (2) newspapers of general circulation.

What is the purpose of government-to-government consultations and when are these conducted?

Upon acceptance of a properly documented application and before initiating an investigation, the DA or DTI Secretary notifies the government of the country of export or origin about the impending application for countervailing measure and invites the same for consultation as well, with the objective of clarifying the situation as to matters referred to in the application and arriving at a mutually agreed upon solution.

Under what circumstances can a petition be rejected, and the investigation terminated?

i. In the case of a product originating from a developed country, when: a. the amount of subsidy is de minimis, i.e., less than one per cent (1%) ad valorem as a percentage of export price; or b. the volume of imports is negligible. The volume of imports shall normally be regarded as negligible if it accounts for less than three per cent (3%) of the total imports of said product in the Philippines, unless countries which individually account for less than three per cent (3%) of the total imports of the said product in the Philippines collectively account for more than seven per cent (7%) of the total imports of that product; or c. injury is negligible.
ii. In the case of a product originating from a developing country, when: a. the amount of the subsidy is de minimis, i.e., for developing countries the threshold shall be two per cent (2%) and for least developed countries, it is three per cent (3%); or b. the volume of imports is negligible. The volume of imports from a developing country shall be considered negligible if it accounts for less than four per cent (4%) of the total imports of the product, unless such developing countries which individually account for less than four per cent (4%) of the total imports of the product collectively account for more than nine per cent (9%) of the total imports of that product; or c. injury is negligible.

ai.title: Under what circumstances can a petition be rejected, and the investigation terminated?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
May iba't ibang de minimis at negligible thresholds depende kung developed o developing ang pinagmulang bansa.

🔍 Breakdown
• Developed: subsidy <1%; volume <3% (maliban kung sama-sama ay >7%)
• Developing: subsidy <2% (3% para sa LDC); volume <4% (maliban kung sama-sama ay >9%)
• Injury ay negligible

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Mas maluwag ang threshold sa developing countries.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung 1.5% ang subsidy mula sa isang developing country, de minimis ito at ititigil ang kaso.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Pinipigilan ang mga case laban sa napakaliit na subsidy.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Kailangang tingnan kung developed o developing ang bansa

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin: 1%/3%/7% (developed) at 2%(3%)/4%/9% (developing).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Pareho ba ang threshold ng AD at CVD?
Sagot: Hindi. May dagdag na developing/developed distinction sa CVD.

🔗 Related Topics
RA 8751; Sec. 713
ai.prompt: Explain this part of the Tariff Commission Primer ("II. Subsidies and Countervailing Measures – Under what circumstances can a petition be rejected, and the investigation terminated?") in simple Taglish. Give the meaning, a breakdown, a practical customs example, why it matters, key numbers and deadlines to remember, a board-exam tip, common confusions, and related CMTA sections, CAO/CMO issuances.

paragraphs.text:
What is meant by disclosure of essential facts?

Before making the final determination, the Tariff Commission is required to disclose to interested parties (e.g., the domestic industry, exporters or foreign producers, their governments, and importers) the essential facts on which the decision to apply a countervailing duty is to be made. The parties are given five (5) days from the date of receipt of the essential facts to defend their interests in writing.

What can the investigating authorities do if the exporting enterprises refuse to cooperate, impede an investigation, or provide incorrect/incomplete information?

The authorities can decide based on the best information available.

What are the four (4) elements of countervailing?

i. Like Product - a product, commodity or article which is identical, i.e., alike in all respects, to the product, commodity or article under consideration, or in the absence of such product, commodity or article, another product, commodity or article which, although not alike in all respects, has characteristics closely resembling those of the imported product, commodity or article under consideration
ii. Subsidy - any specific assistance (e.g., financial contribution, income or price support schemes) provided directly or indirectly by the government of the country of export or origin in respect of the product imported into the Philippines, which confers a benefit to the foreign exporter or producer of said product
iii. Material injury – means material injury to a domestic industry, threat of material injury or material retardation of the growth or the prevention of the establishment of a domestic industry
iv. Causal link - a finding that the material injury suffered by the domestic industry is the direct result of the importation of the subsidized product.

What are the three (3) modalities in determining price effects?

i. Price depression – refers to the extent to which the domestic producer reduces his selling price to compete with the allegedly subsidized product
ii. Price suppression – refers to the extent by which the allegedly subsidized product prevents the domestic producer from increasing his selling price to a level that will allow full recovery of his cost of production
iii. Price undercutting – refers to the extent to which the allegedly subsidized product is consistently sold at a price below the domestic selling price of the like product

What are the remedies/measures imposed against subsidization?

• Provisional measure - takes the form of a security (cash deposit or bond) equal to the amount of the provisionally calculated amount of subsidy. It is applied only after the DA or DTI-BIS has made a preliminary affirmative determination and no sooner than 60 days from initiation of the case.
• Definitive countervailing duty - final countervailing duty imposed, in addition to the regular duty and other charges, on a protested product imported from a specific exporter, following an affirmative final determination

What is the duration of the imposition of countervailing measures?

i. Provisional measure – not exceeding four (4) months.
ii. Definitive countervailing duty – shall not exceed five (5) years from the date of imposition.

What is meant by voluntary undertaking?

Voluntary undertaking is an offer by the government of the exporting country to eliminate or limit the subsidy, or a voluntary commitment by the foreign exporter and/or the producer that they will increase their prices or will cease exporting to the Philippines at the subsidized price. An offer of price undertaking shall be made only after a preliminary affirmative determination of subsidization and injury to the domestic industry has been reached.

Price undertaking is effective for a period of five (5) years unless the foreign exporter proves to the satisfaction of the authorities that the undertaking is no longer necessary.

What are the reviews available to the affected parties of countervailing measures?

i. Interim or Changed Circumstances Review - conducted by the Commission, motu proprio, or upon the direction of the Secretary or upon petition of any interested party to determine whether (i) the imposition of the countervailing duty is no longer necessary to offset subsidization, taking into consideration the need to protect the existing domestic industry against subsidization, or (ii) the existing duty is not sufficient to counteract the subsidization which is causing injury. At least one (1) year should have elapsed since the imposition of the countervailing duty before an interim review can be initiated.
ii. Sunset or Expiry Review - may be initiated by any interested party or upon own motion of the Commission before the sunset date, i.e., the 5th year, to determine whether the expiry of the countervailing duty would lead to a continuation or recurrence of subsidization and injury

What cases have been investigated by the Tariff Commission under RA No. 8751?

Since RA No. 8751 took effect in August 1999, no case has been endorsed to the Tariff Commission for formal investigation.

ai.title: II. Subsidies and Countervailing Measures
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang countervailing measure ay trade remedy laban sa subsidized imports na nagdudulot ng material injury sa lokal na industriya.

🔍 Breakdown
• Batas: RA 8751 (signed 07 Aug 1999; effective 31 Aug 1999); Sec. 713 ng CMTA
• Subsidy: specific assistance ng gobyerno na nagbibigay ng benepisyo
• Green (non-actionable), Red (prohibited), Yellow (actionable)
• Stages: prima facie (10 days), preliminary (20 days), final (120 days)

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Kapag binibigyan ng gobyerno ng ibang bansa ng ayuda ang exporter kaya mas mura ang presyo sa atin, puwedeng magpataw ng countervailing duty para ma-offset ito.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang bansang X ay nagbigay ng export subsidy sa asukal. Kapag nasaktan ang lokal na industriya, maaaring ipetisyon ang countervailing duty.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Pinapantay nito ang laban sa pagitan ng lokal at dayuhang producer.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• De minimis subsidy: <1% (developed); 2% (developing); 3% (LDC)
• Negligible volume: <3% (developed), <4% (developing)
• Provisional: hanggang 4 na buwan; definitive: hanggang 5 taon
• Walang kasong na-endorse sa Commission mula Aug 1999

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Pagkakaiba ng AD at CVD: ang AD ay para sa dumping (presyo); ang CVD ay para sa subsidy (tulong ng gobyerno). Tandaan ang mga timeline (10/20/120 days).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang specific subsidy?
Sagot: Subsidy na limitado sa isang enterprise, industriya, o rehiyon.

🔗 Related Topics
RA 8752; RA 8800; WTO SCM Agreement (GATT Art. XVI)

title: III. Safeguard Measures
subject: PART THREE – TRADE REMEDY MEASURES

paragraphs.text:
What are safeguard measures?

Safeguard measures are trade remedy measures adopted by the government to protect a specific domestic industry from an increase in imports of any product which is causing, or which is threatening to cause, serious injury to the industry.

What are the types of safeguard measures?

i. General safeguard measure – imposed against imports if the products at issue are being imported in such increased quantities, either absolute or relative to domestic production, and under such conditions as to cause or threaten to cause serious injury to the domestic industry
ii. Special safeguard measure – imposed against importations of agricultural products whose quantitative import restrictions were converted (tariffied) into ordinary customs duties and agricultural products and designated with the symbol “SSG” in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) Schedule of Concessions. It may be invoked if (i) the cumulative import volume each year exceeds its trigger volume; or, but not concurrently, (ii) the actual C.I.F. import price is less than its trigger price. In either case, injury to the domestic industry need not be established.

What is the Philippine legislation on the imposition of safeguard measures?

RA No. 8800, otherwise known as the “Safeguard Measures Act”, was signed on 19 July 2000 and took effect on 09 August 2000. It provides for:
i. General safeguard measures to relieve domestic industries suffering from serious injury as a result of increased imports; and
ii. Special safeguard measures on agricultural products marked “SSG” in Schedule LXXV-Philippines when the import volume exceeds its trigger level or when the import price falls below a trigger price level.

The provisions of RA No. 8800 were adopted in Section 712 of the CMTA.

What was the rationale for the passage of RA No. 8800?

i. To transform the domestic safeguard measures law into a more workable and simpler piece of legislation providing the safety nets against the inflow of increased imports
ii. To strengthen the rules governing the investigation of safeguard cases
iii. To align the domestic law with the WTO Agreement on Safeguards (GATT Article XIX) and the WTO Agreement on Agriculture

What other issuances were promulgated to implement RA No. 8800?

i. Joint Administrative Order No. 03, s. 2000 – IRR of RA No. 8800 which took effect on 11 October 2000
ii. Tariff Commission Order No. 00-02 – internal rules and regulations to govern conduct by the Commission of investigations pursuant to RA No. 8800 which took effect on 05 July 2000

Which government agencies administer the Safeguard Measures Act?

i. General safeguard measure
a. DA or DTI-BIS – receives the application/petition (DTI for industrial goods and DA for agricultural products); determines whether or not a prima facie case exists to warrant initiation of investigation; and conducts preliminary investigation to ascertain whether or not to impose provisional measures. The Secretary of either Department decides on the form of safeguard measure to impose and issue a Department Order implementing a safeguard measure pursuant to the results of its preliminary investigation and the formal investigation of the Commission
b. Tariff Commission – conducts the formal investigation and submits its recommendation to the DTI or DA Secretary on the form of definitive safeguard measure to be imposed; monitors the domestic industry’s progress and its efforts to make a positive adjustment to import competition; conducts investigations on any legitimate request for the extension and re-application of safeguard measures and the reduction, modification and/or termination of safeguard action; evaluates the effectiveness of the actions taken by the domestic industry to facilitate its positive adjustment to import competition after the termination of the safeguard measure
c. BOC – collects the safeguard duties
ii. Special safeguard measure
a. DA – receives the application/petition for safeguard measure on sensitive tariffied agricultural products (marked “SSG” in Schedule LXXV-Philippines); conducts verification on whether (i) the volume of imports exceeds a base trigger level, or (ii) the cost insurance and freight (c.i.f.) import price falls below a trigger price level and makes its finding within five (5) working days from receipt of the petition; issues a Department Order for the imposition of a special safeguard duty on subject product
b. BOC – collects the special safeguard duties

What is the coverage of general safeguard measures? Special safeguard measures?

A safeguard measure shall apply to products which are being imported from all sources into the Philippines. Under Chapter II of the IRR of RA No. 8800, a general safeguard measure shall apply where there is an increase in the quantity of a product being imported, whether absolute or relative to the domestic production, which is determined to be a substantial cause of serious injury or threat thereof to the domestic industry.

Under Chapter III of the IRR of RA No. 8800, and consistent with Philippine international treaty obligations, a special safeguard measure on an agricultural product shall apply where:
i. the cumulative import volume, in a given year, exceeds its trigger volume; or but not concurrently,
ii. Its actual c.i.f. import price has gone below its trigger price.

What are the types of products whose importation may be imposed with safeguard measures?

An agricultural product refers to commodities classified under Chapters 1 to 24 of the HS. Non-agricultural or industrial goods refer to products covered under Chapters 25 to 97 of the HS.

Who may file a petition for imposition of safeguard measures?

i. General safeguard measure
Any person, whether natural or juridical, belonging to or representing a domestic industry may file with the Secretary of Agriculture, for agricultural products, or with the Secretary of Trade and Industry, for industrial goods, a verified petition requesting that action be taken to remedy the serious injury or prevent the threat thereof to the domestic industry caused by increased imports. Upon affirmative preliminary findings by the Secretary, the case is endorsed to the Tariff Commission for formal investigation.
ii. Special safeguard measure
Any person, whether natural or juridical may request a verification if a particular agricultural product can be imposed a special safeguard duty.

What is a domestic industry?

The term “domestic industry” refers to the domestic producers, as a whole, of like or directly competitive products manufactured or produced in the Philippines or those whose collective output of like or directly competitive products constitutes a major proportion of the total domestic production of those products.

Under what conditions can a safeguard investigation (general or special) be initiated without a written application from the domestic industry?

i. In special circumstances, the DA or DTI Secretary may, on his own motion, initiate a preliminary safeguard investigation if there is evidence that increased imports of the product under consideration are a substantial cause of, or are threatening to substantially cause, serious injury to the domestic industry.
ii. The Secretary may also initiate action upon the request of the President; or a resolution of the House of Representatives (HOR) or Senate Committee on Agriculture, or HOR or Senate Committee on Trade and Commerce.

What are the stages of investigation for the imposition of a general safeguard measure?

• Prima Facie Determination. The DA or DTI-BIS, upon acceptance of a properly documented petition, has five (5) calendar days to decide whether a prima facie case exists to merit the initiation of a preliminary investigation. If no prima facie case exists, the application is rejected.
• Preliminary Determination. Once a prima facie case has been established, the DA or DTI-BIS initiates the preliminary investigation to include notification to all known interested parties and the government of the exporting country, and distribution of questionnaire to all known concerned parties. DA or DTI-BIS has 30 calendar days, from receipt of properly documented application or a motu proprio initiation (including answers of the respondents, and the respective supporting documents or information), to make its preliminary determination on whether or not to impose a provisional safeguard measure. In the case of an affirmative finding, the DA or DTI Secretary issues written instructions for the imposition of a provisional general safeguard measure. In case of a negative finding, the DA or DTI Secretary terminates the investigation.
• Final Determination. The Tariff Commission has 120 calendar days (or 60 days if the Secretary certifies the case as urgent) from receipt of the endorsement from the Secretary to conclude its formal investigation and submit its report of findings and recommendations to the Secretary on whether or not to impose a definitive general safeguard measure.
• Issuance of Department Order. The Secretary has fifteen (15) calendar days, from receipt of the Commission’s report of findings and recommendation, to make a decision on the level and form of the safeguard measure, if the determination is affirmative. A Department Order is issued to implement the imposition of the general safeguard measure.

In case of a negative determination, the Secretary issues a Department Order for the termination of the case as well as a written instruction to the BOC Commissioner, through the Secretary of Finance, authorizing the return of the cash bond previously collected.

ai.title: What are the stages of investigation for the imposition of a general safeguard measure?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang general safeguard investigation ay may apat na yugto na may mga calendar days.

🔍 Breakdown
• Prima facie: 5 calendar days
• Preliminary: 30 calendar days
• Final determination (Commission): 120 calendar days (60 kung urgent)
• Department Order: 15 calendar days

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Gaya ng AD pero calendar days ang gamit at mas mahaba ang DO.

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag urgent ang kaso, 60 araw lang ang Commission.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Mahalaga sa timeline ng safeguard.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Negative: i-release ang cash bond

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin: 5, 30, 120 (60), 15.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang pagkakaiba sa AD timeline?
Sagot: AD ay may 'working days' sa unang dalawang yugto; safeguard ay 'calendar days'; DO ay 10 vs 15 araw.

🔗 Related Topics
RA 8800; AD timeline

paragraphs.text:
What documents are required in the conduct of formal investigation for the imposition of safeguard duty?

Table 3.4 Formal Investigation for General Safeguard Measure: Checklist of Requirements – (1) Official request for the conduct of formal investigation to determine the merit for the imposition of definitive safeguard duty (1 original copy or electronic copy) – DA Office of the Secretary (agricultural) / DTI Office of the Secretary (industrial); (2) Complete records of the case to include responses to questionnaires, position papers and documentary evidence (1 original set or electronic copy) – DA/DTI; (3) Product description, product specifications, product sample, manufacturing process, production data, trade data, financial data, and market data (3 copies: 1 original, 2 photocopy, and/or 1 electronic copy) – Petitioner/s, domestic producer/s and relevant government agencies; (4) Proof of payment to the publisher of the cost of publication of notices (1 certified true copy, original or electronic copy) – Publisher, two (2) newspapers of general circulation; (5) Adjustment Plan (1 original copy and 1 photocopy or electronic copy) – Petitioner/s, domestic producer/s.

What are the elements for the imposition of safeguard measures?

• General safeguard measure
a. Like product or directly competitive product
i. Like product - shall mean a domestic product which is identical, i.e., alike in all respects, to the imported product under consideration, or in the absence of such a product, another domestic product which, although not alike in all respects, has characteristics closely resembling those of the imported product under consideration
ii. Directly competitive products - shall mean domestically produced substitutable products
b. Increased imports – either in absolute terms or relative to domestic production; the increase should be recent, sharp, and significant
c. Serious injury or threat thereof:
i. Serious injury – shall mean a significant impairment in the position of a domestic industry after evaluation by competent authorities of all relevant factors of an objective and quantifiable nature having a bearing on the situation of the industry concerned, in particular, the rate and amount of the increase in imports of the product concerned in absolute and relative terms, the share of the domestic market taken by increased imports, changes in levels of sales, production, productivity, capacity utilization, profit and losses, and employment
ii. Threat of serious injury – shall be understood to mean serious injury that is imminent
d. Causality – refers to the overall assessment that the serious injury suffered by the domestic industry is the direct result of increased imports of the product under consideration
• Special safeguard measure
a. Volume of imports exceed a base trigger level; or
b. Price of imports fall below a trigger price level.

ai.title: What are the elements for the imposition of safeguard measures?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang elemento ng general safeguard ay iba sa dumping: tinitingnan ang pagdami ng imports at serious injury, hindi ang presyo o unfairness.

🔍 Breakdown
• Like o directly competitive product
• Increased imports (absolute o relative; recent, sharp, significant)
• Serious injury o threat ng serious injury (imminent)
• Causality: ang injury ay direktang bunga ng pagtaas ng imports
• Special safeguard: volume ay lampas sa trigger o presyo ay mas mababa sa trigger price

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Ang safeguard ay para sa 'biglaang bugso' ng imports, kahit patas ang presyo.

📦 Halimbawa
Biglang bumaha ang imported na semento mula sa maraming bansa at nagsara ang mga lokal na planta. Puwedeng safeguard ang remedyo.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Madalas gamitin sa pagkukumpara ng AD/CVD at safeguard.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Sa special safeguard, hindi kailangang patunayan ang injury

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang pagkakaiba ng 'serious injury' (safeguard) at 'material injury' (AD/CVD).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Anong produkto ang puwedeng sakop ng special safeguard?
Sagot: Agricultural products na may 'SSG' sa Schedule LXXV-Philippines.

🔗 Related Topics
RA 8800; Sec. 712; WTO Agreement on Safeguards; AoA Art. 5
ai.prompt: Explain this part of the Tariff Commission Primer ("III. Safeguard Measures – What are the elements for the imposition of safeguard measures?") in simple Taglish. Give the meaning, a breakdown, a practical customs example, why it matters, key numbers and deadlines to remember, a board-exam tip, common confusions, and related CMTA sections, CAO/CMO issuances.

paragraphs.text:
What are the factors in determining serious injury?

The factors in determining serious injury to a domestic industry are the following:
i. rate and amount of the increase in imports of the product concerned in absolute or relative terms;
ii. share of the domestic market taken by increased imports; and
iii. changes in the level of sales, prices, production, productivity, capacity utilization, profits and losses, wages, and employment.

In making their determination with respect to serious injury, the Secretary, and the Commission, at their respective stages of investigation, shall also take into account all economic factors which they consider relevant including but not limited to:
i. significant idling of productive facilities in the domestic industry including the closure of plants or underutilization of production capacity;
ii. inability of a significant number of firms to carry out domestic production at a profit; and
iii. significant unemployment or underemployment within the domestic industry.

What form of general safeguard measure can be imposed?

• Provisional measure - takes the form of a tariff increase either ad valorem or specific, or both, to be paid through a cash bond set at a level sufficient to redress or prevent serious injury to the domestic industry. In the case of non-agricultural products, the Secretary shall first establish that the imposition of the provisional safeguard measure would be in the public interest. In the case of agricultural products, where the tariff increase may not be sufficient to redress or to prevent serious injury to the domestic producer or producers, a quantitative restriction may be applied.
• Definitive safeguard measure - may take any of the following forms:
a. Increase in, or imposition of, any duty on the imported product (not subject or limited to the maximum levels of tariff as set forth in Section 1608 of the CMTA)
b. Decrease in or the imposition of a tariff-rate quota (Minimum Access Volume) on the product
c. Modification or imposition of any quantitative restriction on the importation of the product into the Philippines
d. One or more appropriate adjustment measures, including the provision of trade adjustment assistance
e. Any combination of actions described in items (a) to (d)

The Commission may also recommend other actions, including the initiation of international negotiations, to address the underlying cause of the increase in imports of the product, to alleviate the injury or threat thereof to the domestic industry, and to facilitate positive adjustment to import competition.

What form of special safeguard measure can be imposed (on SSG-denominated agricultural products)?

i. Provisional measure – not applied
ii. Definitive special safeguard measure:
a. Under the volume test, the additional duty should not exceed one-third (1/3) of the applicable out-quota customs duty on the agricultural product under consideration
b. Under the price test, the additional duty is computed as follows:
i) Zero - if the price difference is at most ten percent (10%) of the trigger price
ii) Thirty percent (30%) of the amount by which the price difference exceeds ten percent (10%) of the trigger price, if the said difference exceeds ten percent (10%) but is at most forty percent (40%) of the trigger price
iii) Fifty percent (50%) of the amount by which the price difference exceeds forty percent (40%) of the trigger price, plus the additional duty imposed under paragraph ii, if the said difference exceeds forty percent (40%) but is at most, sixty percent (60%) of the trigger price
iv) Seventy percent (70%) of the amount by which the price difference exceeds sixty percent (60%) of the trigger price, plus the additional duties imposed under paragraphs ii and iii, if the said difference exceeds sixty percent (60%) and is at most, seventy-five percent (75%) of the trigger price
v) Ninety percent (90%) of the amount by which the price difference exceeds seventy-five percent (75%) of the trigger price, plus the additional duties imposed under paragraphs ii, iii, and iv, if the said difference exceeds seventy-five percent (75%) of the trigger price

ai.title: What form of special safeguard measure can be imposed (on SSG-denominated agricultural products)?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang special safeguard sa SSG agricultural products ay additional duty batay sa volume o price test.

🔍 Breakdown
• Volume test: hanggang 1/3 ng out-quota duty
• Price test: zero kung ≤10%; 30%, 50%, 70%, 90% ng bahagi ng pagkakaiba sa trigger price sa mga susunod na band
• Provisional: hindi ipinapataw

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Mas malaki ang idinadagdag na duty kapag mas malaki ang pagbaba ng presyo mula sa trigger.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung bumaba ang import price nang 15% sa trigger, may additional duty na 30% ng sobrang 5%.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Dahil tiered ang formula, madalas itong gawing computation problem.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Hindi kailangang patunayan ang injury

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang mga band: 10%, 40%, 60%, 75% ng trigger price.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Sino ang nag-iisyu ng Department Order?
Sagot: Ang DA.

🔗 Related Topics
AoA Art. 5; RA 8800; Schedule LXXV

paragraphs.text:
What is the duration of imposition of safeguard measures?

i. General safeguard measure
a. Provisional measure – shall not exceed 200 calendar days from the date of imposition
b. Definitive measure – the maximum initial period for the application of a safeguard measure is four (4) years, including the period in which the provisional measure is imposed; the initial period may be extended up to a maximum of ten (10) years
ii. Special safeguard measure
It shall be in effect only until the end of the year in which the measure is imposed.

ai.title: What is the duration of imposition of safeguard measures?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
May magkaibang haba ang bawat uri ng safeguard.

🔍 Breakdown
• General provisional: hanggang 200 calendar days
• General definitive: unang period hanggang 4 na taon (kasama ang provisional); puwedeng i-extend hanggang kabuuang 10 taon
• Special safeguard: hanggang katapusan ng taon na ipinataw

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Pansamantala muna, tapos ang pangunahing proteksyon ay may limitasyon sa taon.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung may provisional na 200 araw at definitive na 4 na taon sa kabuuan, puwedeng i-extend kung may adjustment plan hanggang 10 taon.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Pinipigilan ang walang katapusang proteksyon.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Compensation sa mga apektadong WTO members
• Hindi puwedeng selective (MFN basis)

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Mga numero: 200 days, 4 years, 10 years.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Puwede bang bilateral ang safeguard?
Sagot: Hindi. Dapat non-selective o MFN basis.

🔗 Related Topics
Adjustment plan; WTO compensation; AD/CVD durations
ai.prompt: Explain this part of the Tariff Commission Primer ("III. Safeguard Measures – What is the duration of imposition of safeguard measures?") in simple Taglish. Give the meaning, a breakdown, a practical customs example, why it matters, key numbers and deadlines to remember, a board-exam tip, common confusions, and related CMTA sections, CAO/CMO issuances.

paragraphs.text:
Are there limitations to the application of general safeguard measures?

Yes. General safeguard measures should be limited to: i) the extent of redressing or preventing serious injury to the domestic industry and ii) facilitating the domestic industry’s adjustments from the adverse effects directly attributed to the increased imports.

When quantitative import restrictions are used, such measures shall not reduce the quantity of imports below the average imports for the three (3) preceding representative years, unless clear justification is given that a different level is necessary to prevent or remedy serious injury.

General safeguard measures shall also not be applied to a product originating from a developing country, if that country’s share of total imports of the product is less than three percent (3%), provided that the developing countries with less than three percent (3%) share collectively account for not more than nine per cent (9%) of the total imports.

Can the Tariff Commission recommend the application of general safeguards on a bilateral or selective basis?

No. One of the major guiding principles of the WTO Agreement on Safeguards is that such measures be applied on a non-selective or MFN basis. Safeguard measures shall be applied to a product being imported irrespective of its source. Thus, a WTO Member may not choose specific countries against whose exports it applies the measures.

Does the Philippines have to pay compensation when it applies a general safeguard measure?

Yes. The Philippines, when applying safeguard measures, must generally pay for them through compensation which is substantially the equivalent level of concessions and other obligations with respect to affected exporting WTO members. Any adequate means of trade compensation may be agreed upon with the affected Members through consultation. In the absence of such agreement on compensation within 30 days, the affected exporting Members may individually suspend substantially equivalent concessions and other obligations (i.e., retaliate) unless the Council for Trade in Goods disapproves. However, this right to retaliate may not be exercised for the first three (3) years that a safeguard measure is in effect, provided that the measure has been taken as a result of an absolute increase in imports, and conforms to the provisions of the Safeguards Agreement.

What is an adjustment plan?

An adjustment plan is the action plan of a domestic industry which describes the set of quantified goals, specific plans, and timetables that said domestic industry commits to undertake to facilitate its positive adjustment to import competition.

The domestic industry submits its adjustment plan to the Tariff Commission within 45 calendar days (or 30 calendar days if the investigation is certified as urgent) upon receipt of the notice of submission.

Does the Commission monitor implementation of an industry’s adjustment plan?

Yes. The Commission monitors developments in the domestic industry, including the progress and specific efforts made by workers and firms in the industry to affect a positive adjustment to import competition. The monitoring includes conduct of a public hearing and on-site inspection and data verification to determine compliance by the domestic industry with its adjustment plan. The Commission submits a report of findings and recommendations to the DA or DTI Secretary.

What cases have been investigated by the Tariff Commission under RA No. 8800?

Table 3.5 Summary of Formal Investigations Under RA No. 8800 (Year – Description – Final Determination):
• 2001 – Cement (Original Petition) – Negative
• 2002 – Ceramic Floor and Wall Tiles (Original Petition) – Positive
• 2003 – Figured Glass, Clear and Tinted Float Glass and Glass Mirror (Original Petition) – Positive
• 2004 – Ceramic Floor and Wall Tiles (First Extension) – Positive
• 2006 – Sodium Tripolyphosphate – Technical Grade (Original Petition) – Positive; measure was not imposed for reason of public interest
• 2006 – Figured Glass, Clear and Tinted Float Glass and Glass Mirror (First Extension) – Positive; measures on figured glass and glass mirror were suspended and terminated, respectively, due to non-production of the domestic industry
• 2007 – Ceramic Tiles (Final Extension) – Positive
• 2009 – Steel Angle Bar (Original Petition) – Positive
• 2009 – Clear and Tinted Float Glass (Final Extension) – Positive
• 2010 – Testliner Board (Original Petition) – Positive
• 2011 – Steel Angle Bar (First Extension) – Positive
• 2013 – Testliner Board (First Extension) – Positive
• 2014 – Newsprint (Original Petition) – Positive
• 2014 – Steel Angle Bar (Final Extension) – Positive
• 2016 – Testliner Board (Final Extension) – Positive
• 2019 – Cement (Original Petition) – Positive
• 2019 – Ceramic Tiles (Original Petition) – Negative
• 2020 – Reflective, Clear and Tinted Float Glass (Original Petition) – Negative

ai.title: III. Safeguard Measures
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang safeguard measure ay trade remedy laban sa biglaang pagtaas ng imports na nagdudulot ng serious injury sa lokal na industriya, kahit patas ang kalakalan.

🔍 Breakdown
• Batas: RA 8800 (Safeguard Measures Act); Sec. 712 ng CMTA
• General safeguard at special safeguard (SSG)
• Ang Tariff Commission ay may 120 calendar days (60 kung urgent) para sa final determination
• Definitive: hanggang 4 na taon (extendable hanggang 10)
• Provisional: hindi hihigit sa 200 calendar days

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Kapag biglang bumaha ang imported na semento kahit patas ang presyo, puwedeng maglagay ng pansamantalang proteksyon para hindi magiba ang lokal na industriya.

📦 Halimbawa
Halimbawa: ang special safeguard sa SSG-marked na agricultural products kapag lumampas sa trigger volume o bumaba sa trigger price.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Binibigyan ng pagkakataon ang industriya na mag-adjust sa import competition.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Hindi selective: nakapataw sa lahat ng source (MFN basis)
• Kailangan ng adjustment plan (45 days; 30 kung urgent)
• May compensation sa apektadong WTO members

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Mga numero: 5 (prima facie), 30 (preliminary), 120/60 (final), 15 (DO), 200 days (provisional), 4–10 taon (definitive).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Puwede bang maging bilateral ang safeguard?
Sagot: Hindi. Dapat non-selective o MFN basis.

🔗 Related Topics
RA 8752; RA 8751; WTO Agreement on Safeguards (GATT Art. XIX); WTO AoA Art. 5

title: IV. Safeguard Measures Vis-à-Vis Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Measures
subject: PART THREE – TRADE REMEDY MEASURES

sections.heading: IV. Safeguard Measures Vis-à-Vis Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Measures

paragraphs.text:
Table 3.6 Safeguard Measures Vis-à-Vis Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Measures

Anti-Dumping / Countervailing Measures vs. General / Special Safeguard Measures

Relevant Agreement: AD/CVD – WTO Anti-Dumping Agreement (GATT Article VI); WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (GATT Article XVI). Safeguards – WTO Agreement on Safeguards (GATT Article XIX); WTO Agreement on Agriculture.

Nature of Measure: AD/CVD address unfairly traded imports – export price is lower than the normal value; subsidized production or exportation of the foreign merchandise. Safeguards address fairly traded imports – export price at the level of normal value; increased level of imports absolute or relative to production (general safeguards); volume of imports exceed a base trigger level or price falls below a trigger price level (special safeguards).

Objective: Dumping and countervailing duties seek to level the playing field by providing remedies and protecting domestic industries against the unfair trade practices of dumping and/or subsidization. General safeguards will remove injury and facilitate structural adjustments that will enable an industry to gain competitiveness. Special safeguards will assist farmers whose products were previously protected by quantitative restrictions that have been tariffied.

Coverage of Measure: AD/CVD – limited to like products; country-specific and exporter-specific. Safeguards – all like or directly competitive products; all countries exporting like or directly competitive product; general safeguards can be applied to all goods, whether agricultural or industrial; special safeguards apply only to agricultural products denominated with the acronym “SSG” in the GATT Schedule of Concessions.

Minimum Threshold of Support of Industry for Application: AD/CVD – a domestic industry which is supported by domestic producers whose collective output constitutes more than 50% of the total production of the like product produced by other domestic producers that are expressing either support for or opposition to the application. However, no investigation shall be initiated when domestic producers expressly supporting the application account for less than 25% of the production of the like product produced by the domestic industry. General Safeguards – industry filing the case should be a producer of the like or directly competitive product whose collective output constitutes a major proportion of the total domestic production. Special Safeguards – DA (motu proprio).

Elements to be Established: AD/CVD – like product; price difference / subsidy; material injury or threat of material injury; causal link. General Safeguards – like or directly competitive product; increased imports; serious injury or threat of serious injury; causal link. Special Safeguards – like product; volume of imports exceed a base trigger level, or price falls below a trigger price level.

Forms of Measure: AD/CVD – provisional measure (anti-dumping bond / countervailing bond); definitive anti-dumping duty / countervailing duty. General Safeguards – provisional measure: tariff increase; definitive safeguard measure: tariff increase, quantitative restrictions (e.g., import quota; import licensing). Special Safeguards – additional duty not exceeding one-third of the level of the ordinary customs duty in effect during the year in which the action is taken.

Imposition of Provisional Measure: AD/CVD – requires the conduct of a preliminary investigation (affirmative preliminary determination) prior to imposition of a dumping or countervailing bond for a period of four (4) months or 120 days. General Safeguards – in critical circumstances where delay may cause damage that is difficult to repair, safeguard measure in the form of tariff adjustment may be imposed for 200 days pursuant to a preliminary determination. Special Safeguards – none.

Duration of Definitive Measure: AD/CVD – five (5) years, subject to sunset review to determine whether or not to extend the effectivity of the dumping / countervailing duty. General Safeguards – four (4) years, extendable for another four (4) years provided the industry can show that structural adjustment is being implemented, with an extension of another two (2) years for developing countries. Special Safeguards – shall only be maintained until the end of the year in which it has been imposed.

ai.title: Table 3.6 Safeguard Measures Vis-à-Vis Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Measures
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Magkaibang remedyo ang AD/CVD at safeguard: ang una ay laban sa unfair trade; ang pangalawa ay laban sa patas pero biglang tumaas na imports.

🔍 Breakdown
• Agreement: AD/CVD (GATT VI, SCM) vs safeguard (GATT XIX, AoA)
• Coverage: AD/CVD limitado sa like products at country/exporter-specific; safeguard sa lahat ng source
• Elements: AD/CVD – like product, price difference/subsidy, material injury, causal link; safeguard – like/directly competitive, increased imports, serious injury, causality
• Duration: AD/CVD 5 taon; general safeguard 4 taon (+4; +2 para sa developing); special safeguard hanggang katapusan ng taon
• Provisional: AD/CVD 4 na buwan o 120 days; general safeguard 200 days; special safeguard wala

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Isa laban sa madaya, isa laban sa biglaang pagbaha.

📦 Halimbawa
Dumping ng bakal mula sa isang bansa = AD. Biglang pagbaha ng semento mula sa maraming bansa = safeguard.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Madalas ilagay sa table sa exam.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Sa special safeguard, hindi kailangang patunayan ang injury

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Gumawa ng comparison table: agreement, nature, coverage, elements, forms, provisional, duration.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Selective ba ang safeguard?
Sagot: Hindi. Non-selective o MFN.

🔗 Related Topics

ai.title: IV. Safeguard Measures Vis-à-Vis Anti-Dumping and Countervailing Measures
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ito ang paghahambing ng AD/CVD at safeguard: ang AD/CVD ay laban sa unfair trade, ang safeguard ay laban sa patas na kalakalan na biglang dumami.

🔍 Breakdown
• AD/CVD: unfairly traded imports; country-specific at exporter-specific
• Safeguard: fairly traded imports; lahat ng source
• Elements: AD/CVD – like product, price difference/subsidy, material injury, causal link; Safeguard – like or directly competitive product, increased imports, serious injury, causal link
• Duration: AD/CVD 5 taon; General safeguard 4 taon (extendable 4 pa, +2 para sa developing); Special safeguard hanggang katapusan ng taon

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Dalawang magkaibang 'panangga': isa laban sa madayang presyo, isa laban sa biglaang bugso ng imports kahit patas.

📦 Halimbawa
Dumping ng steel mula sa isang bansa = AD. Biglang pagbaha ng cement mula sa maraming bansa = safeguard.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Madalas ihambing sa board exam ang dalawang ito.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Provisional AD/CVD: 4 buwan o 120 days (bond)
• Provisional general safeguard: 200 days (tariff increase)
• Special safeguard: walang provisional measure

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Gumawa ng comparison table sa isip: relevant agreement, nature, objective, coverage, threshold, elements, forms, provisional, duration.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Kailangan bang patunayan ang injury sa special safeguard?
Sagot: Hindi. Hindi kailangan ang injury sa volume o price trigger.

title: I. Overview of Non-Tariff Measures
subject: PART FOUR – NON-TARIFF MEASURES

paragraphs.text:
What is the mandate of the Tariff Commission on non-tariff measures (NTMs)?

The Tariff Commission’s mandate on non-tariff measures (NTMs) is provided under Section 1603(e) of Republic Act No. 10863, also known as the Customs Modernization and Tariff Act. The particular provision reads:

“(e) Provide the President and Congress with independent analysis, information and technical support on matters related to tariff and nontariff measures affecting Philippine industries and exports for policy guidance;” (underscoring supplied)

What are NTMs?

The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) defines NTMs as “policy measures, other than ordinary customs tariffs, that can potentially have an economic effect on international trade in goods, changing quantities traded, prices, or both” (UNCTAD, 2010).

This definition covers a broad range of policy instruments such as quotas, price controls, and regulatory or technical measures that stem from important non-trade objectives related to health and environmental protection, such as Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) measures and Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) (UNCTAD, 2020).

What is the difference between NTMs and Non-Tariff Barriers (NTB)?

Although there is a perception of NTMs as primarily trade-dampening, the concept of NTMs is neutral and does not necessarily imply a negative impact on trade. Although many NTMs may restrict trade, this is secondary to their primary function of ensuring consumer health and safety and environmental protection. In fact, some NTMs may enhance trade by ensuring that traded products adhere to minimum health and safety guidelines, thus improving consumer confidence. NTBs, on the other hand, are a subset of NTMs that are applied with a protectionist or discriminatory intent or where the restrictiveness of the measures imposed exceeds what is needed for the measure to achieve the underlying non-trade objective (UNCTAD, 2018).

Why is trade regulated?

Trade is an important driver of the modern global economy. One of the benefits for countries is that they can specialize in the production of specific goods and consume more than they otherwise would have without trade. For households, trade allows consumers access to more affordable goods and services that may not have been available domestically, improving consumer choice (World Bank Group, 2018).

Although trade enhances a country’s welfare, regulations are often imposed to safeguard public interest. Trade is regulated to protect consumers, protect the environment, regulate domestic industries, protect domestic firms, and avoid unintended spillovers (UNCTAD, 2018). On the other hand, it is the responsibility of government to balance the benefits and risks that come with trade with the social costs that come with regulation.

How are NTMs classified?

The UNCTAD has classified NTMs into two (2) broad categories: Import Measures and Export Measures (UNCTAD, 2019). Import Measures are further classified into (a) Technical, and (b) Non-Technical Measures. UNCTAD (2019) defines these 16 categories, as follows:

I. Import Measures
• Technical Measures
A. Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS) – measures such as those restricting substances, ensuring food safety, and preventing the dissemination of diseases or pests. Chapter A also includes all conformity-assessment measures related to food safety, such as certification, testing and inspection, and quarantine
B. Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) – measures such as technical specifications and quality requirements; related processes and production methods; and measures such as labelling and packaging in relation to environmental protection, consumer safety, and national security. It also includes all conformity-assessment measures related to technical requirements such as certification, testing, and inspection
C. Pre-Shipment Inspection and Other Formalities – measures related to pre-shipment inspections such as direct consignment requirements, pass-through requirements, import monitoring and surveillance, automatic licensing measures, and other formalities
• Non-Technical Measures
D. Contingent Trade-Protective Measures – measures implemented to counteract the adverse effects of imports in the market of the importing country, including measures aimed at tackling unfair foreign trade practices. These include anti-dumping, countervailing, and safeguard measures or what are more commonly known as trade remedy measures
E. Non-automatic import licensing, quotas, prohibitions, quantity-control measures, and other restrictions not including sanitary and phytosanitary measures or measures relating to technical barriers to trade – control measures aimed at prohibiting or restricting imports, including measures restraining the quantity of goods that can be imported, regardless of whether they come from different sources or specific suppliers. These measures can take the form of non-automatic licensing, fixing of a predetermined quota or prohibitions
F. Price-control measures, including additional taxes and charges – measures implemented to control or affect the prices of imported goods to, among others, support the domestic price of certain products when the import price of these goods are lower; establish the domestic price of certain products because of price fluctuation in domestic markets or price instability in a foreign market; or to increase or preserve tax revenue. This category also includes measures other than tariff measures that increase the cost of imports by a fixed percentage or by a fixed amount, also known as para-tariff measures
G. Finance measures – restrict the payment of imports, such as when the access and cost of foreign exchange is regulated. It also includes restrictions on terms of payment
H. Measures affecting competition – all measures affecting competition such as the grant of exclusive or special preferences or privileges to one or more limited groups of economic operators. These are mainly monopolistic measures such as: state trading, sole importing agencies, or compulsory national insurance or transport
I. Trade-related investment measures – restrict investment by requiring local content or requesting that investment be related to exports to balance imports
J. Distribution restrictions – restrict the distribution channels or sales of a good, e.g., on the sale of goods to certain categories, access to domestic distribution channels, or additional licenses or certification requirements
K. Restrictions on post-sales services – restrictions on exporters’ ability to provide within importing countries’ borders post-sales services through their preferred or desired channels
L. Subsidies and other forms of support – measures or practices by any level of government that involves a financial transfer attributable to an identifiable beneficiary or group of beneficiaries that create or could potentially create an advantage for those beneficiaries
M. Government procurement restrictions – restrictions regarding the selling of products and services to the government
N. Intellectual property – measures imposed to protect intellectual property rights
O. Rules of origin – measures which restrict the origin of products or its inputs

II. Export Measures
P. Export-related measures – all measures applied by a country to the exports of its products, including but not limited to export taxes, export quotas, and export prohibitions.

What are the effects of NTMs?

It can be recalled that NTMs are adopted with specific policy objectives in mind. Effects of NTMs can be broadly grouped into two (2) categories: Effects on Trade and Effects on Other Policy Areas (Figure 4.1).

Effects on Trade: (1) Change influence on market access; (2) Increase trade costs; (3) Change consumers’ demand. Effects on Other Policy Areas: safeguard human, animal, and plant health; safeguard the environment; ensure minimum product quality and safety; safeguard public moral, political, or cultural values; safeguard national security and international peace.

Influence market access – NTMs in the form of prohibitions, quotas and excessively stringent requirements can effectively inhibit or divert trade between countries. Meanwhile, SPS and TBT measures enforce standardization, quality control, and segmentation of markets. Some NTM categories deal specifically with market access such as Measures affecting competition and Trade-related investment measures.

Increase trade costs – NTMs include complex and diverse instruments that add costs to trade in terms of needed information and government impose costs of compliance to firms that wish to enter their market. The increase in trade cost associated with NTMs is calculated as their Ad Valorem Equivalent (NTMAdVAL). In the APEC region, the NTMAdVAL of NTMs was estimated to be around 9.7% compared to an average tariff level of 2.9% (NZIER, 2016). Moreover, the costs of NTMs accumulate along multi-country value chains where raw materials and intermediate products are transferred to various countries for further processing but must comply with the different regulations of each country (UNCTAD, 2018). Technical Measures, such as TBTs, have differential effects on firms with smaller foreign firms generally being priced-out of the market due to the costs of compliance limiting their ability to compete with domestic firms (UNCTAD, 2018).

Change consumers’ demand – NTMs are generally imposed to meet non-trade objectives. These objectives include safeguarding human health and safety and ensuring environmental protection. In meeting these objectives, consumer’s confidence will be enhanced, and minimum standards of product quality are achieved. This may lead to growth in trade despite the associated costs of compliance with NTMs (UNCTAD, 2018).

What are the effects of NTMs on other policy areas?

The World Trade Organization (WTO) leaves substantial policy space for government to put in place domestic policies that promote economic and social development. The core rule of the WTO is non-discrimination: regulatory measures should not be designed to protect domestic producers by discriminating against foreign products. Thus, governments are given wide berth to enact policy measures that satisfy non-trade regulatory objectives such as safeguarding human, animal, and plant health (SPS Agreement and GATT Articles XX(b) and XX(d)), environmental protection (GATT Article XX(g)), minimum standards for product quality and safety (TBT Agreement and, more generally, under GATT Article XX), protect public moral, political, and cultural values (GATT Article XX(a)), and safeguard national security (GATT Articles XX(i) and XX(j)), among others (UNCTAD, 2018).

ai.title: I. Overview of Non-Tariff Measures
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang NTM ay mga polisiya maliban sa ordinaryong taripa na maaaring makaapekto sa kalakalan, tulad ng quota, price control, at technical/regulatory requirements.

🔍 Breakdown
• Mandato ng Commission: Sec. 1603(e) ng CMTA
• Depinisyon: UNCTAD (2010)
• NTB ay subset ng NTM na may protectionist o discriminatory intent
• 16 na kategorya ng UNCTAD (A–O import at P export)

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Hindi laging masama ang NTM. Madalas ito ay pananggalang sa kalusugan, kaligtasan, at kalikasan.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang SPS requirement sa imported na karne ay NTM. Kung sobra-sobra at ginagamit para harangan ang imports, nagiging NTB na ito.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Habang bumababa ang taripa, mas lumalaki ang papel ng NTM sa kalakalan.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• NTM ≠ NTB
• Effects sa trade: market access, trade costs, consumer demand
• NTMAdVAL sa APEC: ~9.7% laban sa average tariff 2.9%

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang depinisyon at ang kaibahan ng NTM at NTB; at ang titulo ng bawat chapter (A=SPS, B=TBT, C=PSI, D=Contingent, E=Non-automatic licensing/quotas, F=Price control, P=Export).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Sinong may mandato sa NTM sa Pilipinas?
Sagot: Ang Tariff Commission ay nagbibigay ng independent analysis at technical support sa Pangulo at Kongreso (Sec. 1603(e)).

SPS at TBT Agreements; UNCTAD; WTO
