title: II. The Philippines’ NTMs Landscape
subject: PART FOUR – NON-TARIFF MEASURES

paragraphs.text:
What is the NTMs Situation in the Philippines?

A study by the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia (ERIA) in 2018 found that 42 agencies in the Philippines have issued various NTMs. The top issuing agencies are shown in Table 4.1:
1. Department of Agriculture – Bureau of Animal Industry – 198
2. Department of Agriculture – Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources – 108
3. Department of Agriculture – Bureau of Plant Industry – 105
4. Philippine National Police – Firearms and Explosives Office – 62
5. Philippine Nuclear Research Institute – 59
6. Food and Drug Administration – 58
7. Department of Agriculture – National Meat Inspection Service – 53
8. National Telecommunications Commission – 49
9. Department of Energy – 45
10. Department of Environment and Natural Resources – 43
Source: “Non-Tariff Measures in ASEAN - An Update” ERIA, 2019

Table 4.2 shows that 1,220 NTMs have been implemented by the different government agencies as of 2018 (Chapter – Number – Proportion): A SPS – 363 – 29.75%; B TBT – 357 – 29.26%; C Pre-shipment inspection and other formalities – 26 – 2.13%; D Contingent trade protective measures – 0 – 0.00%; E Non-automatic licensing, quotas, prohibitions, and quantity control measures for other than SPS or TBT reason – 209 – 17.13%; F Price control measures, including additional taxes and charges – 40 – 3.28%; G Finance measures – 11 – 0.90%; H Measures affecting competition – 3 – 0.25%; I Trade-related investment measures – 1 – 0.08%; J Distribution restrictions – 3 – 0.25%; K Restriction on post-sales services – 0; L Subsidies – 0; M Government procurement restrictions – 0; N Intellectual Property – 0; O Rules of origin – 0; P Export-related measures – 207 – 16.97%. Total: 1,220 – 100.00%.

How does the Philippine situation compare with the global NTMs landscape?

NTMs Situation of the Philippines vs. ASEAN
A study found that 9,502 NTMs were in force in the ASEAN region in 2018 (Reyes, 2019). These NTMs are summarized in Table 4.3 (Number – Proportion): A SPS – 2,795 – 29.40%; B TBT – 3,443 – 36.20%; C PSI – 325 – 3.4%; D Contingent – 0; E Non-automatic licensing etc. – 819 – 8.60%; F Price control – 438 – 4.60%; G Finance – 18 – 0.20%; H Competition – 27 – 0.30%; I TRIMs – 7 – 0.10%; J Distribution – 8 – 0.10%; K–O: 1 each or 0; P Export-related – 1,619 – 17.00%; Total 9,502 – 100.00%.

A comparison of the composition of ASEAN NTMs and Philippine NTMs shows some differences in policy. Most notably, the proportion of TBTs is much higher for ASEAN (36.20%) than for the Philippines (29.26%). On the other hand, the Philippines has a larger composition of non-automatic licensing measures in place (17.13%) compared to the rest of the region (8.60%). It should be noted that said measures are aimed specifically at restricting the flow of imported goods.

In comparing the NTMs policies of various countries, the following indicators are used: Frequency Index (FI), coverage ratio (CR), prevalence score (PS), and ad valorem equivalent (AVE). The definitions of these indicators are shown in Box 4.1:
• Frequency Index (FI) – captures a country’s share of traded product lines subject to at least one NTM
• Coverage Ratio (CR) – captures a country’s share of trade subject to NTMs. It is weighted by import values, rather than using traded product lines
• Prevalence Score (PS) – indicates the number of distinct NTMs applied on regulated product. It measures the diversity NTM types applied and provides an indication regarding the intensity of regulation in a country
• Ad Valorem Equivalent (AVE) – indicates the increase in trading costs associated with the imposition of NTMs
Source: UNCTAD NTMs Hub

The Philippines has a high CR of 71%: this means that 71% of all tariff lines have an associated NTM. It has an FI of 75%: this means that 75% of all imported products are subject to at least one (1) NTM. Finally, a PS of 3.2 means that, on average, 3.2 distinct measures are applied to all regulated products. Except for Laos, these scores are among the highest among ASEAN Member States, revealing the broad scope and intensity of NTMs policy in the Philippines (Fig. 4.2).

On the other hand, the study found that the ad valorem equivalent (AVE) of Technical NTMs in the Philippines is among the lowest in the ASEAN region. For example, its AVE of 3.7% for SPS Measures is the lowest in ASEAN. Its AVE of 3.4 for TBTs is 3rd lowest (only Myanmar (3.1%) and Cambodia (2.8%) have lower figures) (Fig. 4.3).

What are some illustrative examples of NTMs in the Philippines?

a. NTMs on Essential Medical Products
As the COVID-19 Pandemic accelerated in early April 2020, the WTO issued a report outlining, among others, medical products deemed necessary in the fight against the coronavirus. Under the Philippines’ 2017 ASEAN Harmonized Tariff Nomenclature (AHTN 2017), products of this nature were found in seven hundred and eighty-five (785) distinct tariff lines. In accordance with the WTO report, these products were grouped into the following general categories:
1. Medicines (Pharmaceuticals) – including both dosified and bulk medicines. Table 4.4: Chapter 30 – SPS 22; TBT 35; Pre-shipment inspection 2; Contingent trade protective measures 2; Quantity control measures 18; Price control measures 12; Export-related measures 27; Other measures 4; Total 122.
2. Medical Supplies - refers to consumables for hospital and laboratory use (e.g. alcohol, syringes, gauze, reagents, etc.). Table 4.5: HS 8421.29, 2207.10, 2208.90 – total NTMs 66 (TBT, pre-shipment inspection, quantity control, price control, export-related).
3. Medical Equipment and Technology (Table 4.6: HS 3002.15, 3822.00, 9018.11, 9018.12, 9018.18, 9018.19, 9018.39, 9018.90, 9019.20) – total NTMs 80; and
4. Personal Protective Products – hand soap, sanitizers, face masks, and protective spectacles. Table 4.7: HS 9004.90 – TBT 1; quantity control measures 2; total 3.

b. NTMs on Meat and Processed Food Products
As the COVID-19 Pandemic continued to intensify in mid-July, a review of NTMs on meat and processed food products issued in response to the pandemic was undertaken by the Tariff Commission. It was found that only one (1) NTM for was issued between 13 March 2020 and 15 July 2020 (Table 4.8): Meat and edible offal; fresh, chilled, or frozen – Chapter A (Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures) – 1 new regulation: imposes additional measures to ensure proper cold chain management, thereby safeguarding food safety of food commodities. The following additional documents shall be required from all importers: a. Certificate of Availability of Space of Accredited Cold Storage Warehouse (CSW); b. Meat Importation Usage Report – to ensure that the importers have fully utilized their meat imports every year. Source: WTO ePING Alerts System.

ai.title: II. The Philippines’ NTMs Landscape
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ipinapakita ng bahaging ito kung ilan at anong klase ang NTMs sa Pilipinas at kung paano ito ikinukumpara sa ASEAN.

🔍 Breakdown
• 42 ahensya ang nag-isyu ng NTMs; 1,220 NTMs in force (2018)
• SPS (29.75%) at TBT (29.26%) ang pinakamarami
• Coverage ratio 71%, frequency index 75%, prevalence score 3.2
• Mababa ang AVE ng technical NTMs kumpara sa ASEAN

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang inventory ng mga patakaran sa hangganan. Marami ang bilang pero medyo mababa ang dagdag-gastos nito sa kalakalan.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang karne na kailangan ng SPS clearance at dagdag na cold chain documents ay halimbawa ng NTM sa panahon ng COVID-19.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Nakakatulong ito sa pagbuo ng polisiya na hindi nagiging sagabal sa kalakalan.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Mas marami ang non-automatic licensing sa Pilipinas (17.13%) kumpara sa ASEAN (8.60%)
• Mas mataas ang TBT share ng ASEAN (36.20%) kaysa Pilipinas (29.26%)

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang top issuing agencies at ang mga indicator (FI, CR, PS, AVE).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang ibig sabihin ng coverage ratio na 71%?
Sagot: 71% ng tariff lines ay may kaugnay na NTM.

UNCTAD TRAINS; ERIA; WTO ePing

title: I. The World Trade Organization
subject: PART FIVE – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: MULTILATERAL

paragraphs.text:
What is the World Trade Organization?

The World Trade Organization (WTO) is the only formal and international organization, composed of member governments, dealing with the rules of trade between nations. Trade liberalization is the main approach that WTO Members have adopted to promote economic growth and development. The WTO deals with the regulation of trade between participating countries by providing a framework for negotiating trade agreements and a dispute settlement mechanism aimed at enforcing participants’ adherence to the WTO agreements signed by WTO members. The WTO also covers trade in services and trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights.

How was the WTO created?

The history of the WTO begins with the signing of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) in 1947 which provided the rules for the bulk of world trade and presided over periods that saw some of the highest growth rates in international trade. The initial objective was to create an International Trade Organization (ITO) to handle the trade side of international economic cooperation, to complement the two Bretton Woods Institutions, namely the World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). However, with the failure of the creation of the ITO, the GATT served as an interim organization and took the functions originally intended for the ITO.

The GATT developed rules for the Multilateral Trading System (MTS) through eight (8) rounds of trade negotiations. In the early years, the GATT trade rounds focused on reducing tariffs. The following GATT trade rounds covered not only tariffs, but also other trade barriers. The eighth round, known as the Uruguay Round (UR), was the most comprehensive round that eventually led to the creation of the WTO and the current set of WTO Agreements.

When did the WTO enter into force and what is its present membership?

The WTO was instituted on 01 January 1995 after the long and intense Uruguay Round of Negotiations. The Philippines is one of the founding members of the WTO, alongside several AMSs, namely Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, Singapore, and Thailand. Currently, 164 countries have ratified their accession to the WTO with the newest Members being Liberia and Afghanistan who acceded to the WTO on 14 July 2016 and 29 July 2016, respectively. As of 2018, there are 23 more countries negotiating accession to the WTO.

What are the fundamental principles of the WTO?

• Non-discrimination – Members shall not discriminate between their trading partners (MFN principle); or between national and foreign like products, services, or nationals (national treatment principle).
• More open trade – involves efforts in reducing or eliminating obstacles to trade.
• Transparency and predictability – traders and Members need to know trade rules around the world (transparency) and that trade measures will not be raised/introduced arbitrarily (predictability)
• Special and differential treatment for less developed Members – developing and least developing Members face particular challenges when dealing with trade liberalization; therefore, they are provided greater flexibility, given more time to adjust to the rules, and granted other special rights.

ai.title: What are the fundamental principles of the WTO?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Apat na pangunahing prinsipyo ang gabay ng WTO.

🔍 Breakdown
• Non-discrimination: MFN (pantay sa lahat ng trading partners) at national treatment (pantay ang imported at lokal na produkto)
• Mas bukas na kalakalan: pagbabawas o pag-aalis ng hadlang
• Transparency at predictability: alam ng lahat ang patakaran at hindi basta-basta itinataas
• Special and differential treatment: mas maluwag at mas mahabang panahon para sa developing at least-developed countries

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Patas, bukas, malinaw, at may konsiderasyon sa mahihirap na bansa.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung binigyan ng 5% duty ang produkto ng bansa A, dapat gayundin sa bansa B (MFN).

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Dito nakabatay ang karamihan ng trade rules at disputes.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• MFN ay para sa pagitan ng trading partners; national treatment ay para sa imported laban sa lokal

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang apat na prinsipyo at ang kaibahan ng MFN at national treatment.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang MFN?
Sagot: Pantay na trato sa lahat ng trading partners.

🔗 Related Topics
GATT Art. I at III; WTO Agreements

paragraphs.text:
What is the organizational structure of the WTO?

a. Highest Authority: The Ministerial Conference
The highest decision-making body of the WTO, the Ministerial Conference (MC) shall meet at least once every two (2) years to review the ongoing work, provide political guidance and direction to that work, and set the agenda for further work as necessary. The MC is composed of the Trade Ministers of all the Members (except for some, e.g., the EU Trade Commissioner and the US Trade Representative for the European Union and the United States of America, respectively).

b. Second Level: The General Council
The General Council (GC) is composed of representatives from all Members; they are usually Members’ Ambassadors or Permanent Representatives based in Geneva. The GC meets as appropriate to adopt decisions, on behalf of the MC, when the latter is not in session.

The GC has authority over the Trade Negotiations Committee (TNC), which is in-charge of the negotiations mandated by the Doha Development Agenda (DDA). The GC also meets as:
• Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) - establishes panels of independent experts to resolve the disputes, adopts the rulings of the panels, and oversees the implementation of those rulings
• Trade Policy Review Body (TPRB) - administers trade policy reviews as mandated by the Trade Policy Review Mechanism of the WTO

c. Third level: The Councils and Subsidiary Bodies
Three more councils, each handling a different area of trade, report to the General Council:
• The Council for Trade in Goods (Goods Council) - oversees all the issues related to the WTO Agreement on Trade in Goods. It supervises the work of various committees responsible for specific matters (e.g., agriculture, market access, customs validations, rules of origin, sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures).
• Council for Trade in Services (Services Council) - oversees all issues related to the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS)
• Council for Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS Council) - oversees all issues related to the Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) Agreement

Several other subsidiary bodies which focus on horizontal issues also report directly to the GC. Usually called Committees, Working Groups or Working Parties, these are the following:
• Committee on Trade and Development (CTD);
• Committee on Trade and Environment (CTE);
• Committee on Regional Trade Agreements (CRTA);
• Committee on Balance-of-Payment Restrictions (BOP Committee);
• Committee on Budget, Finance and Administration (CBFA);
• Working Parties on Accession;
• Working Group on Trade, Debt and Finance; and
• Working Group on Trade and Technology Transfer.

ai.title: What is the organizational structure of the WTO?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Tatlong antas ang organisasyon ng WTO: Ministerial Conference, General Council, at mga Councils/Committees.

🔍 Breakdown
• MC: pinakamataas; hindi bababa sa isang beses kada 2 taon; mga Trade Ministers ng lahat ng Members
• GC: mga Ambassador sa Geneva; nagiging DSB at TPRB; may awtoridad sa TNC (DDA)
• Goods Council, Services Council (GATS), TRIPS Council; at mga Committees (CTD, CTE, CRTA, BOP, CBFA) at working groups

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Mula sa mga Ministro (itaas) pababa sa mga komite (ibaba).

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag may reklamo sa paglabag sa WTO rules, ang GC bilang DSB ang magtatayo ng panel.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Madalas itanong sa exam kung alin ang highest authority at ano ang DSB at TPRB.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Desisyon: consensus; kung hindi, majority vote; 1 boto kada Member

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Highest: MC. Second level: GC. Third level: Councils at Committees.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang DSB?
Sagot: Ang GC kapag tinatalakay ang mga hindi pagkakaunawaan; nagtatayo ng panel at nag-aadopt ng rulings.

paragraphs.text:
How are decisions made at the WTO?

The WTO continues GATT’s tradition of making decisions not by voting but by consensus. Where consensus is not possible, the WTO Agreement allows for voting - a vote being won by a majority of the votes cast, unless otherwise provided in said Agreement. At meetings of the MC and the GC, each WTO Member shall have one vote.

Decisions in the WTO are taken through its various councils and committees, whose memberships consist of all WTO Members. The highest decision-making body is the MC.

In what ways does the WTO operate?

• As a set of multilaterally agreed rules governing the trade behavior of governments providing the main rules of the road for trade
• As a forum for trade negotiations in which the trade environment is liberalized and made more predictable either through the opening of national markets or through the reinforcement and extension of the rules themselves
• As an international court where governments can resolve disputes with other WTO members

How does the WTO promote trade liberalization?

Trade liberalization is promoted through the conduct of Multilateral Trade Negotiations, referred to as “Rounds”, to remove or reduce barriers to world trade. Since the creation of the GATT in 1948, eight (8) Rounds of negotiations have been held, with the earlier Rounds focusing on the reduction of tariff barriers that resulted in the lowering of industrial tariffs in developed countries to about 7% on the average.

By the 1980s, negotiations were expanded to cover non-tariff barriers on goods (Tokyo Round) and new areas such as trade in services, investments, and intellectual property (UR).

What is the Uruguay Round (UR)?

The UR was the eighth Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations conducted within the framework of the GATT, spanning from 1986 to 1994 and including 123 countries as “contracting parties.” It covered areas that were never integrated into the GATT before, such as agriculture, textiles and clothing, services, trade-related intellectual property rights, and trade-related investment measures. The UR transformed the GATT into the WTO which was established in 1995.

The Final Act embodying the thirty (30) agreements and 22 ministerial decisions resulting from the UR, and the Agreement to establish the World Trade Organization, was signed on 15 April 1994 at Marrakesh, Morocco. The UR came into effect in 1995 and was implemented up to 2000. In the case of developing country contracting parties, implementation was extended to 2004 under the administrative direction of the newly created WTO.

What are the three (3) key result areas of the Uruguay Round?

a. Market Access – includes negotiations in industrial tariffs, agriculture, textiles and clothing, and services
b. Rules and Disciplines – negotiating topics ranged from trade measures against unfair trade (such as anti-dumping and countervailing measures), trade measures to protect a country against import surges and a deterioration of its balance-of-payments (e.g., safeguards), trade restrictions, customs valuation, subsidies, intellectual property rights, and investment measures
c. Institutional Topics – includes dispute settlement and ways by which to improve the conduct of the MTS, e.g., trade policy review

What are the emergency measures sanctioned by the WTO?

a. Trade Remedy Measures: Anti-Dumping; Countervailing; Safeguard Measures (see Part Three of this publication)
b. Balance-of-Payments Measures: The UR reaffirmed that a country can restrict imports if its balance-of-payments is threatened by increased imports. Restrictions can come in the form of price-based measures (import surcharges, import requirements) over the bound duty rates of a member under the Understanding on the Balance-of-Payments Provisions of GATT 1994. Consultations are required four (4) months from the adoption of a balance-of-payments measure.
c. Renegotiation of Tariff Concessions: The WTO allows a renegotiation of bound tariffs subject to the requirement that a return to higher tariffs be compensated for. For example, if import surges of, say, apples plague the local fruit industry, the bound tariff on apples of 45% can be renegotiated. In exchange for an increase in the bound tariff on apples, a trading partner affected by such increase could probably request that it be compensated by a reduction in the tariff on, say, paper products.

ai.title: What are the emergency measures sanctioned by the WTO?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Tatlong emergency measures ang pinapayagan ng WTO: trade remedies, balance-of-payments measures, at renegotiation ng tariff concessions.

🔍 Breakdown
• Trade remedies: anti-dumping, countervailing, safeguard
• BOP: puwedeng i-restrict ang imports kapag banta ang BOP; price-based measures (import surcharges) sa bound duty rates; consultation 4 na buwan mula adoption
• Renegotiation: puwedeng itaas ang bound tariff basta may kompensasyon

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Tatlong 'emergency exit' sa mga commitment.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung bumaha ang apples at gustong itaas ang bound tariff na 45%, puwedeng mag-renegotiate pero babayaran ng kapalit sa ibang produkto.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Alam mo kung kailan puwedeng lumabag nang legal sa taripa commitments.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Kailangan ang kompensasyon sa renegotiation

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang tatlo at ang 4 na buwang consultation sa BOP measures.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Pareho ba ang trade remedy at BOP measure?
Sagot: Hindi. Magkaiba ang batayan: unfair/injurious imports vs balance-of-payments.

🔗 Related Topics
GATT Art. XXVIII; XIX; BOP Understanding

paragraphs.text:
What laws have been issued to implement the Philippine commitments under the WTO?

Table 5.1 Laws Issued to Implement Philippine Commitments Under the WTO:
• RA 8181 – 28 March 1996 – Changed the basis of dutiable value of imported articles subject to an ad valorem rate of duty from home consumption value to transaction value
• RA 8178 – 28 March 1996 – Replaced quantitative import restrictions on agricultural products, except rice, with tariffs, and created the Agricultural Competitiveness Enhancement Fund
• EO 313 – 29 March 1996 – Set the tariff rates on agricultural products previously covered by quantitative restrictions, except rice, to complement the lifting of quantitative restrictions under RA No. 8178
• EO 465 – 13 January 1998 – Re-calibration of tariff rates for deserving industries and corrected remaining distortions in the tariff structure
• RA 8751 – 07 August 1999 – Strengthened the mechanism for the imposition of countervailing duties, amending Section 302 of the TCCP
• RA 8752 – 12 August 1999 – Provided the rules for the imposition of an anti-dumping duty, amending Section 301 of the TCCP
• RA 8800 – 19 July 2000 – Provided safeguard measures against increased imports
• RA 9135 – 27 April 2001 – Amended RA No. 8178
• EO 395 – 31 December 2004 – Modified the nomenclature and MFN duties on certain IT products under the ITA
• EO 190 – 05 November 2015 – Reduced the MFN duties on certain agricultural products to implement Philippine tariff commitments under the WTO Decision on Waiver Relating to Special Treatment for Rice
• EO 21 – 27 April 2017 – Modified the nomenclature and MFN duties on certain IT products under its ITA Expansion Schedule
• EO 23 – 27 April 2017 – Extended the effectivity of the MFN duty on certain agricultural products and implemented other Philippine commitments under the WTO decision on Waiver Relating to Special Treatment for Rice
• RA 11203 – 14 February 2019 – Lifted quantitative restrictions on rice and provided for the tariff equivalent thereof
• EO 82 – 13 June 2019 – Modified the nomenclature and rates of import duties of certain agricultural products under Section 1611 of RA No. 10863

ai.title: I. The World Trade Organization
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang WTO ay ang nag-iisang pormal na internasyonal na organisasyon na namamahala sa mga patakaran ng kalakalan sa pagitan ng mga bansa.

🔍 Breakdown
• Itinatag: 01 January 1995 matapos ang Uruguay Round
• Pinalitan ang GATT (1947)
• Pilipinas ay founding member
• Mga prinsipyo: non-discrimination (MFN at national treatment), mas bukas na kalakalan, transparency at predictability, special and differential treatment
• Estruktura: Ministerial Conference > General Council > Councils/Committees

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'referee at rulebook' ng world trade: may mga patakaran, may lugar para sa negosasyon, at may korte para sa hindi pagkakaunawaan.

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag ang isang bansa ay lumabag sa taripa nito (bound rate), puwedeng magreklamo ang ibang bansa sa Dispute Settlement Body.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Dito nakabatay ang karamihan ng trade agreements ng Pilipinas at ang mga commitments sa taripa.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Ministerial Conference: hindi bababa sa isang beses kada 2 taon
• Desisyon: consensus; kung hindi, majority vote; 1 boto kada Member
• 164 ang miyembro (ayon sa primer)

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Tandaan ang timeline: GATT 1947 > Uruguay Round 1986–1994 > WTO 1995; 8 rounds; Marrakesh 15 April 1994.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang pagkakaiba ng MFN at national treatment?
Sagot: MFN: pantay ang trato sa lahat ng trading partners. National treatment: pantay ang trato sa imported at lokal na produkto.

title: II. Tariff Bindings on Industrial Products
subject: PART FIVE – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: MULTILATERAL

sections.heading: II. Tariff Bindings on Industrial Products

paragraphs.text:
What is a tariff binding?

“Tariff binding” refers to a commitment by WTO Members not to increase a tariff rate beyond its bound rate, i.e., the tariff ceiling or maximum tariff rate. The binding of tariffs in the WTO provides a stable and predictable basis for trade. Once a rate of duty is bound, a Member may not raise it beyond the tariff ceiling, or bound rate, without compensating adversely affected Members.

What was the outcome of the tariff negotiations in the Uruguay Round?

The UR achieved an across-the-board reduction in tariffs of at least a third (33%) of the 1986 levels. Japan cut its overall tariffs by a weighted average of 61%, the European Union by 37%, and the United States of America by 34%.

For certain sectors such as construction and agricultural equipment, medical equipment, steel, beer, distilled spirits, paper, toys, pharmaceuticals and furniture, industrialized countries committed to eliminate tariffs over five (5) to ten (10) years. For semi-conductors, computer parts and chip making equipment, tariff cuts were anywhere from 50% to 100%.

Did the Philippines cut its tariffs in the Uruguay Round?

The Philippines did not reduce its applied tariffs. Instead, a commitment to bind some 2,800 industrial tariff lines at ceiling rates of ten (10) percentage points above the 1995 applied rate was undertaken. This number represents around 50% of total tariff lines. If the commitment to bind agricultural tariff lines were included, numbering some 744 lines, the scope of bindings would reach 63%.

In 2004, the tariffs on 66 tariff lines accounting for 0.01% of total tariff lines and referring to agricultural (42 lines) and textiles and clothing (24 lines) products, were reduced.

How were local industries affected by the tariff bindings committed under the UR?

Since the applied tariff rates fall way below the bound rates committed by the Philippines under the UR, there was no change in the structure of tariff protection to domestic industries.

Insofar as the tariff bindings/cuts undertaken by other WTO Members, however, especially for major trading partners of the Philippines, their lower tariff barriers mean greater commercial opportunities for Philippine businesses to diversify and grow their exports, encourage micro-, small-, and medium-scale enterprises to expand into the international market through participation in global supply networks, and ultimately, allow the Philippine economy to reap the economic benefits of innovation and efficiency from increasing foreign trade.

ai.title: II. Tariff Bindings on Industrial Products
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang tariff binding ay pangako ng WTO Member na hindi tataasan ang taripa lampas sa bound rate (tariff ceiling).

🔍 Breakdown
• Bound rate = maximum tariff
• UR: hindi bababa sa 33% na kabuuang bawas ng taripa (1986 levels)
• Pilipinas: nag-bind ng ~2,800 industrial tariff lines sa 10 percentage points sa ibabaw ng 1995 applied rate (~50% ng tariff lines)

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'kisame' sa presyo: puwede kang magtakda ng mas mababa, pero hindi ka puwedeng lumampas nang hindi nagbabayad ng kompensasyon.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang applied rate ng Pilipinas sa isang produkto ay 10%, pero ang bound rate ay 20%. Hindi puwedeng itaas ang taripa nang lampas sa 20% nang walang renegotiation.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Nagbibigay ito ng predictability sa kalakalan.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Hindi binawasan ng Pilipinas ang applied tariffs sa UR
• Hindi nagbago ang protection structure dahil mas mababa ang applied sa bound

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang kahulugan ng bound vs applied rate at ang 63% scope ng bindings kung kasama ang agri.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Nabawasan ba ang taripa ng Pilipinas dahil sa UR?
Sagot: Hindi. Nag-bind lang ito ng mga rate sa ceiling na mas mataas kaysa applied.

🔗 Related Topics
WTO Schedule LXXV-Philippines; GATT Art. II

title: III. The Agreement on Agriculture
subject: PART FIVE – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: MULTILATERAL

paragraphs.text:
What is the Agreement on Agriculture?

The WTO Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) is an agreement covering agricultural products (HS Chapters 1 to 24 excluding fish and fish products plus certain products in Chapters 29, 33, 35, 38, 41, 43, 50, 51, 52, and 53) negotiated during the UR. Parties to the Agreement, including the Philippines entered into binding commitments on market access, domestic support, export competition, and an agreement on sanitary and phytosanitary issues.

What are the objectives of the AoA?

• Establish a fair and market-oriented agricultural trading system and initiate a reform process through the negotiation of commitments on support and protection and through the establishment of strengthened and more operationally effective GATT rules and disciplines
• Provide for substantial progressive reductions in agricultural support and protection sustained over an agreed period of time, resulting in the correction and prevention of any restrictions and distortions in world agricultural markets
• Achieve specific binding commitments in the areas of market access, domestic support, export competition, and reach an agreement on sanitary and phytosanitary issues

What is the market access commitment for agricultural products under the AoA?

The current rule for market access in agricultural products is tariffs only. Before the UR, agricultural imports were restricted by import quotas, import licensing, import prohibition and other non-tariff measures. Under the AoA, all non-tariff border measures would have to be removed and converted into ordinary customs duties corresponding to their ad valorem equivalents. This is the process known as “tariffication”.

How does tariffication of agricultural products operate?

The tariffication system operates through a mechanism called “tariff quotas.”

Pre-negotiated Minimum Access Volumes (MAVs) are set for agricultural products at low tariff rates, also called “in-quota tariffs.” Volumes to be imported outside of the MAV are levied higher tariff rates, called “out-quota-tariffs,” which are set at more-or-less the equivalent level of protection afforded by the quantitative restrictions which were removed or “tariffied.”

ai.title: How does tariffication of agricultural products operate?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Tariffication ang pagpapalit ng non-tariff barriers sa agri imports ng taripa. Dito pumapasok ang tariff quotas.

🔍 Breakdown
• MAV (Minimum Access Volumes) na may mababang in-quota tariff
• Out-quota tariff para sa lampas sa MAV, katumbas ng dating proteksyon
• Lahat ng non-tariff border measures ay dapat gawing customs duties

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Bago ang UR, may quota o ban. Ngayon, taripa na lang, na may mababang rate sa unang bahagi ng volume at mataas na rate pagkatapos.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang pork na may MAV na 10,000 metric tons ay mababa ang rate; ang lampas ay mataas.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Ito ang sanhi kung bakit may in-quota at out-quota rates sa AHTN.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Ang MAV ay itinatakda sa Schedule LXXV Section I-B

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang MAV, in-quota, out-quota at ang kahulugan ng tariffication.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang in-quota tariff?
Sagot: Mababang taripa sa loob ng MAV.

🔗 Related Topics
RA 8178; AoA; Schedule LXXV

paragraphs.text:
What was the implementation period of the tariff commitments under the AoA?

• For developing countries like the Philippines entitled to special and differential treatment – tariff concessions/commitments were implemented over a ten (10)-year period from 1995 up to 2004. This meant that out-quota tariffs, which were really tariff ceilings, were reduced by a minimum of 10% for each tariff line and by a simple average of 24% for all tariff lines within ten (10) years.
• For developed countries – tariff rates were reduced by a minimum of 15% per product and by an average cut of 36% for all products over six (6) years from 1995 to 2000.

ai.title: What was the implementation period of the tariff commitments under the AoA?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Magkaiba ang panahon ng implementasyon at bawas ng taripa para sa developing at developed countries.

🔍 Breakdown
• Developing (Pilipinas): 10 taon (1995–2004); bawas ng out-quota tariffs na hindi bababa sa 10% kada line at 24% average
• Developed: 6 na taon (1995–2000); hindi bababa sa 15% bawat produkto at 36% average

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Mas mahaba at mas magaan ang commitment ng developing countries.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang Pilipinas ay may hanggang 2004 para tapusin ang pagbabawas.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Madalas itanong ang pagkakaiba ng dalawa.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Special and differential treatment

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin: 10 yrs/10%/24% vs 6 yrs/15%/36%.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ilang taon ang implementation ng developing countries sa AoA?
Sagot: 10 taon (1995–2004).

AoA; special and differential treatment

paragraphs.text:
What laws were issued to implement Philippine tariff binding commitments under the Agreement on Agriculture?

• RA 8178 signed on 28 March 1996 - implements the tariffication of agricultural products
• EO 313 - specifies the products whose quantitative restrictions were “tariffied” and the applicable tariffs to be levied; it took effect on 03 May 1996.

Which agricultural products have MAVs?

The sensitive agricultural products on which MAVs were provided are listed in Section I-B Tariff Quotas of Schedule LXXV – Philippines. The initial and final bound rates of duty are also indicated in Schedule LXXV.

In case of commodity shortages or abnormal price increases of products with MAVs, what action can be taken?

RA 8178 provides for a mechanism called “MAV Plus” which authorizes the President to increase the MAV with the concurrence of Congress. In effect, the in-quota volumes of products which have been forecast to be in short supply, or whose domestic prices have risen abnormally during a given year, will be increased to pre-set levels based on prevailing demand and supply conditions.

Who administers the MAV?

The MAV Management Committee, composed of the Secretary of Agriculture as Chairman, and the Secretaries of Agrarian Reform, Science and Technology, Trade and Industry and the Director-General of NEDA as members, implements and administers all importations under the MAV scheme.

What out-quota tariffs apply to non-sensitive agricultural products?

Out-quota tariffs on non-sensitive products, which are bound at higher levels than those for sensitive agricultural products, are set forth in Section I-A Tariffs of Schedule LXXV – Philippines. The initial rates ranged from a minimum of 10% to a maximum of 100%, to be reduced over time to the level of the final bound rates also indicated in the schedule.

What is the tariff treatment of rice for the Philippines under the WTO?

As special and differential treatment to developing countries, the predominant staple in the traditional diet of a developing country shall be exempt from tariffication. However, a MAV has to be provided corresponding to 1% of the base period domestic consumption of the product concerned and increasing over time to up to 4% of domestic consumption in the final year of implementation.

As the basic staple grain of the Philippines, rice was not “tariffied” under the UR.

In view of the expiration of the ten-year rice quota under Annex 5 of the AoA on 30 June 2005, the Philippine Government requested the extension of the special treatment on rice until June 2012. The WTO approved the request and the quantitative restriction on rice was maintained until June 2012. In line with this, EO 627 was issued on 15 June 2007 to reduce the MFN rates on certain agriculture products (e.g., mechanically deboned meat) to compensate other WTO member countries for the requested seven (7)-year extension of the special treatment on rice until 2012.

With the expiration of the special treatment on rice in June 2012, the Philippines notified the Council on Trade in Goods of its request for the continuance of the waiver on special treatment for rice until June 2017. The WTO General Council approved the request for extension of the waiver on 24 July 2014.

In line with this, EO Nos. 190 and 191 were issued, both on 05 November 2015. EO No. 190 provides a temporary modification of MFN rates on rice and non-rice products. Adjustments on the rates of duty start on 01 January 2015 to 30 June 2017 with subsequent adjustments on 01 July 2017. Under EO No. 190, in-quota rates of rice products (HS 10.06) will decrease to 35% starting 01 January 2015 and revert back to 40% starting 01 July 2017.

Meanwhile, EO No. 191 modified the preferential tariff rates on certain agricultural products under EO No. 851 (s. 2009), in effect accelerating the tariff reductions under the AANZFTA on certain agricultural products as concession for the requested extension of the waiver.

EO No. 23 issued on 27 April 2017 extended the effectivity of the temporary modification of the MFN tariffs on rice and non-rice products. Under EO No. 23, in-quota rates of rice products will remain at 35% starting July 2017 and shall be applicable until 30 June 2020 or until such time that a law amending certain provisions relating to rice tariffication in RA No. 8178 is enacted, whichever comes first, after which the tariffs shall revert back to 40%.

On 14 February 2019, the President signed RA No. 11203, also known as “An Act liberalizing the importation, exportation and trading of rice, lifting for the purpose the quantitative import restriction on rice, and for other purposes”. Effective 05 March 2019, this new law amends RA No. 8178, otherwise known as the “Agricultural Tariffication Act.” RA No. 11203 provides for the repeal of all other laws, and provisions of law, prescribing quantitative import and export restrictions, or granting government agencies the power to impose such import restrictions on agricultural products, or hindering the liberalization of the importation, exportation and trading of rice and the tariffication of quantitative import restrictions.

What measures can be taken in case of import surges that injure Philippine farmers?

Article 5 of the AoA provides for special safeguards action in the form of an additional duty that may be imposed on a temporary basis on top of the existing tariffs in cases (i) where the actual import volume exceeds a base trigger level, or (ii) where the import price falls below a base trigger price. The level of additional duty to be levied shall not exceed 33% of the level of the ordinary customs duty applied on imports of the product in question at the time of importation. The SSG inscriptions of the Philippines cover “tariffied” agricultural products and are listed in Section I-A Tariffs of Schedule LXXV – Philippines.

ai.title: What measures can be taken in case of import surges that injure Philippine farmers?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang special safeguard (SSG) ay pansamantalang additional duty laban sa import surge sa tariffied agri products.

🔍 Breakdown
• Trigger: volume lampas sa base trigger level o presyo mas mababa sa base trigger price
• Additional duty: hindi lalampas sa 33% ng ordinary customs duty
• Saklaw: SSG inscriptions sa Schedule LXXV Section I-A

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Panangga laban sa biglang bugso ng imports o biglang bagsak ng presyo.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung bumagsak ang presyo ng imported na manok, puwedeng magpataw ng karagdagang duty.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Mahalaga sa proteksyon ng magsasaka.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Ang Pilipinas ang tanging ASEAN member na may special safeguards sa agri (ayon sa Part 10)

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin: 33%, volume o price trigger.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Kailangan bang patunayan ang injury?
Sagot: Hindi.

🔗 Related Topics
AoA Art. 5; RA 8800

ai.title: III. The Agreement on Agriculture
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) ng WTO ay naglalagay ng pangako sa market access, domestic support, export competition, at SPS para sa agricultural products.

🔍 Breakdown

• Tariff quotas: MAV (mababang in-quota) at out-quota (mataas)

Imbes na harangan ang imports, mag-uuri ang bansa: may mababang taripa sa takdang dami (MAV), at mataas kapag lampas na.

Ang pork na MAV 10,000 metric tons ay mababa ang taripa. Kapag lumampas, out-quota na ang rate.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit may in-quota at out-quota rates sa mga agri product sa AHTN.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• MAV Plus: puwedeng taasan ang MAV ng Pangulo na may concurrence ng Congress
• Special safeguard: additional duty na hindi lalampas sa 33% ng ordinary duty

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Mga numero: 10%, 24% (developing); 15%, 36% (developed); 1% hanggang 4% MAV ng rice; 33% SSG.

Tanong: Ano ang SSG?
Sagot: Special Safeguard na nakatala sa Schedule LXXV para sa tariffied agri products.

title: IV. The Information Technology Agreement
subject: PART FIVE – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: MULTILATERAL

paragraphs.text:
What is the Information Technology Agreement? ITA Expansion?

The Information Technology Agreement (ITA) is a multilateral agreement enforced by the WTO which aims to eliminate tariff and non-tariff barriers to trade on information technology (IT) products.

The product coverage of ITA has been expanded (ITA Expansion) to include new categories of IT products.

The ITA is solely a tariff-cutting mechanism. The commitments undertaken under the ITA and ITA Expansion in the WTO are on an MFN basis. While both the ITA and ITA Expansion Declarations provide for the review of non-tariff barriers, there are no binding commitments concerning these.

When was the ITA concluded? When did it enter into force?

The Ministerial Declaration on Trade in Information Technology Products, which provided for the elimination/binding of tariffs on certain IT products beginning 01 July 1997 and ending on 01 January 2000 (with extended staging of tariff reductions up to the year 2005 for developing countries), was concluded at the Singapore Ministerial Conference on 13 December 1996.

It officially entered into force on 01 July 1997.

Who were the original signatories of the ITA? What is its present membership?

Fourteen (14) countries (counting the 5 member states of the European Union as one) signed the ITA Declaration, namely: Australia, Canada, Chinese Taipei, European Communities, Hong Kong, Iceland, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Norway, Singapore, Switzerland, Turkey, and United States of America.

The ITA membership has grown to 82 as of September 2017.

When was the ITA Expansion concluded? When did it enter into force?

The Ministerial Declaration on the Expansion of Trade in Information Technology Products, providing for the elimination/binding of tariffs on IT products beginning 01 July 2016 and ending on 01 July 2019 (with flexibility for sensitive products until 01 July 2023), was concluded at the Nairobi Ministerial Conference in December 2015.

There were 53 WTO Members that participated in the negotiations for the ITA Expansion.

It officially entered into force on 01 July 2016.

What are the three (3) basic principles that an ITA and ITA Expansion participant must abide by?

• All products listed in the Declarations must be covered.
• All products listed in the Declarations must have their tariffs reduced to and bound at zero.
• All other duties and charges must be bound at zero.

ai.title: What are the three (3) basic principles that an ITA and ITA Expansion participant must abide by?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Tatlong prinsipyo ang dapat sundin ng mga kalahok sa ITA at ITA Expansion.

🔍 Breakdown
• Lahat ng produkto sa Declarations ay saklaw
• Ang taripa ng mga ito ay ibinababa at ibina-bind sa zero
• Lahat ng ibang duties at charges ay naka-bind sa zero

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Zero tariff para sa lahat ng nakalistang IT products, at walang ibang dagdag na singil.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang semiconductor na nasa listahan ay dapat zero ang taripa.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Ito ang pinakapuso ng ITA.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• May staging at puwedeng extension para sa developing countries

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Tandaan: covered, zero, at all other duties zero.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Kasama ba ang non-tariff barriers?
Sagot: Walang binding commitment sa NTBs.

🔗 Related Topics
ITA; ITA Expansion; EO 21; EO 395

paragraphs.text:
What were the timeframes for the staging of concessions in the ITA and ITA Expansion?

The Declarations provide in principle for the staging-in of concessions in equal rate reductions based on the following timeframe (Table 5.2):
• 1st stage – ITA: By 01 July 1997; ITA Expansion: By 01 July 2016
• 2nd stage – ITA: By 01 January 1998; ITA Expansion: By 01 July 2017
• 3rd stage – ITA: By 01 January 1999; ITA Expansion: By 01 July 2018
• 4th stage – ITA: Complete elimination of duties not later than 01 January 2000; ITA Expansion: Complete elimination of duties not later than 01 July 2019

Were the timeframes strictly implemented?

No. A number of developing countries requested for extensions beyond the years 2000 (for the ITA) and 2019 (for the ITA Expansion) during the negotiations. Approved by the other participants, said extensions were reflected in the concerned developing countries’ schedules of commitments. In no case, however, were the extended staging periods allowed to go beyond year 2005 for the ITA and year 2023 for the ITA Expansion.

What is the product landscape of the ITA?

• Computer hardware products
• Semiconductor and integrated circuits
• Computer software
• Telecommunication equipment
• Other IT products, e.g., semiconductor manufacturing equipment

What is the product landscape of the ITA Expansion?

• New generation multi-component integrated circuits (MCOs)
• Touch screens
• Global Positioning Systems (GPS) navigation equipment
• Medical equipment, such as magnetic resonance imaging products and ultrasonic scanning apparatus
• Portable interactive electronic education devices
• Video game consoles
• Other IT products, e.g., semiconductor manufacturing equipment and parts

What are the benefits from membership in the ITA and ITA Expansion?

• Easier access to the latest technology in computer hardware and software products as well as certain telecommunications equipment
• Heightened speed and accuracy of information exchange; increased network utilization
• Accelerated development of the information technology highway
• Improved productivity
• Lower cost of IT products covered by the ITA and ITA Expansion

Who oversees the implementation of the ITA and ITA Expansion?

Established in March 1997, the Committee of Participants on the Expansion of Trade in Information Technology Products (ITA Committee) oversees the implementation of the provisions of the ITA. It serves as the forum for meetings and collective consultations among the participants concerning the following issues: (i) examination of classification divergences; (ii) consultations on non-tariff barriers; (iii) invitation of new participants; and (iv) discussions on implementation plans. All decisions of the ITA Committee are arrived at by consensus.

How are problems arising from product coverage between and among participants resolved?

Both Declarations provide that participants shall meet periodically to review the product coverage specified in the Attachments. The objective is to agree, by consensus, whether, in the light of technological developments or experience in applying the tariff concessions, or changes to the HS Nomenclature, the Attachments should be modified to incorporate additional products. Another objective of the periodic meetings is to consult on non-tariff barriers to trade in IT products.

Is the Philippines a signatory/participant to the ITA and ITA Expansion?

Yes, but the Philippines did not participate in the ITA negotiations and was not one of the original signatories. Instead, the Philippines acceded and formally signed the ITA on 01 April 1997. The Philippine Senate concurred in the ratification of the Agreement on 03 December 1998.

The Philippines participated in the ITA Expansion negotiations. Its Schedule of Concessions was approved by participants on 08 December 2015. Following the issuance of EO 21 on 27 April 2017, the Philippines notified the WTO on 19 June 2017 of the completion of its domestic procedures.

How did the Philippines implement its commitments under the ITA?

The Philippines adopted a tariff phase-out schedule, as follows:
• for products which are not locally produced, whether bound or unbound under the WTO, tariffs were eliminated in year 2000;
• for products which are locally produced and considered non-sensitive, tariff elimination/binding were undertaken earlier than 2005; and
• for products which are locally produced and considered sensitive, tariffs were eliminated beginning year 2005.

How will the Philippines implement its commitments under the ITA Expansion?

The Philippines requested to defer for one (1) year its implementation of the ITA Expansion to complete its domestic procedures. It adopted a tariff phase-out schedule for products covered by the ITA Expansion, as follows:
• for products which are non-sensitive, whether bound or unbound, tariffs were eliminated on 01 July 2017 or in year 2019;
• for products which are sensitive and bound under the WTO, tariffs were reduced starting 01 July 2017 and will be eliminated in year 2021 or 2023; and
• for products which are sensitive and unbound under the WTO, tariffs would be reduced starting 01 January 2019 or 01 January 2020 and eliminated in year 2021 or 2023.

What is the role of the Commission in Philippine participation in the ITA and ITA Expansion?

Pursuant to Sections 1608 and 1609 of the CMTA (formerly Sections 401 and 402 of the TCCP, as amended), the Commission conducts public hearings/consultations to afford interested parties the opportunity to present their views and submit position papers on the following, among others:
• products agreed to be included in the negotiations with their corresponding timeframes;
• sensitive products whose inclusion cannot be accepted;
• sensitive products which may be included but need longer timeframes to eliminate/bind their tariffs; and
• advantages and disadvantages Philippine participation.

The Commission submits its reports of findings and recommendations to NEDA, for consideration by CTRM, after which it prepares the implementing EO upon final approval by the NEDA Board.

What Executive Orders were issued granting tariff concessions under the ITA? ITA Expansion?

a. Under the ITA
• EOs 465 and 163 were issued on 13 January 1998 and 18 October 1999, respectively, to implement the Philippines’ commitment to liberalize tariffs on IT products starting 01 January 2000.
• EO 395 was issued on 31 December 2004 binding the duty at zero on the remaining tariff lines.
b. Under the ITA Expansion
• EO 21 was issued on 27 April 2017 to implement the Philippines’ commitment to liberalize tariffs covered by the ITA Expansion starting 01 July 2017.

What is the progress of the work on non-tariff barriers?

The ITA Committee approved on 13 November 2000 a one-year work program on non-tariff measures on ITA products consisting of three (3) phases:
a. Phase I - the Committee compiled in March 2001 an inventory of non-tariff barriers which had been identified by participants as impediments to trade in IT products
b. Phase II - participants examined the economic and developmental impact of the aforementioned non-tariff barriers and the benefits which would accrue to said participants from addressing the trade-distorting effects of these non-tariff barriers
c. In November 2001, the Committee met to consider the outcomes of Phases I and II.

Based on a proposal from Australia, the work program was adopted after intensive consultations conducted by the ITA Committee. Among the non-tariff barriers cited by the IT industry which adversely affect the expansion of trade in IT products are redundant testing and certification requirements by various countries and problems with import licenses.

Participants to the ITA Expansion agreed to intensify consultations concerning non-tariff barriers in the IT sector by supporting the development of an upgraded work program on non-tariff barriers.

ai.title: IV. The Information Technology Agreement
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang ITA ay multilateral agreement ng WTO para alisin ang taripa at non-tariff barriers sa IT products. Ang ITA Expansion ay nagdagdag ng bagong kategorya ng produkto.

🔍 Breakdown
• ITA: concluded Dec 1996 (Singapore); in force 01 July 1997
• ITA Expansion: concluded Dec 2015 (Nairobi); in force 01 July 2016
• 3 principles: lahat ng products covered, taripa ay zero, at lahat ng ibang duties ay zero
• Pilipinas: nag-accede sa ITA 01 April 1997; EO 21 (27 April 2017) para sa Expansion

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'zero tariff club' para sa computers, chips, telecom equipment, at iba pa.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang importer ng semiconductor ay hindi na magbabayad ng taripa dahil sa ITA commitments.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Mas mura at mas mabilis ang access ng bansa sa teknolohiya.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• MFN basis ang commitments
• Solely tariff-cutting; walang binding commitment sa non-tariff barriers
• Decisions ng ITA Committee: consensus

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Mga petsa at bilang: 14 original signatories; 82 members (Sept 2017); 53 sa Expansion; staging 1997–2000 at 2016–2019.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Kasali ba ang Pilipinas sa original signatories?
Sagot: Hindi. Nag-accede ito noong 01 April 1997.

🔗 Related Topics
EO 465, 163, 395, 21; WTO; AHTN

title: V. The Doha Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations
subject: PART FIVE – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: MULTILATERAL

sections.heading: V. The Doha Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations

paragraphs.text:
What is the Doha Round?

The Doha Round, semi-officially known as the Doha Development Agenda (DDA), is the latest round of multilateral trade negotiations at the WTO, launched on 9-13 November 2001 in Doha, Qatar. The Doha Round seeks to address issues of special interest to developing and least developed countries. Its aim is to achieve a major reform of the international trading system through the introduction of lower trade barriers and revised trade rules.

What are the areas of negotiation in the Doha Development Agenda?

The main areas of the DDA are: (i) Agriculture; (ii) Non-agricultural market access (NAMA); (iii) Services; (iv) Intellectual property; (v) Trade and development; (vi) Trade and environment; (vii) Trade facilitation; (viii) WTO rules; and (ix) Dispute Settlement Understanding.

What are the areas for negotiation in Agriculture?

Negotiations on agriculture began in early 2000. At the November 2001 Doha Ministerial Conference, the agriculture negotiations became part of the single undertaking, i.e., all linked negotiations were to end by 01 January 2005. Member governments committed to comprehensive negotiations on:
• Market access - substantial reductions on trade barriers
• Export subsidies - reductions with a view to phasing out; and
• Domestic support - substantial reductions for support that distort trade.

What were the Philippines’ initial positions on Agriculture?

On Market Access: Two (2)-stage tariff reduction as follows:
• Stage 1 (Harmonization): All tariff peaks harmonized at 150% for developing countries and 50% for developed countries within three (3) years
• Stage 2 (Further Reduction): Choice of Swiss or Uruguay formula over six (6) years based on final UR bound rates; further reductions for developing countries to commence only after developed countries complete a similar Stage 1 for export competition and domestic support; and retention of SSG for developing countries only including expansion of SSG access and coverage

Export Competition:
• Elimination of export subsidies over three (3) years for developed countries and six (6) years for developing countries
• No roll-over to next year of unused commitments; caps for each product category
• Compliance with reduction commitments on other export subsidies with similar trade-distorting effects; and
• Flexibility for developing countries to apply specific types of export subsidies.

On Domestic Support:
• De minimis to be retained for developing countries only
• Commitments shall be product specific

What are the areas for negotiation in Non-Agricultural Market Access?

At Doha, the Ministers agreed to initiate negotiations to further liberalize trade on non-agricultural goods. To this end, the Negotiating Group on Market Access was created at the first meeting of the Trade Negotiating Committee, in early 2002.

The NAMA negotiations aim to reduce or, as appropriate, eliminate tariffs, including the reduction or elimination of tariff peaks, high tariffs, and tariff escalation, as well as non-tariff barriers particularly on products of export interest to developing countries.

What techniques have been employed for tariff reduction purposes in the negotiations on NAMA?

The history of the GATT has seen the development of techniques in tariff negotiations. The bilateral item-by-item/country-by-country modality is the oldest, involving submission of request lists followed by offer lists. This technique was used in GATT negotiations from 1947 until the 1960-61 Dillon Round. It is still being used for bilateral negotiations and for those countries in the process of accession as new WTO Members.

Other techniques/methods are the following:
• Linear reduction - method whereby all tariffs, regardless of their levels, are reduced by an agreed percentage; was applied for industrial products in the 1960s during the Kennedy Round;
• Harmonization formula - seeks to reduce high tariffs more than lower ones; was used during the Tokyo Round in the 1970s;
• Sector formula - aims to complete the elimination (or harmonization) of tariffs in a given sector; was applied during the UR and 1997 ITA negotiations; and
• Cocktail approach - combines the above three (3) techniques to achieve more meaningful tariff reductions; this technique was used during the UR.

What is the Swiss Formula?

The Swiss Formula was proposed by Switzerland in the 1973-79 Tokyo Round negotiations as a method to achieve tariff harmonization. It uses a single mathematical formula that produces a narrow range of maximum final tariff rates from a wide set of initial tariffs, i.e., no matter how high the original tariffs are. The final tariff rates are reached through equal annual reductions.

At the 6th Ministerial Conference held in Hong Kong on 13-18 December 2005, it was agreed that a Swiss Formula be applied as follows:

t1 = (a × t0) / (a + t0)

where:
t1 = new bound rate
a = coefficient
t0 = base rate

In the agreed formula, the value of the coefficient is the unknown variable. Two (2) values for the coefficient have been proposed: (i) a lower one for developed Members which would mean higher tariff cuts for them and (ii) a higher value for developing Members which would mean lower tariff reductions.

ai.title: What is the Swiss Formula?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang Swiss Formula ay ginagamit para mag-harmonize ng taripa: t1 = (a × t0) / (a + t0).

🔍 Breakdown
• t1 = bagong bound rate
• a = coefficient
• t0 = base rate
• Mas mababang coefficient = mas malaking bawas
• Napagkasunduan sa Hong Kong Ministerial (Dec 2005) na gumamit ng dalawang halaga ng coefficient (mas mababa sa developed; mas mataas sa developing)

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Kapag mas mataas ang base rate, mas malaki ang bawas, kaya nagiging pantay ang ending rates.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung a = 8 at t0 = 120, ang t1 ay halos 7.5.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Madalas itanong ang pormula at ang epekto ng coefficient.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Ang bound rates ang base rates; para sa unbound, 2001 MFN plus mark-up

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang pormula at ang kahulugan ng bawat letra.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Alin ang mas mababang coefficient: developed o developing?
Sagot: Developed (mas malaking bawas).

🔗 Related Topics
NAMA; Doha; Tokyo Round

paragraphs.text:
What are the effects of the Swiss Formula?

The Swiss Formula would result in harmonization within schedules, but not necessarily across schedules. If a single coefficient is used for all Members, harmonization across schedules would be achieved, but this would also mean that there would be higher average cuts for schedules with higher tariff rates, i.e., countries with higher tariffs will have to undertake substantially larger tariff reductions. If different coefficients across schedules would occur to a lesser extent but there is greater flexibility in the magnitude of cuts that would be required for schedules characterized by higher tariffs.

How are bound and unbound tariff lines factored in the Swiss Formula?

Bound tariff lines:
The bound rates are used as the base rates in the Swiss Formula. Use of the Swiss Formula is intended to reduce the “binding overhang”, or the gap between the bound rate and the currently applied tariff rate of bound tariff lines. A new bound rate that is lower than the current applied rate would indicate attainment of real market access.

Unbound tariff lines:
The base rate for unbound lines would be their 2001 MFN tariffs plus a mark-up. The appropriate value of the mark-up is being negotiated. The Swiss Formula would be used to calculate the bound rates of previously unbound tariff lines. Depending on the values of the coefficient and the mark-up, the new bound rates may be lower than the currently applied tariffs thus leading to real market access.

The Philippines’ unbound tariff lines (virtually all NAMA products) account for 41% of total tariff lines based on the HS and 47% based on the AHTN.

What tariff reduction approaches have been proposed in the NAMA negotiations aside from the Swiss Formula?

The general modality that has been proposed is use of formula that is supplemented by sectoral/zero-for-zero approaches and with provision for special and differential treatment for developing and least-developed Members:

Table 5.3 Proposed Tariff Reduction Approaches in the NAMA Negotiations:
• United States – Two-step approach: 1) elimination of tariffs below 5% (nuisance tariffs); 2) use of Swiss formula using a coefficient of 8, so ending rates, even with initial average duties of 120%, will be from zero to a maximum of 7.5%. Phasing can be discussed; special and differential treatment is customized; “no less than full reciprocity” would result to a cap of 8% on tariffs; to be supplemented by sectoral / zero-for-zero approaches
• Japan and Korea – Trade-weighted average tariff reduction: 1) Japan – no parameters were submitted; 2) Korea – 40% average tariff reduction with a minimum 20% reduction per bound tariff line; after the initial cut, tariff peaks will be addressed through further line-by-line reduction of all tariff rates that are twice the national average using a formula (there will be a slightly higher rate of reduction for tariffs above 25% the national average); to be supplemented by sectoral / zero-for-zero approach
• European Union – Compression formula that will reduce high tariffs and tariff escalation; phasing can be discussed; special and differential treatment and “less than full reciprocity” are not for discussion
• China – Uniform formula but with different coefficients to address fully the needs and interests of Members, particularly the least developed ones
• India – Simple tariff cuts on bound tariffs, with the developing countries’ tariff reduction at only 2/3 the level of tariff reduction to be undertaken by developed countries, as special and differential treatment

What were the Philippines’ initial positions on NAMA?

• Keep tariff rates equal to year 2000 levels to obtain maximum flexibilities, i.e., the overall average nominal tariff in 2000 is 16% compared to only 6% in January 2003
• Support the elimination of high tariffs on agricultural and industrial exports of the Philippines
• Obtain maximum flexibilities to maintain tariffs where warranted within the context of special and differential treatment
• Oppose any move to eliminate nuisance tariffs
• Strongly espouse that in the context of developing countries with limited revenue base, tariffs serve to generate government revenues that finance developmental expenditures

What is the present status of the DDA negotiations?

Much remains to be done. Members continue to attach priority to the multilateral trading system, but their attention is also being diverted by bilateral and regional trade initiatives. There is also the perception that the WTO process is too slow, and it takes too long to realize concrete results. Members need to continue the work, however, i.e., make compromises and adjust negotiating positions to strengthen the multilateral trading system and make it more responsive and relevant to businesses globally.

What is the Philippine position on the Doha Development Agenda?

The Philippines joins the rest of the Members in pushing for the conclusion of the DDA. Despite setbacks in such areas as agriculture, industrial goods, and services, Members continue to exert great effort to bridge their differences and build on past convergences.

ai.title: V. The Doha Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang Doha Round (Doha Development Agenda o DDA) ay pinakabagong round ng WTO na inilunsad noong November 2001 sa Doha, Qatar, na nakatuon sa interes ng developing countries.

🔍 Breakdown
• 9 na lugar ng negosasyon: agriculture, NAMA, services, IP, trade and development, trade and environment, trade facilitation, WTO rules, dispute settlement
• NAMA: pagbawas ng taripa sa non-agricultural goods
• Swiss formula: t1 = (a × t0) / (a + t0)
• Mabagal ang usad; maraming nananatiling isyu

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Isang malaking negosasyon para ibaba pa ang trade barriers at ayusin ang mga patakaran, na may espesyal na konsiderasyon sa mahihirap na bansa.

📦 Halimbawa
Sa Swiss formula, kapag mas mataas ang base rate, mas malaki ang bawas. Ang resulta ay mas pantay-pantay na taripa.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Nakakaapekto ito sa kung gaano kataas ang taripa na puwedeng panatilihin ng Pilipinas.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• 41% ng tariff lines (HS) ng Pilipinas ang unbound
• 6th Ministerial (Hong Kong, 2005) ang pumili ng Swiss formula

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang mga technique (linear, harmonization, sector, cocktail), ang Swiss formula, at ang posisyon ng Pilipinas.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang 'coefficient' sa Swiss formula?
Sagot: Ito ang variable na nagtatakda ng pinakamataas na ending rate. Mas mababa ang coefficient, mas malaki ang bawas.

🔗 Related Topics
WTO DDA; NAMA; AoA; Schedule LXXV

title: VI. The Trade Facilitation Agreement
subject: PART FIVE – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: MULTILATERAL

paragraphs.text:
What is the Trade Facilitation Agreement?

The WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) is the first multilateral trade agreement to be concluded since the establishment of the WTO.

The TFA contains provisions for expediting the movement, release, and clearance of goods, including goods in transit. It also sets out measures for effective cooperation between customs and other appropriate authorities on trade facilitation and customs compliance issues. It further contains provisions for technical assistance and capacity building in this area.

When did the Trade Facilitation Agreement enter into force?

The TFA entered into force on 22 February 2017 after two-thirds of the WTO membership completed their domestic ratification processes.

What are the benefits of implementing the Trade Facilitation Agreement?

Estimates show that the full implementation of the TFA could reduce trade costs by an average of 14% and boost global trade by up to $1 trillion per year, with the biggest gains in the poorest countries. For the first time in WTO history, the requirement to implement the Agreement is directly linked to the capacity of the country to do so. A Trade Facilitation Agreement Facility (TFAF) has been created by the WTO to help ensure that developing and least-developed countries can obtain the needed assistance to reap the full benefits of the TFA.

Does the WTO provide technical assistance and capacity building on trade facilitation?

Technical assistance for trade facilitation is provided by the WTO, WTO members, and other intergovernmental organizations including the World Bank, the WCO and the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). In July 2014, the WTO announced the launch of the TFAF, which will assist developing and least-developed countries in implementing the TFA. The Facility became operational with the adoption of the Trade Facilitation Protocol on 27 November 2014.

ai.title: VI. The Trade Facilitation Agreement
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) ang unang multilateral trade agreement mula nang itatag ang WTO.

🔍 Breakdown
• In force: 22 February 2017
• Saklaw: paggalaw, release at clearance ng goods, kasama ang transit
• Pagtutulungan ng customs at iba pang awtoridad
• May TFAF para tulungan ang developing at least-developed countries

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Layunin nitong pabilisin at padaliin ang customs procedures para bumaba ang gastos sa kalakalan.

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag simple at transparent ang customs procedures, mas mabilis ang release ng kargamento.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Tinatayang puwedeng bawasan ng 14% ang trade costs at itaas ang global trade ng hanggang $1 trillion kada taon.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Unang pagkakataon na ang obligasyon ay nakadepende sa kapasidad ng bansa
• TFAF operational noong 27 November 2014

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Mga numero: 22 Feb 2017, 14%, $1 trillion, 27 Nov 2014.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Sino ang tumutulong sa technical assistance?
Sagot: WTO, WTO members, WB, WCO, UNCTAD at iba pang intergovernmental organizations.

🔗 Related Topics
WTO; Revised Kyoto Convention; CMTA
