title: I. Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation
subject: PART SIX – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: REGIONAL

paragraphs.text:
What is the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum?

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum refers to the association created in 1989 for economies that share the boundaries of the Pacific Ocean. APEC Member economies work together to reduce barriers to trade, ease the exchange of goods, services, resources, and technical know-how, and strengthen economic and technical cooperation between and among Members.

APEC as an organization envisions full trade and investment liberalization and facilitation by 2010 for industrialized economies and 2020 for developing Members. With respect to tariffs, the goal is zero tariffs in 2010 and 2020 for developed and developing countries, respectively.

APEC currently has 21 Member countries, namely: Australia; Brunei Darussalam; Canada; Chile; People’s Republic of China; Hong Kong, China; Indonesia; Japan; Republic of Korea; Malaysia; Mexico; New Zealand; Papua New Guinea; Peru; the Philippines; Russia; Singapore; Chinese Taipei; Thailand; United States of America; and Viet Nam.

What are the four (4) objectives of APEC?

• Sustain the growth and development of the region for the common good of its peoples thus contributing to the growth of the world economy
• Enhance the gains of both the regional and world economies by encouraging the flow of goods, services, capital, and technology
• Develop and strengthen the open multilateral trading system in the interest of Asia-Pacific Member economies and all other economies
• Reduce barriers in goods and services, and minimize hindrance to investment among its participants in a manner consistent with GATT/WTO principles, where applicable, and without detriment to other economies

What are the programs to achieve APEC’s objectives?

• Liberalization to dismantle those obstacles to international economic transactions which are imposed as customs barriers
• Facilitation of trade and investment to reduce needless divergences in approaches to domestic policies influencing international commerce
• Technical cooperation to share the information and expertise needed to implement proposals for facilitation and to enhance the availability and efficiency of regional infrastructure
• Economic policy coordination to reduce uncertainties that add to the costs of international economic transactions

What were the major results of the Annual APEC Economic Leaders’ Meetings?

Table 6.1 Major Results of the Annual APEC Economic Leaders’ Meetings (AELM) (condensed; full table in PDF pp. 144–148):
• 1993, Blake Island, USA – APEC’s vision of stability, security, and prosperity for the people of the Asia-Pacific was outlined.
• 1994, Bogor, Indonesia – The Bogor Declaration of Common Resolve identified the Bogor Goals of “free and open trade and investment in the Asia-Pacific by 2010 for developed economies and by 2020 for developing economies”. The Bogor Goals refer to the ambitious manifestation of APEC’s common belief that free and open trade and investment are essential to realize the growth potential of the region. The APEC Policy Support Unit was tasked to prepare short reports and a dashboard on progress; APEC member economies are requested to submit their Individual Action Plans (IAP) regularly.
• 1995, Osaka, Japan – The Osaka Action Agenda was adopted which provided a framework for meeting the Bogor Goals through trade and investment liberalization, business facilitation and sectoral activities, underpinned by policy dialogues and economic and technical cooperation.
• 1996, Manila, Philippines – The Manila Action Plan for APEC was adopted outlining the trade and investment liberalization and facilitation measures to reach the Bogor Goals; compiled the first Collective and Individual Action Plans.
• 1997, Vancouver, Canada – The Vancouver Framework endorsed the proposal for Early Voluntary Sectoral Liberalization (EVSL) in 15 sectors and decides that Individual Action Plans should be updated annually.
• 1998, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – APEC Ministers agreed on a Blueprint for Action on Electronic Commerce, including a commitment to paperless trading by 2005 in developed economies and by 2010 in developing economies.
• 1999, Auckland, New Zealand – APEC Principles to Enhance Competition and Regulatory Reform; APEC Business Travel Card scheme approved.
• 2000, Bandar Seri Begawan, Brunei Darussalam – electronic Individual Action Plan system.
• 2001, Shanghai, China – Shanghai Accord; e-APEC Strategy.
• 2002, Los Cabos, Mexico – Trade Facilitation Action Plan; Secure Trade in the APEC Region (STAR) Initiative.
• 2003, Bangkok, Thailand – agreed to re-energize the WTO-Doha Development Agenda (DDA) negotiations.
• 2004, Santiago, Chile – APEC Best Practices for RTAs and FTAs; Santiago Commitment to Fight Corruption and Ensure Transparency.
• 2005, Busan, South Korea – Mid-Term Stock-take: average tariffs in the APEC region reduced to 5.5 per cent, down from 16.9 per cent in 1989; Busan Roadmap to the Bogor Goals; APEC Privacy Framework.
• 2006, Hanoi, Viet Nam – Ha Noi Action Plan.
• 2007, Sydney, Australia – major report on closer regional economic integration; APEC Trade Facilitation Action Plan to further reduce trade transaction costs by 5% in 2010.
• 2008, Lima, Peru; 2009, Singapore – Supply-Chain Connectivity Framework and Ease of Doing Business Action Plan (25% cheaper, faster and easier by 2015); 2010, Yokohama, Japan – Yokohama Vision and assessment of progress toward the Bogor Goals.
• 2011, Honolulu, United States – Honolulu Declaration; agreed to facilitate trade in remanufactured goods.
• 2012, Vladivostok, Russia – endorsed an APEC List of 54 Environmental Goods with a commitment to reduce applied rates to 5% or less by 2015.
• 2013, Bali, Indonesia – Framework on Connectivity and Multi-Year Plan on Infrastructure Development and Investment.
• 2014, Beijing, China – Beijing Roadmap for APEC’s Contribution to the Realization of the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP).
• 2015, Manila, Philippines – Boracay Action Agenda to Globalize Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs).
• 2016, Lima, Peru – Lima Declaration (FTAAP).
• 2017, Da Nang, Viet Nam – welcomed the entry-into-force of the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement; 2018, Port Moresby, PNG – Era Kone Statement; 2019, Santiago, Chile – Leaders meeting was not convened in November 2019 due to some unforeseen circumstances; a Host Economy Leader’s Statement was released.

What were the operational targets set by the APEC leaders in Osaka to achieve the goal of free and open trade and investment in the Asia-Pacific region by 2020?

• Trade in goods: Zero tariffs for all goods and the removal of all quantitative restrictions
• Trade in services: Unlimited rights of establishment, national treatment or travel related to the provision of services for visits of up to two (2) years
• International investment: (i) National treatment of all firms and unrestricted rights of establishment in all sectors of production including national treatment of international investors in terms of fiscal policy (taxation and/or subsidies); and (ii) Accession of all APEC governments to existing international conventions for the settlement of disputes relating to international investment
• Transport: (i) Full harmonization of air traffic control procedures and safety standards; (ii) Uninhibited landing rights for carriers (“open skies”); and (iii) Accession of all APEC governments to international legal conventions for the carriage of goods by air, sea and land
• Tourism: (i) Introduction of smart card passports and electronic processing of international passengers; and (ii) Visa-free travel by residents of APEC economies within the region for visits of up to six (6) months
• Telecommunications: (i) Mutual recognition of all technical telecommunications standards; (ii) Unhampered trans-border transmissions; and (iii) National treatment for connections to local telecommunications networks
• Dispute settlement: Adoption of an APEC Code of Practice for the settlement of disputes relating to trade policy or international investments based on mediation and the reinforcement of existing multilateral mechanisms
• Competition policy: Rejection of anti-dumping measures by APEC governments against imports from any other APEC participant following the adoption of an agreed code of minimum standards for competition policy
• Administrative procedures: (i) Full compatibility and Electronic Data Interchange of customs documentation and clearance procedures; and (ii) Full documentation and on-line access to texts of all significant commercial legislations, regulations, tariffs or quantitative restrictions influencing international economic transactions of all participants, including patents, standards and testing procedures

What are the proposed Philippine Action Plans for the Trade and Investment Liberalization and Facilitation areas in the implementation of the Osaka Action Agenda?

a. On tariffs
a) Reduce tariffs progressively
• Gradual phase down/elimination of preferential tariffs under various FTAs on substantially all goods by the agreed end-dates
• Conduct of a comprehensive tariff review at least every five (5) years
• 144 tariff lines classified as sensitive agricultural products excluded from tariff reduction
ii) Ensure transparency of tariff regime: Active participation in the APEC Tariff Database to update its tariff data notifications

b. On non-tariff measures
(i) Reduce non-tariff measures progressively
• Non-tariff measures imposed for reasons of public security, health and safety, are allowed to remain from 1997-2020; and
• Periodic review of residual non-tariff measures to assess the need for continued application.
(ii) Ensure transparency of non-tariff measures: Exchange information with APEC on residual non-tariff measures

Arising from the 2011 AELM, what are the proposed definitions of remanufactured goods?

• Non-agricultural goods that are entirely or partially comprised of parts that: (i) have been obtained from the disassembly of used goods; and (ii) have been processed, cleaned, inspected, and tested to the extent necessary to ensure they have been restored to original working condition or better; and for which the remanufacturer has issued a warranty
• Product that goes through a recovery process where it is transformed through cleaning, testing, and other operations so that it meets the same specifications as a new good
• Industrial goods assembled in the territory of a Party classified under HS Chapter 84, 85, 87, or 90 or heading 94.02, except goods classified under HS heading 84.18 or 85.16, that: (i) are entirely or partially comprised of recovered goods; and (ii) have a similar life expectancy and enjoy a factory warranty similar to such new goods
• Industrial good assembled in the territory of a Party as listed in Annex 4.A, that: (i) is entirely or partially composed of recovered goods; (ii) has the same life expectancy and meets the same performance standards as a new good; and (iii) enjoys the same factory warranty as such a new good

What are the issues being discussed on remanufactured goods?

• Provision of specific Harmonized System tariff line
• Treatment of remanufactured goods as used good and waste
• Imposition of trade-restrictive non-tariff measures due to a lack of understanding or concern over public safety
• Opening up of developing markets to remanufactured goods which could lead to dumping of sub-standard goods
• Application of import prohibition against all remanufactured goods or against remanufactured goods in specific sectors
• Application of technical regulations, conformity assessment procedures, and documentation and import licensing requirements concerning new goods to remanufactured goods
• Facilitation of trade by making existing and future tariff and non-tariff measures applied to goods that are not newly-manufactured publicly available.

What is the relevant use of advance rulings to the APEC economies?

Through the use of advance rulings, APEC economies can help to address chokepoints in the supply chain by providing businesses operating in the region a more transparent and predictable environment in which to operate across borders.

What Executive Orders have been issued to implement the liberalization measures adopted by the Philippine Government under APEC?

Table 6.2 EOs Issued to Implement Liberalization Measures Adopted by the Philippines under APEC (EO No. – Philippine Commitment – Effectivity Date):
• EO 264 – Tariff reduction program on industrial products under Chapters 25 to 97 of the TCCP – 22 July 1995
• EO 288 – Tariff reduction on non-sensitive agricultural products (those not covered by quantitative restrictions) falling under Chapters 1 to 24 of the TCCP – 12 December 1995
• EO 465 – Re-calibration of tariff rates for deserving industries and corrected remaining distortions in the tariff structure – 22 January 1998
• EO 486 – Re-calibration of tariff schedules for residual items not covered under EO 465 to achieve a coordinated phased tariff reduction program – 10 July 1998
• EO 334 – Reduction of tariff levels across all sectors towards 0%-5% by 2004, excluding sensitive agricultural products – 01 January 2001
• EO 241 – Comprehensive tariff review that prescribed the 2003-2005 tariff schedules for industrial finished products – 03 November 2003
• EO 264 – Provided the tariff schedules for residual items – 30 December 2003
• EO 574 – Set the tariff structure on all products for 2006 to 2010 – 03 December 2006
• EO 678 – Reduced the rates of duty on certain imported manufacturing inputs – 31 October 2007
• EO 790 – Reduced the rates of duty to 1% on raw material inputs which are not locally available – 07 April 2009
• EO 890 – Tariff elimination on crude oil to address tariff distortion – 10 June 2010
• EO 896 – Reduced the rate of duty on raw material inputs which are not locally available – 18 June 2010
• EO 898 – Tariff elimination on hot-rolled coils and cold-rolled coils to support the construction industry – 22 June 2010
• EO 61 – Provided the tariff structure on all products for 2012 to 2015 – 15 December 2011
• EO 185 – Reduced the tariff rates of certain environmental goods to 5% – 03 July 2015
• EO 20 – Prescribed the MFN tariff schedule from July 2017 to 2020 – 17 June 2017

What are Individual Action Plans?

Individual Action Plans are annual reports that record the unilateral steps taken by Members to meet the Bogor Goals. These are prepared for each of the fifteen (15) policy action areas of the Osaka Action Agenda.

Why do Members need to submit Individual Action Plans?

• To improve the transparency of trade and investment regimes, providing valuable information to business and thereby facilitating intra-APEC trade and investment
• To encourage Members to focus on policy issues which need to be addressed to achieve the Bogor Goals through annual reporting and a peer review process
• To maintain and demonstrate the momentum of APEC trade and investment efforts, thereby encouraging liberalization in non-APEC economies through WTO processes
• To enable Members to learn from the liberalization and facilitation experiences of others

Have there been changes to the format of the Individual Action Plans?

Yes. The May 2011 Senior Officials Meeting endorsed recommendations prepared by the Committee on Trade and Investment for a more robust mechanism to track progress towards the Bogor Goals.

Economies will report on new trade and investment policies and procedures and the improvements planned for the remaining areas to fill the gap in moving closer to achieving the Bogor Goals. Electronic versions of the Individual Action Plans are posted on the APEC website (http://www.apec-iap.org/).

Is there a legal obligation to abide by tariff commitments?

There is none. APEC Members are not bound by the tariff liberalization measures they commit to undertake. Trade liberalization/facilitation measures committed under the Individual Action Plans are unilateral and voluntary and subject to best-endeavour implementation.

Are the tariff commitments under APEC over and above the concessions granted by the Philippines under the WTO and ASEAN?

No. The Philippines did not commit anything new in APEC outside of what is already being unilaterally implemented.

Does the Philippines intend to include in its revised Individual Action Plans a commitment to reduce tariff rates to zero by 2020?

At present, there is no definite commitment to reduce tariffs to zero across-the-board by 2020 although the Philippines intends to promote free and open trade through progressive reduction of tariffs in pursuit of national development goals, and will continue to maintain the transparency of its tariff regime.

What are the transparency obligations and how is the work on tariffs progressing?

A computerized tariff database called the “APEC Tariff Database” is available online and is accessible to all interested parties. Each economy is required to keep this database current by providing both regular updates of tariff information as changes occur and annual updates of trade and other agreed-upon data.

What are Environmental Goods and Services?

The term Environmental Goods and Services (EGS) refers to the industry sector devoted to solving, limiting, or preventing environmental problems. EGS companies may be involved in manufacturing and/or services related to water or air pollution, waste management, recycling, renewable energy, monitoring, and analysis and assessment.

The development of an EGS industry in transition economies is instrumental in eliminating preventable diseases, enhancing quality of life, protecting natural resources and attracting in-bound investment.

What is the tariff schedule for environmental goods?

Paragraph 31 of the Doha Development Agenda provides for the reduction, or as appropriate, elimination of tariff and non-tariff barriers on environmental goods and services.

With the endorsement of the APEC Environmental Goods List in 2012, AELM also committed to reduce applied rates to 5% or less by the end of 2015 on said goods, taking into account Members’ economic circumstances, and without prejudice to APEC economies’ positions in the WTO.

As of January 2016, APEC economies have published details on their respective implementation of said tariff commitment. This APEC initiative has lowered the cost of environmental goods such as solar panels, wind turbines and air pollution control equipment.

What is the Philippines’ Environmental Goods Schedule?

On 26 June 2015, EO 185 was issued, modifying the MFN rate of certain environmental goods, in compliance with the Philippines’ commitment. Items subjected to 5% MFN rates included condensers for steam or other vapour power units, waste incinerators, and filtering machinery and apparatus for liquids or gases.

What are the implications of the APEC Work Programme on Environmental Goods to the Philippines?

Reduction of tariffs to 5% in 2015 on the environmental goods in the APEC List will improve market access of Philippine exports to USA, Taiwan and Mexico on six (6) tariff lines.

What is the Environmental Services Action Plan?

On 01 March 2016, APEC Members launched a multi-year Environmental Services Action Plan (ESAP) to facilitate trade in environmental services by minimizing associated regulatory and trade policy barriers in APEC economies. The ESAP takes the following two-track approach:
a. First, a survey will be undertaken to provide APEC economies with necessary information to gain greater insights about efficient regulatory and trade promotion policies in environmental services.
b. Second, APEC economies will continue to consider and study broader environmental industries/businesses with a view to build and enhance a common understanding of the roles of services in these industries/businesses. This study is expected to contribute towards both the discussions on the scope of environmental services and identifying challenges relating to environmental businesses.

ai.title: I. Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang APEC ay forum ng 21 ekonomiya (itinatag 1989) para bawasan ang trade barriers at palakasin ang kooperasyong pang-ekonomiya.

🔍 Breakdown
• Layunin: free and open trade and investment sa 2010 (industrialized) at 2020 (developing)
• Bogor Goals (1994); Osaka Action Agenda (1995); Manila Action Plan (1996)
• Individual Action Plans (IAPs): boluntaryo at unilateral
• APEC List of 54 Environmental Goods (2012): rate na 5% o mas mababa pagsapit ng 2015

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'pangako ng kapitbahay': bawat ekonomiya ay may sariling plano, walang legal na pananagutan kung hindi matupad.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang EO 185 (2015) ay nagbaba ng MFN rate ng ilang environmental goods sa 5% bilang pagtupad sa APEC commitment.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Mahalaga ito para sa pag-unawa kung paano nakaaapekto ang regional commitments sa taripa.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Walang legal na obligasyon sa APEC commitments
• Walang bagong commitment ang Pilipinas sa APEC lampas sa WTO at ASEAN

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Tandaan ang Bogor Goals (2010/2020), ang Osaka Action Agenda, at ang mga EO na nag-implement (264, 288, 465, 486, 334).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Legal bang obligado ang APEC members sa tariff commitments?
Sagot: Hindi. Unilateral, voluntary, at best-endeavour.

🔗 Related Topics
WTO; ASEAN; EO 185; EO 264, 288, 465, 486, 334

title: II. Association of Southeast Asian Nations
subject: PART SIX – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: REGIONAL

paragraphs.text:
What is the Association of Southeast Asian Nations?

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) was established on 08 August 1967 through the Bangkok Declaration and is a regional organization created to promote political and economic cooperation and regional stability among the countries in the Southeast Asian region. Among the founding members of the ASEAN were Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand. Brunei Darussalam joined on 07 January 1984, Viet Nam on 28 July 1995, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic (Lao PDR) and Myanmar on 23 July 1997, and Cambodia on 30 April 1999 – thus constituting what is today the ten (10) Member States of the ASEAN.

ASEAN’s main objectives are to accelerate economic growth, enhance social progress and cultural development, and to promote regional peace and stability in the region.

What is the ASEAN Charter?

The ASEAN Charter refers to the legal document that provides the legal status and institutional framework for cooperation within the ASEAN region and towards the formation of the ASEAN Community. The Charter also codifies ASEAN norms, rules and values; sets clear targets for ASEAN; and presents accountability and compliance.

Overall, the ASEAN Charter establishes the rules-based systems and structures for the conduct of ASEAN affairs.

The ASEAN Charter was signed by the Governments of the ten (10) AMSs on 20 November 2007 and entered into force on 15 December 2008.

What are the main declarations of the ASEAN Charter?

• To maintain and enhance peace and security in the region, and to preserve Southeast Asia as a nuclear weapon-free zone
• To create a single market and production base, which is highly competitive and economically integrated with free flow of goods, services and investment, facilitated movement of labour, and freer flow of capital
• To strengthen democracy, enhance good governance and the rule of law, and to promote human rights. The ASEAN shall establish a human rights body, with terms to be decided by the foreign ministers.
• To respect the independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and national identity of all AMSs
• Renunciation of aggression and threat or use of force in any matter inconsistent with international law, and reliance on peaceful settlement of disputes
• Non-interference in the internal affairs of Member States
• To alleviate poverty and narrow the development gap within ASEAN
• To promote sustainable development to protect the environment, natural resources, and cultural heritage
• To develop human resources and well-being through co-operation on education, equitable access to development opportunities, social welfare and justice
• To promote an ASEAN identity through awareness of culture

What are the rights and obligations of AMSs under the ASEAN Charter?

• AMSs have equal rights and obligations.
• AMSs must take all necessary measures, including the enactment of appropriate domestic legislation, to effectively implement the provisions of the Charter and to comply with all obligations of Membership.
• In the case of a serious breach of the Charter or noncompliance, refer the matter for consultation under Article 20 (Consultation and Consensus) of the Charter.

What are the procedures for application and admission of new Members?

a. The procedure for application and admission to ASEAN shall be prescribed by the ASEAN Coordinating Council (ACC).
b. Admission shall be based on the following criteria: • location in the recognized geographical region of Southeast Asia; • recognition by all AMSs; • agreement to be bound and to abide by the ASEAN Charter; and • ability and willingness to carry out the obligations of Membership.
c. Admission shall be decided by consensus by the ASEAN Summit, upon the recommendation of the ACC.
d. An applicant State shall be admitted to ASEAN upon signing an Instrument of Accession to the Charter.

What are the general principles for the settlement of disputes?

• Member States shall endeavor to resolve peacefully all disputes in a timely manner through dialogue, consultation, and negotiation.
• ASEAN shall maintain and establish dispute settlement mechanisms in all fields of ASEAN cooperation.

What will happen to unresolved disputes?

When a dispute remains unresolved, after the application of the preceding provisions of this Chapter, this dispute shall be referred to the ASEAN Summit, for its decision.

What bodies comprise the ASEAN Summit?

a. ASEAN Coordinating Council – comprises the ASEAN Foreign Ministers and meets at least twice a year. Supported by the relevant senior officials, the Council shall: • prepare the meetings of the ASEAN Summit; • coordinate the implementation of agreements and decisions of the ASEAN Summit; • coordinate with the ASEAN Community Councils to enhance policy coherence, efficiency, and cooperation among them; • coordinate the reports of the ASEAN Community Councils to the ASEAN Summit; • consider the annual report of the Secretary-General on the work of ASEAN; • consider the report of the Secretary-General on the functions and operations of the ASEAN Secretariat and other relevant bodies; • approve the appointment and termination of the Deputy Secretaries-General upon the recommendation of the Secretary-General; and • undertake other tasks provided for in this Charter or such other functions as may be assigned by the ASEAN Summit.
b. ASEAN Community Councils – comprise the three (3) pillars of the ASEAN Community: (i) ASEAN Political-Security Community Council (APSCC); (ii) ASEAN Economic Community Council (AECC); and (iii) ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community Council (ASCCC). To realize the objectives of each Council, each ASEAN Community Council should: • ensure the implementation of the relevant decisions of the ASEAN Summit; • coordinate the work of the different sectors under its purview, and on issues which cut across the other Community Councils; and • submit reports and recommendations to the ASEAN Summit on matters under its purview. Each ASEAN Community Council should have under its purview the relevant ASEAN Sectoral Ministerial Bodies and meet at least twice a year to be chaired by the appropriate Minister from the Member State holding the ASEAN Chairmanship.
c. ASEAN Sectoral Ministerial Bodies - implement the agreements and decisions of the ASEAN Summit under their respective purview; strengthen cooperation in their respective fields in support of ASEAN integration and community building; and submit reports and recommendations to their respective Community Councils.

Who appoints the Secretary-General of ASEAN and what is his term of office?

• The ASEAN Summit appoints the Secretary-General of ASEAN, with the rank and status of Minister, who will serve with the confidence and at the pleasure of the ASEAN Heads of State or Government upon the recommendation of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers Meeting.
• The Secretary-General is appointed for a non-renewable term of office of five (5) years, selected from among nationals of the AMSs based on alphabetical rotation, with due consideration to integrity, capability, professional experience, and gender equality.
• The Secretary-General’s mandate is to initiate, advise, coordinate and implement ASEAN activities. He is responsible to the Heads of Government Meeting and to all Meetings of ASEAN Ministers when they are in session and to the Chairman of the ASEAN Standing Committee. He also chairs all meetings of the ASEAN Standing Committee on behalf of the ASEAN Standing Committee Chairman.

What is the ASEAN Community?

The ASEAN Community is a community of opportunities under the three community pillars of the ASEAN: (i) ASEAN Economic Community (AEC); (ii) ASEAN Political-Security Community (APSC); and (iii) ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community (ASCC).

The ASEAN Community ascertains that the goal of ASEAN’s founding fathers of improving the lives of its people is reflected in the region’s economic and cultural development, social progress, regional peace and security, collaboration, mutual assistance in training and research, improvement of living standards, promotion of Southeast Asian studies, and cooperation with regional and international organizations.

At the 9th ASEAN Summit in October 2003, ASEAN Leaders resolved that an ASEAN Community shall be established in 2020 and signed the Bali Concord II Declaration. The establishment of the ASEAN Community is the main goal of the ASEAN Vision 2020.

In January 2007 at the 12th ASEAN Summit in Cebu, the Leaders affirmed their strong commitment to accelerate the establishment of an ASEAN Community by 2015 and signed the Cebu Declaration.

What is the ASEAN Economic Community?

The ASEAN Economic Community is the end goal of economic integration as espoused in the Vision 2020, which is based on a convergence of interests of AMS to deepen and broaden economic integration through existing and new initiatives with clear timelines. The AEC remains part of the ASEAN community realization procedure comprised of three pillars that work in tandem, namely, the APSC, the AEC, and the ASCC.

At the 12th ASEAN Summit in January 2007, Leaders signed the Cebu Declaration on the Acceleration of the Establishment of an ASEAN Community by 2015. In particular, the Leaders agreed to hasten the establishment of the AEC by 2015 and to transform ASEAN into a region characterized by the free movement of goods, services, investment, skilled labour, and freer flow of capital.

What is the AEC Blueprint?

Adopted in 2007, the AEC Blueprint serves as a coherent master plan guiding the establishment of the AEC. It identifies the characteristics and elements of the AEC with clear targets and timelines for implementation of various measures as well as pre-agreed flexibilities to accommodate the interests of all AMSs.

The implementation of the first AEC Blueprint (2015-2018), adopted in 2007, has been substantially achieved in eliminating tariffs and facilitating free trade; advancing the services trade liberalization agenda; liberalizing investment; streamlining and harmonizing capital market regulatory frameworks and platforms; facilitating skilled labour mobility; promoting the development of regional frameworks in competition policy, consumer protection and intellectual property rights; promoting connectivity; narrowing the development gap; and strengthening ASEAN’s relationship with external parties.

Moreover, as the ASEAN recognizes that regional economic integration is a dynamic, on-going process as economies as well as domestic external environments are constantly evolving, it has developed the AEC Blueprint 2025. The AEC Blueprint 2025, adopted by the ASEAN Leaders at the 27th ASEAN Summit on 22 November 2015 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, is built upon the AEC Blueprint 2015 and will provide broad directions through strategic measures to guide the next phase of ASEAN economic integration from 2016 to 2025. The AEC Blueprint 2025 forms part of ASEAN 2025: Forging Ahead Together.

What are the key characteristics of AEC 2025?

• Highly Integrated and Cohesive ASEAN Economy
• A Competitive, Innovative, and Dynamic ASEAN
• Enhanced Connectivity and Sectoral Cooperation
• A Resilient, Inclusive, People-Oriented, and People-Centered ASEAN
• A Global ASEAN

What are the elements comprising a highly integrated and cohesive ASEAN economy?

• Trade in goods
• Trade in services
• Investment environment
• Financial integration, financial inclusion, and financial stability
• Facilitated movement of skilled labour and business visitors
• Enhanced participation of global value chain

What are the elements comprising an innovative and dynamic ASEAN?

• Effective competition policy
• Consumer protection
• Strengthened intellectual property rights cooperation
• Productivity-driven growth, innovation, research and development, and technology commercialization
• Taxation cooperation
• Good governance
• Effective, efficient, coherent, and responsive regulation, and good regulatory practices
• Sustainable economic development
• Global megatrends and emerging trade-related issues

What are the elements comprising enhanced connectivity and sectoral cooperation?

• Transport • Information and communication technology • E-commerce • Energy • Food agriculture and forestry • Tourism • Healthcare • Minerals • Sciences and technology

What are the elements comprising a resilient, inclusive, people-oriented, and people-centered ASEAN?

• Strengthened role of micro, small, and medium enterprises • Strengthened role of the private sector • Enhanced Public-private partnership • Narrowed development gap • Intensified contribution of stakeholders on regional integration efforts

What are the approaches for the ASEAN to be fully integrated into the global economy?

• ASEAN is continuing to make steady progress towards integrating the region into the global economy through FTAs and comprehensive economic partnership agreements (CEPs) with Hong Kong, China, Japan, Republic of Korea, India, Australia and New Zealand. Negotiations to conclude the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is also ongoing.
• Building on the gains from ASEAN’s global engagement and its economic integration initiatives, ASEAN shall work towards further integrating the AEC into the global economy.

What is the status of tariff reduction and/or elimination within ASEAN?

Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand have eliminated intra-ASEAN import duties on 99.65% of their tariff lines. Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, and Viet Nam have reduced their import duties to 0%-5% on 98.86% of their tariff lines. Today, focus is given to addressing non-tariff measures that could have non-tariff barrier effects on the region’s trade and business activities.

What is the ASEAN Political-Security Community?

The APSC, the first pillar of the ASEAN, aims to ensure that countries in the region live at peace with one another and with the world in a just, democratic and harmonious environment. The members of the Community pledge to rely exclusively on peaceful processes in the settlement of intra-regional differences and regard their security as fundamentally linked to one another and bound by geographic location, common vision and objectives.

The political and security cooperation in ASEAN is based on, among other things, the 1976 Treaty of Amity on Cooperation (TAC) in Southeast Asia, the 1995 Treaty of SEA Nuclear Weapon-Free Zone, and the ASEAN Charter which provides principles of shared commitments and collective responsibility in enhancing regional peace, security, and prosperity. Enhanced consultations seriously affecting the common interests of the AMSs, and adherence to the rule of law, good governance, the principles of democracy and constitutional government are also taking place. Details and cooperation program of the APSC can be found in the APSC Blueprint adopted in March 2009.

What are the components of the ASEAN Political-Security Community?

• Political development • Shaping and sharing of norms • Conflict prevention • Conflict resolution • Post-conflict peace building • Implementing mechanisms

What are the three (3) key characteristics of the APSC Blueprint?

At the 14th ASEAN Summit on 01 March 2009 in Cha-am/Hua Hin, Thailand, the APSC Blueprint was adopted by the ASEAN Leaders with the following characteristics:
• rules-based Community of shared values and norms;
• a cohesive, peaceful, stable, and resilient region with shared responsibility for comprehensive security; and
• a dynamic and outward-looking region in an increasingly integrated and interdependent world.

What is the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community?

The ASCC, the third pillar of the ASEAN, aims to contribute to realising an ASEAN Community that is people-oriented and socially responsible with a view to achieving enduring solidarity and unity among the peoples and Member States of ASEAN.

The ASCC seeks to forge a common identity and build a caring and sharing society which is inclusive and where the well-being, livelihood, and welfare of the ASEAN peoples are enhanced. Its main focus is on nurturing human, cultural and natural resources for sustained development in a harmonious and people-oriented ASEAN.

What is the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community Blueprint?

The ASCC Blueprint represents the human dimension of ASEAN cooperation and upholds ASEAN’s commitment to address the region’s aspiration to lift the quality of life of its peoples. The ASCC Blueprint was adopted by the ASEAN Leaders during the 14th ASEAN Summit held in Cha-am/Hua Hin, Thailand on 01 March 2009.

The goals of the ASCC are envisioned to be achieved by implementing concrete and productive actions that are people-centred and socially responsible. A set of cooperative activities has been developed based on the assumption that the three (3) pillars of the ASEAN Community are interdependent and interrelated and that linkages are imperative to ensure complementarity and unity of purpose.

What are the characteristics of the ASCC Blueprint?

• Human Development • Social Welfare and Protection • Social Justice and Rights • Environmental Sustainability • Building the ASEAN Identity • Narrowing the Development Gap

ai.title: II. Association of Southeast Asian Nations
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang ASEAN ay regional organization ng 10 bansa sa Southeast Asia na itinatag noong 08 August 1967 sa pamamagitan ng Bangkok Declaration.

🔍 Breakdown
• Founding members: Indonesia, Malaysia, Pilipinas, Singapore, Thailand
• ASEAN Charter: nilagdaan 20 Nov 2007; in force 15 Dec 2008
• 3 pillars: AEC, APSC, ASCC
• ASEAN Summit: pinakamataas na policy-making body
• AEC Blueprint 2025 ang gabay ng integrasyon 2016–2025

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'pamilya ng mga bansa' na may sariling konstitusyon (Charter) para sa kapayapaan, kaunlaran, at malayang kalakalan.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang ATIGA at AFTA ay bahagi ng AEC, kung saan inalis ang taripa sa halos lahat ng produkto sa pagitan ng mga miyembro.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Dito nanggagaling ang karamihan sa preferential tariff schemes na ginagamit ng Pilipinas.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Desisyon: consensus
• Chairmanship: umiikot taun-taon (alphabetical)
• Secretary-General: 5 taon, non-renewable

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang mga petsa ng pagsapi (Brunei 1984, Viet Nam 1995, Laos at Myanmar 1997, Cambodia 1999) at ang tatlong pillars.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ilan ang ASEAN Summit meeting kada taon?
Sagot: Dalawang beses kada taon, at puwedeng ad hoc.

ATIGA; AFTA; RCEP; ASEAN FTAs

title: III. The ASEAN Free Trade Area
subject: PART SIX – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: REGIONAL

paragraphs.text:
What is the ASEAN Free Trade Area?

The ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) is a trade bloc agreement which seeks to remove obstacles to freer trade among AMSs through the abolition of tariffs on traded goods and the scrapping of quantitative restrictions and other non-tariff barriers that limit the entry of imports. The ASEAN Heads of Government agreed the establishment of AFTA by the year 2008 at the 4th ASEAN Summit held in Singapore on 28 January 1992.

What are the primary goals of AFTA?

• To increase ASEAN’s competitive edge as a production base in the world market through the elimination, within ASEAN, of tariffs and non-tariff barriers
• To attract more foreign direct investments to ASEAN

sections.heading: B. The Common Effective Preferential Tariff Scheme

paragraphs.text:
What is the Common Effective Preferential Tariff Scheme?

The Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) Scheme is the main implementing mechanism of AFTA. This means that AMSs shall have common effective tariffs among themselves in AFTA, but the level of tariffs vis-a-vis non-ASEAN countries shall continue to be determined individually.

It is a cooperative arrangement among AMSs to reduce intra-regional tariffs and remove non-tariff barriers over a 15-year period commencing 01 January 1993.

In September 1994 at the ASEAN Economic Ministers Meeting, the target date of 2008 was accelerated to 2003. The goal of the Scheme is to reduce tariffs on all manufactured goods to 0%-5% by the year 2003.

ai.title: What is the Common Effective Preferential Tariff Scheme?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang CEPT ay ang pangunahing mekanismo ng AFTA para babaan ang intra-ASEAN tariffs.

🔍 Breakdown
• Common effective tariffs sa pagitan ng AMSs; hiwalay na tinutukoy ang taripa sa non-ASEAN
• 15-year period mula 01 January 1993
• Sa Sept 1994 AEM, in-accelerate ang target mula 2008 patungong 2003
• Layunin: 0%–5% sa lahat ng manufactured goods pagsapit ng 2003

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Magkapareho ang taripa sa loob ng ASEAN, pero magkakaiba pa rin ang sa labas.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang Pilipinas ay nagpapatupad ng CEPT rates sa produktong galing Thailand.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Pinalitan ito ng ATIGA noong 2010.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• AFTA: 28 Jan 1992 (4th ASEAN Summit, Singapore)

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin: 1993, 15 taon, 2003, 0%–5%.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Anong agreement ang pumalit sa CEPT?
Sagot: ATIGA.

🔗 Related Topics
ATIGA; TEL; IL; AISP

paragraphs.text:
What EOs have been issued to implement the Philippine CEPT Scheme?

Table 6.3 EOs Issued to Implement the Philippine CEPT Scheme (summary; full table in PDF pp. 166–168):
• EO 388 (27 December 1996) – modified the nomenclature and rates of import duty on zinc oxide, zinc peroxide and dioctylorthophthalates under the CEPT-AFTA
• EO 453 (31 October 1997) – 1997-2003 Philippine schedule of tariff reduction of products transferred from the Temporary Exclusion List (TEL) to the Inclusion List (IL) under the new timeframe of the Accelerated CEPT-AFTA
• EO 487 (11 June 1998) – 1998-2003 schedule; TEL to IL
• EO 71 (15 January 1999); EO 234 (27 April 2000); EO 254 (12 June 2000) – Bold Economic Measure Initiatives of the Accelerated CEPT-AFTA; EO 49 (03 November 2001)
• EO 163 (10 January 2003) – ICT products to implement the e-ASEAN Framework Agreement; EO 165 and EO 166 (10 January 2003) – 2002 schedule; ASEAN Integration System of Preferences (AISP) Package of the Philippines
• EO 230 (26 July 2003) and EO 484 (29 December 2005) – sugar preferential rates
• EO 263 (30 December 2003); EO 268 (09 January 2004) – reduce the tariff rates on 60% of the products in the IL to 0%; EO 316 (21 May 2004); EO 448 (22 July 2005); EO 486 (12 January 2006); EO 489 and EO 490 (12 January 2006)
• EO 617 (23 April 2007); EO 703 (22 January 2008) – 80% of the IL to 0%; EO 704; EO 768 (07 November 2008)
• EO 850 (23 December 2009) – eliminate the tariff rates on the remaining products in the IL in year 2010 under the CEPT-AFTA/ATIGA; footnote: Section 3 of EO 850, s. 2009 states that the tariff rates listed in the Annex and all relevant EOs issued in compliance with CEPT tariff reduction/elimination commitments are in accordance with the obligations under Article 19 (Reduction or Elimination of Import Duties) and 21 (Issuance of Legal Enactments) of the ATIGA
• EO 892 (17 June 2010) – sugar; EO 894 (18 June 2010) – rice, through the invocation of the Protocol to Provide Special Consideration for Rice and Sugar under the CEPT-AFTA/ATIGA

sections.heading: C. ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement

paragraphs.text:
What is the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement?

An improvement over the CEPT Scheme, the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) consolidates into one comprehensive agreement the existing initiatives, obligations, and commitments made by the AMSs with regard to both trade in goods (tariffs) and non-tariff elements (e.g., trade disciplines on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures, customs procedures, and trade facilitation). The ATIGA was signed in February 2009 and entered into force on 17 May 2010 upon the notification of the ratification of all AMSs.

With ATIGA, certain ASEAN agreements relating to trade in goods, such as the CEPT Agreement and selected Protocols, were superseded.

What is the objective of ATIGA?

ATIGA seeks to achieve free flow of goods in ASEAN, and considered as one of the principal means to establish a single market and production base for the deeper economic integration of the region towards the realization of the ASEAN Economic Community by 2015.

What are the key elements of the ATIGA?

a. The ATIGA consolidates and streamlines all the provisions in the CEPT-AFTA (CEPT, TEL, SL/HSL Protocols), and formalizes several Ministerial decisions.
b. The ATIGA Annex provides the full tariff reduction schedule of each AMS and spells out the tariff rates to be applied on each product for each year up to 2015. This makes tariff reduction schedules transparent and predictable for the business community. A single legal enactment to effectively implement the stipulated reduction schedule up to 2015 is also expected.
c. The ATIGA comprises elements to ensure the realisation of free flow of goods in ASEAN, including the following: tariff liberalisation, removal of non-tariff barriers, rules of origin, trade facilitation, customs, standards and conformance, and sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures. The ATIGA contains comprehensive coverage of commitments related to trade in goods, mechanisms for its implementation, and institutional arrangements. This would allow for synergy of actions being undertaken by the various ASEAN sectoral bodies.
d. With the objective of eliminating non-tariff barriers, the provisions on non-tariff measures in the ATIGA have been enhanced further through codification of measures, as well as establishment of a mechanism to monitor the committed elimination of non-tariff measures.
e. The ATIGA places emphasis on trade facilitation measures by including the ASEAN Framework on Trade Facilitation. Subsequently, ASEAN developed the Trade Facilitation Work Programme for the period of 2009-2015.

ai.title: What are the programs for tariff reduction or elimination of import duties?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang ATIGA ay may iskedyul ng pag-aalis ng duties ayon sa schedules A hanggang H.

🔍 Breakdown
• ASEAN-6: zero duty sa 2010; CLMV: 2015 (flexibility hanggang 2018)
• Schedule A: eliminate by 2010 (ASEAN-6)/2015 (CLMV); ilang CLMV lines hanggang 7% hanggang 2018
• Schedule B (ICT, CLMV): 2008, 2009, 2010
• Schedule C (Priority Integration Sector): 2012
• Schedule D (unprocessed agri): 0%–5% sa 2010 (ASEAN-6), 2013 (Viet Nam), 2015 (Lao PDR, Myanmar), 2017 (Cambodia)
• Schedule H: General Exceptions; walang reduction
• Reduction ay tuwing 01 January; base: CEPT rates

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang listahan ng mga produkto na bawat isa ay may sariling 'deadline' ng zero duty.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang ICT products ng Cambodia ay inalis ang duties sa tatlong tranches.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Dito malalaman kung kailan zero ang taripa ng produkto.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Hindi puwedeng itaas ang existing duty sa originating goods

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang 2010 at 2015 (2018) at ang schedules A, B, C, D, H.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Sino ang may flexibility hanggang 2018?
Sagot: CLMV.

🔗 Related Topics
ATIGA Annex 2; CEPT
ai.prompt: Explain this part of the Tariff Commission Primer ("III. The ASEAN Free Trade Area – What are the programs for tariff reduction or elimination of import duties?") in simple Taglish. Give the meaning, a breakdown, a practical customs example, why it matters, key numbers and deadlines to remember, a board-exam tip, common confusions, and related CMTA sections, CAO/CMO issuances.

paragraphs.text:
What is the status of the tariff reduction/elimination initiatives in ASEAN?

Progress in tariff elimination is demonstrated by the average ATIGA rate for all AMSs of only 0.54% in 2014, compared with the Most Favoured Nation (MFN) average of 6.90%. In the case of ASEAN-6, the average ATIGA rate is now negligible, while for CLMV, the average continues to decline until tariff elimination for several products is implemented in 2018. The share of ATIGA tariff lines with ATIGA rate of 0% is (i) 99.2% for ASEAN-6 and (ii) 72.6% and 90.8% for CLMV in 2014 and 2015, respectively.

What are the exclusions/exceptions allowed under the ATIGA?

a. General Exceptions – An AMS may exclude a product based on the following considerations: • to protect public morals; • to protect human, animal or plant life or health; • importations or exportations of gold or silver; • to secure compliance with laws or regulations which are not inconsistent with the provisions of the ATIGA including those relating to customs enforcement, the enforcement of monopolies operated under paragraph 4 of Article II and Article XVII of GATT 1994, the protection of patents, trademarks and copyrights, and the prevention of deceptive practices; • products of prison labour; • to protect national treasures of artistic, historic, or archaeological value; • to conserve exhaustible natural resources if such measures are made effective in conjunction with restrictions on domestic production or consumption; • to pursue obligations under any intergovernmental commodity agreement which conforms to criteria submitted to the WTO and not disapproved by it or which is itself so submitted and not so disapproved; • restrictions on exports of domestic materials necessary to ensure essential quantities of such materials to a domestic processing industry during periods when the domestic price of such materials is held below the world price as part of a governmental stabilization plan, provided that such restrictions shall not operate to increase the exports of or the protection afforded to such domestic industry, and shall not depart from the provisions of the ATIGA relating to non-discrimination; and • essential to the acquisition or distribution of products in general or local short supply, provided that any such measures shall be consistent with the principle that all AMSs are entitled to an equitable share of the international supply of such products, and that any such measures, which are inconsistent with the other provisions of the ATIGA shall be discontinued as soon as the conditions giving rise to them have ceased to exist.
The Philippines excludes from ATIGA all products falling under HS Chapter 93 (Arms and Ammunition; Parts and Accessories Thereof), except for goods classified under HS Heading No. 93.07 (Swords, cutlasses, bayonets, lances and similar arms and parts thereof and scabbards and sheaths therefor).
b. Security Exceptions – These refer to the following: • To require any AMS to furnish any information, the disclosure of which it considers contrary to its essential security interests; • To prevent any AMS from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests; or • To prevent any AMS from taking any action in pursuance of its obligations under the United Nations Charter for the maintenance of international peace and security.

What are the programs for elimination of tariff rate quotas and non-tariff barriers?

a. Each AMS undertakes not to introduce Tariff Rate Quotas (TRQs) on the importation of any goods originating in other AMSs or on the exportation of any goods destined for the territory of the other AMSs.
b. Viet Nam and Thailand shall eliminate their existing TRQs in three (3) tranches: • Thailand - by 01 January 2008, 2009 and 2010; and • Viet Nam - by 01 January 2013, 2014 and 2015, with flexibility up to 2018.
c. Each AMS undertakes not to adopt or maintain any prohibition or quantitative restriction on the importation of any goods of the other AMSs or on the exportation of any goods destined for the territory of the other AMSs, except in accordance with its WTO rights and obligations or other provisions in the ATIGA. To this end, Article XI of GATT 1994, shall be incorporated into and form part of the ATIGA mutatis mutandis.
d. The identified non-tariff barriers shall be eliminated in three (3) tranches as follows: • Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand - by 01 January 2008, 2009 and 2010; • the Philippines - by 01 January 2010, 2011 and 2012; and • CLMV - by 01 January 2013, 2014 and 2015, with flexibility up to 2018.

What is the ASEAN Trade Repository?

The ASEAN Trade Repository (ATR) contains trade-related information such as (i) tariff nomenclature; (ii) MFN tariffs and preferential tariffs offered under the ATIGA and other Agreements of ASEAN with its Dialogue Partners; (iii) Rules of Origin; (iv) non-tariff measures; (v) national trade and customs laws and rules; (vi) procedures and documentary requirements; (vii) administrative rulings; (viii) best practices in trade facilitation applied by each AMS; and (ix) list of authorized traders of AMSs and made accessible to the public through the internet.

The ASEAN Secretariat maintains and updates the ATR based on the notifications submitted by AMSs.

What are the Rules of Origin for the ATIGA?

Rules of Origin (ROO) are sets of criteria used to determine the origin of a good or service and the eligibility of a product to receive concessions.

The ATIGA ROO is based on the Regional Value Content (RVC) of not less than 40% (RVC 40) or if all non-originating materials used in the production of the goods have undergone a Change in Tariff Classification at four-digit level (i.e., a change in tariff heading or CTH) of the HS.

ai.title: What are the Rules of Origin for the ATIGA?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang ATIGA ROO ay nakabatay sa Regional Value Content (RVC) na hindi bababa sa 40% o sa Change in Tariff Heading (CTH).

🔍 Breakdown
• RVC 40: hindi bababa sa 40% regional value content
• CTH: ang non-originating materials ay nagbago ng 4-digit heading
• Kailangan ng CO Form D
• Produkto ay nasa Inclusion List at ≤20% ang taripa sa exporting AMS

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Para makuha ang ASEAN preferential rate, dapat 'sapat na ASEAN' ang produkto: alinman sa 40% value ng ASEAN o nagbago ang heading nito.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang biskwit na gawa sa Thailand mula sa imported na harina at ASEAN na asukal ay maaaring mag-qualify kung RVC ≥40% o nagbago ang tariff heading.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Dito nakadepende kung makukuha ang ATIGA rate sa customs.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Accumulation rule: puwedeng bilangin ang originating inputs mula sa ibang ASEAN country

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin: 40%, 4-digit CTH, Form D, ≤20%.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Sapat na ba ang Form D lang?
Sagot: Hindi. Kailangan ding pasok sa ROO at nasa Inclusion List ang produkto.

🔗 Related Topics
Rules of Origin; AHTN; Certificate of Origin; ATIGA Annex 2

Give the meaning, a breakdown, a practical customs example, why it matters, key numbers and deadlines to remember, a board-exam tip, common confusions, and related CMTA sections, CAO/CMO issuances.

paragraphs.text:
What are the criteria for a product to be eligible for concession under the ATIGA?

a. Products in the Inclusion List on which tariffs of the exporting AMS have reached or are at the rate of 20% or below;
b. If the product conforms to the origin requirements specified in the ATIGA ROO; and
c. Preferential tariff treatment shall be supported by a Certificate of Origin (CO) Form “D” issued by a government authority designated by the exporting AMS.

ai.title: What are the criteria for a product to be eligible for concession under the ATIGA?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Tatlong kondisyon para makakuha ng ATIGA concession.

🔍 Breakdown
• Produkto ay nasa Inclusion List at ang taripa ng exporting AMS ay ≤20%
• Sumusunod sa ROO ng ATIGA (RVC 40 o CTH)
• May Certificate of Origin Form D

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Kailangan ng tatlo: tamang listahan, tamang pinagmulan, at patunay.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung nasa Inclusion List ang produkto pero walang Form D, walang concession.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Madalas itanong sa classification at origin.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Ang CO ay galing sa government authority ng exporting AMS

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang 20%, RVC 40, Form D.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Kailangan ba ng Form D kahit nasa Inclusion List?
Sagot: Oo.

🔗 Related Topics
ATIGA ROO; Form D

paragraphs.text:
When and how can a Member State apply for a temporary modification or suspension of concessions?

An AMS may temporarily modify or suspend a concession when it faces unforeseen difficulties in implementing its tariff commitments. It shall notify, in writing, of such temporary modification or suspension of concessions to the AFTA Council at least 180 days prior to the date when the temporary modification or suspension of concessions is to take effect.

What are the rights and obligations of a Member State concerning trade remedy measures?

• Safeguard Measures. AMSs affirm their rights and obligations under Article XIX of GATT 1994, the Agreement on Safeguards, and Article 5 of the Agreement on Agriculture.
• Anti-Dumping Duties. AMSs affirm their rights and obligations with respect to each other under Article VI of GATT 1994.

What is the frequency distribution of Philippine ATIGA rates?

Table 6.4 Frequency Distribution of Philippine Tariffs under ATIGA: 2017-2022 (Number of AHTN 2017 tariff lines; unchanged 2017–2022): 0% – 10,931 (98.85%); 5% – 79 (0.71%); 35% – 19 (0.17%); GE (General Exclusion – excluded from any tariff concessions) – 29 (0.26%); Grand Total 11,058 (100.00%).

sections.heading: D. Protocol to Provide Special Consideration for Rice and Sugar

paragraphs.text:
What is the Protocol for Rice and Sugar and what is its objective?

The Protocol for Rice and Sugar was signed on 23 August 2007 in recognition of the political sensitivity of certain basic commodities and the domestic policy framework of individual AMSs to ensure self-sufficiency and food security.

The protocol allows AMSs, under exceptional cases, to request for waiver from the obligations imposed under the CEPT Agreement and its related Protocols, with regards to rice and sugar.

How does a Member State invoke the Protocol?

An AMS requesting for a waiver shall make a written submission to the AFTA Council at least 90 days prior to the date the waiver is to take effect.

The submission shall include the following information: (i) product or list of products with the corresponding tariff nomenclature in AHTN; (ii) justification for the request; (iii) latest available three (3) years of import statistics, by origin, of the product in question; and (iv) indicative modality for tariff reduction.

A copy of the submission shall be forwarded immediately by the ASEAN Secretariat to the Senior Economic Officials Meeting (SEOM) as well as to the Coordinating Committee on the Implementation of the ATIGA (CCA).

When and how can a request of waiver be considered?

Unless otherwise directed by the AFTA Council, the request for waiver shall be considered within the CCA. The CCA shall submit its report on the outcome of the discussions, including its recommendations, to SEOM within 30 days from the date of the receipt of the request.

The SEOM shall consider the report of the CCA and forward its own report, including its recommendations, to the AFTA Council within 30 days from the date of receipt of the report from the CCA.

The AFTA Council shall consider and decide on the request for waiver, within a time period not exceeding 30 days from the date of receipt of the report from SEOM. The decision of the AFTA Council granting the waiver shall state the exceptional circumstances justifying such decision, the terms and conditions governing the grant of the waiver, if any, and the time period within which the waiver shall prevail.

What are the rights of affected ASEAN Member States under the Protocol?

a. An AMS which has been granted a waiver pursuant to Article 3 shall provide adequate opportunity for bilateral consultations with AMSs having export interests on the product in question so that these interests are considered in the implementation of the Protocol.
b. Whilst compensatory adjustment measures are not available under the Protocol, such bilateral consultations may include, inter alia, measures aimed at providing continued market access for the product in question and joint economic cooperation activities that would facilitate the eventual restoration of the obligations under the CEPT Agreement and its related Protocols.
c. Any AMS affected by the outcomes of such bilateral consultations may request for bilateral consultations with the AMS which has been granted with waiver.

Is there a time limit to the waiver granted a Member State?

Yes. The AFTA Council shall, at its annual meeting, review the waiver to determine whether the exceptional circumstances justifying such waiver still exist and whether the terms and conditions attached to the waiver, if any, are being met. The AMS which has been granted with the waiver shall submit an annual report for review by the AFTA Council.

Based on the outcome of the annual review, the AFTA Council shall render its decision on whether to continue, modify or terminate the waiver.

In cases of disputes, is there a settlement mechanism available?

Yes. The Protocol on Enhanced Dispute Settlement Mechanism for ASEAN shall apply in relation to any dispute arising from, or any difference between AMSs, concerning the interpretation or application of the Protocol.

What Executive Orders have been issued by the Philippines to implement its tariff commitments on rice and sugar?

Table 6.5 EOs Issued to Implement the Philippines’ Commitments on Rice and Sugar:
• EO 892 – 17 June 2010 – Modified the rates of import duty on sugar products to implement the tariff reduction schedule on sugar products through the invocation of the Protocol to Provide Special Consideration for Rice and Sugar under the CEPT-AFTA/ATIGA
• EO 894 – 18 June 2010 – Modified the rates of import duty on rice products to implement the tariff reduction schedule on rice products through the invocation of the Protocol to Provide Special Consideration for Rice and Sugar under the CEPT-AFTA/ATIGA

ai.title: III. The ASEAN Free Trade Area
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang AFTA ay trade bloc agreement ng ASEAN para alisin ang taripa at non-tariff barriers sa pagitan ng mga miyembro. Ang CEPT ang pangunahing mekanismo at ang ATIGA ang pumalit sa CEPT.

🔍 Breakdown
• AFTA: 28 January 1992 (4th ASEAN Summit, Singapore)
• CEPT: 15 taon mula 01 January 1993; target ng 0%–5% sa manufactured goods pagsapit ng 2003
• ATIGA: nilagdaan Feb 2009; in force 17 May 2010
• ATIGA ROO: RVC 40 o CTH; Certificate of Origin Form D
• Protocol for Rice and Sugar (23 August 2007)

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'ASEAN-wide discount': kapag may Form D at pasok sa rules of origin, mababa o zero ang taripa sa ASEAN goods.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang importer ng produktong gawa sa Thailand na may RVC 40% at Form D ay puwedeng makakuha ng ATIGA preferential rate.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Ito ang pinakamalaking trade agreement na ginagamit sa araw-araw na customs operations sa Pilipinas.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• ASEAN-6 zero duty pagsapit ng 2010; CLMV 2015 (flexibility hanggang 2018)
• Inclusion list na ≤20% ang taripa ang puwedeng i-concession
• Pilipinas: Chapter 93 (Arms and Ammunition) excluded maliban 93.07

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Mga petsa at numero: 1992, 1993, 2003, 2010, 2015, 2018; RVC 40; Form D; 20% o mas mababa; 180 days (notice ng suspension); 90 days (waiver Rice and Sugar).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang Form D?
Sagot: Certificate of Origin para sa ATIGA preferential treatment.

🔗 Related Topics
AHTN; Rules of Origin; ACFTA, AKFTA, AIFTA, AJCEPA, AANZFTA

title: IV. ASEAN and Its Free Trade Area Partners
subject: PART SIX – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: REGIONAL

sections.heading: A. ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Area

paragraphs.text:
What is the ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Area?

The ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Area (AANZFTA) is a trade agreement among the ten (10) AMSs, Australia and New Zealand. The Agreement was signed on 27 February 2009 and entered into force on 01 January 2010.

The AANZFTA is a comprehensive single undertaking FTA covering trade in goods, trade in services, and investment. It also includes chapters on: (i) rules of origin; (ii) customs procedures; (iii) sanitary and phytosanitary measures; (iv) standards, technical regulations and conformity assessment procedures; and (v) safeguard measures.

What is the objective of the AANZFTA?

The AANZFTA seeks to establish deeper economic integration between the two regions through (i) progressive liberalization and facilitation of trade in goods, trade in services, and investments, and (ii) trade and investment facilitation and economic cooperation measures.

What is the product coverage of the Trade in Goods (TIG) Chapter of the AANZFTA?

Except for rice, sugar and selected articles of iron and steel, all products falling under HS Chapters 1 to 97 are covered in the TIG Chapter.

What are the two (2) programs of tariff reduction under the AANZFTA TIG Chapter?

a. Normal Track (NT) - products included in NT comprise 90% of total tariff lines. The tariff reduction program was set to commence on 01 January 2008 and by 2015, all products under NT are expected to be duty-free.
b. Sensitive Track (ST) - contains the remaining ten percent (10%) of total tariff lines. It is subdivided into two (2) categories: Sensitive List (SL) and Highly Sensitive List (HSL). Products falling under the SL category have end rates of 0%-5% by 2015, 2018 or 2020 while tariffs of products in the HSL shall be reduced by 20%, from their base rates, by 2020.

ai.title: What are the two (2) programs of tariff reduction under the AANZFTA TIG Chapter?
ai.content:

Dalawang programa ng tariff reduction sa AANZFTA: Normal Track at Sensitive Track.

🔍 Breakdown
• Normal Track: 90% ng tariff lines; simula 01 January 2008; duty-free sa 2015
• Sensitive Track: 10%; Sensitive List (end rates 0%–5% sa 2015, 2018 o 2020) at Highly Sensitive List (20% na bawas mula base rates sa 2020)

📦 Halimbawa

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Mahalaga para malaman ang taripa ng produkto mula Australia/NZ.

Kabisaduhin: 90%/10%, 2015, SL at HSL.

What are the Rules of Origin (ROO) under AANZFTA?

Products which are wholly produced or obtained in the exporting Party or produced in the exporting Party exclusively from originating materials from one or more of the Parties, shall be deemed originating and eligible for preferential tariff treatment.

The “General Rule” of RVC 40 or all non-originating materials used in the production of the good have undergone a change in tariff classification at the four-digit level (i.e., change in tariff heading or CTH) is applicable to all other goods except where there is a Product Specific Rule (PSR). The PSR becomes either the exclusive rule, or an alternative to, or in combination with the General Rule, depending on the provisions of Annex 2 of the Agreement.

Table 6.6: ROO Criteria – General Rule: RVC 40 or Change in Tariff Heading; Certificate of Origin (CO) Form: Form AANZ; Reciprocity Rule: None.

What are the criteria for products to be eligible for concession under AANZFTA?

• Product should be in the Inclusion List;
• Product should be wholly produced or obtained in the exporting party, or meets the RVC 40 or CTH or PSR criterion, to be deemed originating; and
• Submission of CO Form AANZ

What EOs implement the Philippines’ tariff commitments under AANZFTA?

• EO 851 issued on 23 December 2009 and which took effect on 01 January 2010.
• EO 191 issued on 05 November 2015 and which took effect on 12 November 2015

What is the frequency distribution of Philippine tariffs under the AANZFTA?

Table 6.7 (2017–2022, number of AHTN 2017 tariff lines; 2017 vs 2020–2022): 0% – 10,371 (92.37%) in 2017 and 10,542 (93.89%) in 2020–2022; U (Unbound – excluded from any tariff concessions) – 116 (1.03%); Grand Total 11,228. Rates range from 0% up to 50% (2%, 3%, 4%, 5%, 6%, 7%, 8%, 10%, 12%, 15%, 16%, 20%, 24%, 25%, 28%, 30%, 32%, 35%, 40%, 50%). [Full table: see PDF pp. 178–179]

What is the ASEAN-China Free Trade Area?

The ASEAN-China Free Trade Area (ACFTA) is a trade agreement among the ten (10) AMSs and China.

The Framework Agreement on Comprehensive Economic Cooperation between ASEAN and China covering trade in goods, trade in services, investments and other measures to develop new areas of economic cooperation was signed in Cambodia on 04 November 2002.

The Agreement on Trade in Goods (TIG) containing the Parties’ commitment to establish the ACFTA covering trade in goods by 2010 for ASEAN-6 and China and by 2015 for CLMV was signed on 29 November 2004.

What are the objectives of the ACFTA?

• To strengthen and enhance economic, trade and investment co-operation between the Parties
• To progressively liberalize and promote trade in goods and services as well as create a transparent, liberal and facilitative investment regime
• To explore new areas and develop appropriate measures for closer economic co-operation between the Parties
• To facilitate the more effective economic integration of the newer AMSs and bridge the development gap among the Parties

What is the ACFTA Early Harvest Programme and what is its product coverage?

The Early Harvest Program (EHP) aims to accelerate the implementation of Article 6 of the Framework Agreement on trade in goods.

The EHP covers all products falling under HS Chapters 1 to 8 (live animals, meat and edible meat offal, fish, dairy produce, other animal products, live trees, edible vegetables, and edible fruits and nuts). Parties were allowed to have an Exclusion List.

What is the modality for tariff reduction and elimination under the EHP?

Table 6.8 EHP Tariff Rate (%) not later than 01 January 2004 / 2005 / 2006: With applied MFN tariffs higher than 15% – 10 / 5 / 0; between 5% and 15% (inclusive) – 5 / 0 / 0; lower than 5% – 0 / 0 / 0.

Implementation began on 01 January 2004 for ASEAN, except for the Philippines and China. On 29 December 2005, the Philippines issued EO 485 to implement its EHP.

What are the timeframes for the TIG Agreement?

Implementation began on 01 July 2005 with two (2) programs of tariff reduction:
a. Normal Track (NT): Reduction to 0%
• ASEAN-6 and China: 2005 to 2010, with flexibility up to 01 January 2012. For ASEAN-6 and China, NT products were classified as belonging to either NT1 (2007 to 2010) or NT2 (tariff elimination in 2012).
Table 6.9 modality (tariff rate X: 2005 / 2007 / 2008 / 2009 / 2010): X ≥ 20% – 20 / 12 / 10 / 5 / 0; 15% ≤ X < 20% – 15 / 8 / 8 / 5 / 0; 10% ≤ X < 15% – 10 / 8 / 5 / 5 / 0; 5% < X < 10% – 5 / 5 / 3 / 0 / 0; X ≤ 5% – Standstill / 0 / 0.
Thresholds: a. 40% of NT tariff lines at 0%-5% by 01 July 2005; b. 60% at 0%-5% by 01 January 2007; c. 100% at 0% by 01 January 2010, with flexibility to eliminate tariffs on tariff lines not exceeding 150 by 01 January 2012 (except for the Philippines whose tariff lines can exceed 150 and which list shall be determined after a review in 2008).
• CLMV: 2005 to 2015, with flexibility up to 01 January 2018
b. Sensitive Track (ST)
• Sensitive List (SL): ASEAN-6 and China: 20% by 01 January 2012 to 0%-5% by 01 January 2018; CLMV: 20% by 01 January 2015 to 0%-5% by 01 January 2020
• Highly Sensitive List (HSL): For ASEAN-6 and China: 50% by 01 January 2015; For CLMV: 50% by 01 January 2018

What is the reciprocal tariff treatment under the ACFTA?

Reciprocal tariff treatment is not automatically applied. Products that have been placed in ST may be accorded reciprocal tariff treatment as governed by Paragraphs 6 of Annex 2 of the TIG, after notification has been received from the Party/ies that the rates of duty on its products in ST are at 10% and below.

How is reciprocal tariff rate treatment applied?

The following conditions must apply:
• the product to be imported is in the NT of the importing country and in the ST of the exporting FTA partner;
• the ST rate of the exporting FTA partner should be 10% and below;
• the applicable rate is whichever is higher between the exporting FTA partner’s ST rate and the importing party’s NT rate; and
• the applicable rate should not be greater than the importing party’s MFN rate.

Table 6.10 (Country A = exporting; Country B = importing): A: EHP / B: EHP, NT or ST – applicable rate is EHP rate of Country B, NT rate of Country B, or ST rate of Country B, respectively; A: NT / B: EHP, NT or ST – EHP rate, NT rate, or ST rate of Country B; A: ST ≤ 10% / B: EHP – EHP rate of Country B or ST rate of Country A, whichever is higher (provided that the rate shall not exceed the MFN rate of Country B); B: NT – NT rate of Country B or ST rate of Country A, whichever is higher (not exceeding MFN of Country B); A: ST > 10% / B: ST or EHP or NT – ST rate of Country B / MFN rate of Country B / MFN rate of Country B / ST rate of Country B (as printed; verify in PDF pp. 181–182).

Table 6.11 Sample Reciprocal Tariff Treatment (Philippines importing from China): 0409.00.00 Natural honey – China MFN 15, ACFTA 0 (NT); PH MFN 7, ACFTA 0 (NT1) – Applicable rate 0; 0705.11.00 Cabbage lettuce – China ACFTA 0 (NT); PH MFN 25, ACFTA 20 (SL) – 20; 1005.10.00 Maize seed – China MFN 20 (ST); PH MFN 1, ACFTA 0 (NT1) – 1; 3901.20.00 Polyethylene – China 6.5 (ST); PH MFN 10, ACFTA 10 (SL) – 10; 1006.20.10A Thai Hom Mali Rice, husked (brown) rice, In-Quota – China 65 (ST); PH MFN 35, ACFTA 50 (2017) (HSL) – 50; 1006.20.10B Out-Quota – PH MFN 50, ACFTA 50 (2015) (HSL) – 50.

ai.title: How is reciprocal tariff rate treatment applied?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang reciprocal tariff treatment sa ACFTA ay hindi awtomatiko at may apat na kondisyon.

🔍 Breakdown
• Nasa NT ng importing country at nasa ST ng exporting FTA partner
• ST rate ng exporter ≤10%
• Applicable rate ay alinman ang mas mataas sa pagitan ng ST rate ng exporter at NT rate ng importer
• Hindi lalampas sa MFN rate ng importing party

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Kung may 'trade-off', ang mas mataas na rate ang susundin pero hindi lalampas sa MFN.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang honey (NT sa PH, 0%) mula China ay 0%. Ang bigas ay 50% (HSL).

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Mahalaga sa pagtukoy ng tamang preferential rate.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Hindi awtomatiko; kailangan ng notification mula sa exporting party

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang apat na kondisyon, lalo na ang 10% at ang pagiging 'mas mataas' na rate na hindi lalampas sa MFN.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Awtomatiko ba ang reciprocal treatment?
Sagot: Hindi.

ACFTA; AKFTA reciprocity; PTF

What are the ROO under ACFTA?

Products which are wholly obtained or produced in the exporting Party shall be deemed originating and eligible for preferential tariff treatment.

The General Rule of RVC 40 is applicable to all other goods except where there is a Product Specific Rule (PSR). The PSR becomes either the exclusive rule or an alternative to the General Rule depending on the provisions of Annex 3 of the TIG Agreement.

Table 6.12 ROO under ACFTA: ROO Criteria – General Rule: RVC 40; Certificate of Origin (CO) Form: Form E; Reciprocity Rule – Conditions: the product to be imported is in the NT of the Philippines and in the ST of the exporting FTA partner; the ST rate of FTA partner should be 10% and below; the applicable rate is whichever is higher between the FTA partner’s ST rate and the Philippines’ NT rate; the applicable rate should not be greater than the Philippines’ MFN rate.

What are the criteria for products to be eligible for concessions under the ACFTA?

• Product should be in the NT of both the exporting and importing country, otherwise the product should comply with the criteria for reciprocal tariff treatment;
• Product should be wholly obtained or produced in the exporting party or meets the RVC 40 or PSR to be deemed originating; and
• Submission of CO Form E

What EOs have been issued to implement the Philippines’ commitments under the Agreement on Trade in Goods of the ACFTA?

Table 6.13 Executive Orders Issued to Implement Philippine Commitments under ACFTA:
• Early Harvest Program: EO 485 (29 Dec. 2005) – implements the tariff commitments to reduce tariffs to 0% for certain products under Chapters 1 to 8
• Normal Track: EO 487 (12 January 2006) – covers the 2005-2008 tariff reduction schedule; EO 613 (17 April 2007) – 2006-2008 tariff reduction schedule; EO 814 (30 June 2009) – 2009-2012 tariff reduction schedule; transfer of certain tariff lines from ST to NT for tariff elimination by 2010, with flexibility in 2012
• Sensitive Track: EO 618 (23 April 2007) – covers the commitment to grant reciprocal tariff treatment on tariff lines included in the ST; EO 71 (16 April 2012) – implements the tariff commitments on certain products included in HSL; EO 72 (16 April 2012) – implements the tariff commitments on certain products included in SL and the transfer of certain tariff lines from ST to NT

What is the frequency distribution of Philippine tariffs under the ACFTA?
