sections.heading: C. ASEAN-Hong Kong, China Free Trade Area

paragraphs.text:
What is the ASEAN-Hong Kong, China Free Trade Area?

The ASEAN – Hong Kong, China Free Trade Area (AHKFTA) is a trade agreement among the ten (10) AMSs and Hong Kong, China.

The Agreement establishing the AHKFTA was signed by the Economic Ministers of ASEAN and the Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development of Hong Kong, China on 12 November 2017 at the sidelines of the 31st ASEAN Summit in Manila, Philippines.

What is the product coverage of the Trade in Goods (TIG) Chapter of the AHKFTA?

Tariff reduction commitments under the AHKFTA cover different kinds of commodities, including jewelry, articles of apparel and clothing accessories, watches and clocks, and toys.

The tariff reduction commitments of each AMS and Hong Kong, China are set out in the Schedules of Tariff Commitments in Annex 2-1 of the Agreement.

What are the timeframes for the TIG Chapter?

Implementation began on 01 January 2019 with tariff lines subject to tariff reduction and/or elimination categorized according to the following modalities (Table 6.15):
• Normal Track 1 – End rate 0%: ASEAN-6 (Brunei/Malaysia/Philippines/Thailand) 85% – 65% within 3 years; Indonesia/Viet Nam 75% – 50% within 3 years; Cambodia/Lao PDR/Myanmar 65% – 50% within 8 years
• Normal Track 2 – End rate 0%: 20% within 10 years; 25% within 10 years; 15% within 15 years
• Sensitive Track – Sensitive List (end rate 0-5%): 10% – 5% within 12 years; 10% – 5% within 12 years; 20% – 10% within 17 years
• Highly Sensitive List (≤50%): 5 years; 14 years; 20 years (as printed; verify in PDF p. 185)
• Exclusion List – no tariff commitments: 5% (ASEAN-6), 15% (Indonesia/Viet Nam), 5% (CLM)

What are the Rules of Origin under the AHKFTA?

• Wholly obtained or produced;
• Produced exclusively from originating materials from one or more of the Parties; or
• RVC 40.

Products which are wholly obtained or produced in the exporting Party or produced exclusively from originating materials from one or more of the Parties shall be deemed originating and eligible for preferential tariff treatment. The General Rule of RVC 40 is applicable to all other goods except where there is a Product Specific Rule (PSR).

Table 6.16 ROO under AHKFTA: ROO Criteria – General Rule: RVC 40; Certificate of Origin (CO) Form: Form AHK; Reciprocity Rule: None.

What are the criteria for products to be eligible for tariff concession under the AHKFTA?

• Product should be in the Inclusion List;
• Product should be wholly produced or obtained in the exporting party, or meets the “General Rule” of RVC 40 and Change in Tariff Subheading, to be deemed originating.
• Submission of Certificate of Origin Form AHKFTA

Which Executive Order implemented Philippine tariff commitments under the AHKFTA?

EO No. 102 was issued on 10 January 2020 and took effect on 10 February 2020 following its complete publication in the Official Gazette.

What is the frequency distribution of Philippine tariffs under the AHKFTA?

Tables 6.17A and 6.17B Frequency Distribution of Philippine Tariffs Under AHKFTA: 2019–2032 (number of tariff lines and percentage shares; Grand Total 11,127 tariff lines; EL = Exclusion List). In 2019, 478 lines at 0% (4.30%) and 917 lines in the Exclusion List (8.24%); in 2021, 6,803 lines at 0% (61.14%); by 2032, 8,997 lines at 0% (80.86%), 141 lines at 1% (1.27%), 132 lines at 3%, 335 lines at 5%, 364 lines at 15%, 229 lines at 20%, and the Exclusion List remains 917 lines (8.24%). [Full tables: see PDF pp. 186–187]

What is the ASEAN-India Free Trade Area?

The ASEAN-India Free Trade Area (AIFTA) is a trade agreement among the ten (10) AMSs and India.

The Framework Agreement on Comprehensive Economic Cooperation between ASEAN and India signed on 08 October 2003, supports the establishment of an FTA by: (i) year 2013 for Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and India, and (ii) year 2018 for the Philippines, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Viet Nam, and India, with flexibility on sensitive sectors and commodities.

The Agreement on Trade in Goods (TIG) under the AIFTA entered into force on 01 January 2010, was ratified on 10 April 2010, and implemented on 17 May 2011.

Negotiations for Trade in Services and Investment are still ongoing. Future negotiations will include other areas of economic cooperation such as agriculture, mining and energy, science and technology, standards and conformity assessment, travel facilitation, non-tariff measures and customs cooperation. The Parties agreed not to pursue an Early Harvest Programme.

What is the product coverage and program of tariff reduction under the Trade in Goods Agreement of the AIFTA?

Except for about 14% of tariff lines in AHTN 2012 nomenclature, all products falling under HS Chapters 1 to 97 are covered by a program of progressive reduction/elimination of tariffs.

The applied MFN tariffs as of 01 July 2007 (base rates) are subject to reduction and/or elimination under the following categories:
a. Normal Track (NT): Applied MFN tariffs for tariff lines placed in the NT will be reduced and subsequently eliminated in accordance with the following tariff reduction and elimination schedules:
(i) NT 1: 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2013 for Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and India; 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2018 for the Philippines and India; 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2013 for India, and 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2018 for CLMV
(ii) NT 2: 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2016 for Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and India; 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2019 for the Philippines and India; 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2016 for India and 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2021 for CLMV
b. Sensitive Track: (ii) Base rates above 5% will be reduced to 5% in accordance with the following tariff reduction schedules: 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2016 for Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and India; 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2019 for the Philippines and India; 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2016 for India and 01 January 2010 to 31 December 2021 for CLMV. (iii) Base rates of 5% can be maintained for up to 50 tariff lines. For the remaining tariff lines, base rates are reduced to 4.5% upon entry into force of the Agreement for ASEAN-6 and five (5) years from entry into force of the Agreement for CLMV. The AIFTA preferential tariffs for these tariff lines are further reduced to 4% in accordance with the end-date set in subparagraph (i). (iv) Base rates on 4% of the tariff lines placed in the ST, will be identified by each Party on its own accord and exchanged with other Parties, will be eliminated by: 31 December 2019 for or Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and India.

[Paragraphs 30–33 (rules of origin, eligibility criteria and Executive Orders under AIFTA; Table 6.18) and Table 6.19 Frequency Distribution of Philippine Tariffs under AIFTA 2017–2022 are not covered by the screenshots provided. AIFTA ROO per Table 6.31 of the ASEAN Plus FTAs: Form AI.]

sections.heading: E. ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement

paragraphs.text:
What is the ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement?

The ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (AJCEPA) between the ten (10) AMSs and Japan covers chapters on (i) Trade in Goods (TIG), (ii) Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures, (iii) Technical Barriers to Trade, (iv) Trade in Services, (v) Trade in Investment, and (vi) Economic Cooperation and Trade Facilitation.

The Agreement provides for the establishment of an FTA between ASEAN and Japan over a period of ten (10) years taking into account the outcomes of bilateral negotiations between each AMS and Japan and the further progress of the ASEAN integration process.

The Philippines signed and ratified the Agreement on 02 April 2008 and 24 December 2008, respectively.

What are the basic principles underlying AJCEPA?

• The AJCEPA should involve all AMSs and Japan and include a broad range of sectors focusing on liberalization, facilitation and co-operation activities, noting the principle of reciprocity, transparency and mutual benefits to both ASEAN and Japan.
• The integrity, solidarity and integration of ASEAN shall be maintained in the realization of the AJCEPA.
• The AJCEPA should be consistent with the rules and disciplines of the WTO Agreements.
• Special and differential treatment should be provided to AMSs in recognition of their different levels of economic development. Additional flexibility should be accorded to the newer AMSs.
• Flexibility should be given to address the sensitive sectors in each AMS and Japan.
• Technical co-operation and capacity building programs should also be considered.

What are the objectives of the AJCEPA?

• Strengthen economic integration between ASEAN and Japan through the creation of a CEP
• Enhance the competitiveness of ASEAN and Japan in the world market through strengthened partnership and linkages
• Progressively liberalize and facilitate trade in goods and services as well as create a transparent and liberal investment regime
• Explore new areas and develop appropriate measures for further co-operation and economic integration
• Facilitate the more effective economic integration of the newer AMSs and bridge the development gap among AMSs.

What other areas of trade facilitation and cooperation initiatives are included in the AJCEPA?

Trade-Related Procedures; Business Environment; Intellectual Property Rights; Energy; Information and Communications Technology (ICT); Human Resource Development; Small and Medium Enterprises; Tourism and hospitality; Transportation and logistics; Standards and conformance and mutual recognition arrangement; and other possible technical cooperation projects including environment, automobile, bio-technology, science and technology, sustainable forest management, competition policy, food security, and financial services cooperation.

What is the product coverage under the Trade in Goods Chapter of the AJCEPA?

All products falling under HS Chapters 1 to 97, under the following categories and schedule of tariff reduction (Table 6.20): A – Immediate tariff elimination; B4* – 4 years grace period, zero in fifth year; B5 – 5 years = 6 equal annual installments; B5* – 5 years; 1 year grace period; 5 equal annual installments; B5** – 5 years grace period; zero on the sixth year; B7 – 7 years = 8 equal annual installments; B10 – 10 years = 11 equal annual installments; B10* – 10 years; 1 year grace period; 10 equal annual installments; B10** – 10 years; 5 years grace period; 6 equal annual installments; R(a) – 11 equal annual installments, 5% end rate; R(b) – 1 year grace period; reduced to 20% in the second year; R(c) – 8 years grace period; 5% on the ninth year; X – Excluded from any tariff commitments.

The Philippines excluded rice, salt, certain chemical products, articles of iron and steel, and motor vehicles of Heading 87.03.

What are the ROO in the AJCEPA?

Products which are wholly obtained or produced in the exporting party shall be deemed originating and eligible for preferential tariff treatment. The “General Rule” of RVC 40 is applicable to all other goods except where there is a product specific rule (PSR). The PSR becomes either the exclusive rule or an alternative to the “General Rule” depending on the provisions of the FTA.

Table 6.21 ROO under AJCEPA: ROO Criteria–General Rule: RVC 40 or Change in Tariff Heading; Certificate of Origin (CO) Form: Form AJ; Reciprocity Rule: None.

What are the criteria for products to be eligible for concession under AJCEPA?

• Product should be in the Inclusion List;
• Product should be wholly produced or obtained in the exporting party, or satisfaction of RVC 40 or Change in Tariff Heading or Product Specific Rule (PSR), to be deemed originating; and
• Submission of Certificate of Origin Form AJ

What Executive Order implements Philippine tariff commitments under the TIG Chapter?

EO 852 issued on 23 December 2009 and which took effect on 01 July 2010

What is the frequency distribution of Philippine AJCEPA rates?

Table 6.22 Frequency Distribution of Philippine Tariffs under AJCEPA 2017-2022 (Number of AHTN 2017 tariff lines; 2017 vs 2018–2022): 0% – 7,364 (63.80%) vs 10,215 (88.50%); 1% – 2,558 vs 44; 2% – 140 vs 0; 3% – 104 vs 4; 5% – 26 vs 93; 7% – 15 vs 3; 10% – 53; 15% – 43; 20% – 345; 30% – 151; X* (Exclusion List) – 591 (5.12%); Grand Total 11,542.

What is the ASEAN-Korea Free Trade Area?

The ASEAN-Korea Free Trade Area (AKFTA) refers to the trade agreement among the ten (10) AMSs and Korea. The AKFTA was signed on 29 November 2004 in Vientiane, Lao PDR. The Agreement on Trade in Goods (TIG) reflecting the Parties’ commitment on goods was signed in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia on 24 August 2006.

The AKFTA covers economic cooperation projects on selected areas, i.e., effective trade and investment facilitation measures, and procedures and mechanisms for their effective implementation. It also provides for special and differential treatment to the newer AMSs to compensate for different levels of economic development and to enable them to fully participate in and take advantage of the benefits of an FTA with Korea.

What are the objectives of the AKFTA?

• Strengthen and enhance economic, trade and investment cooperation among the Parties
• Progressively liberalize and promote trade in goods and services as well as create a transparent, liberal and facilitative investment regime
• Explore new areas and develop appropriate measures for closer economic cooperation and integration
• Facilitate the more effective economic integration of the new AMSs and bridge the development gap among the Parties
• Establish a cooperative framework for further strengthening the economic relations among the Parties

What is the product coverage of the AKFTA?

All products, except arms and ammunitions, clinical and municipal wastes and specialized medicine for cancer, AIDS and other dreaded diseases, and 185 tariff lines in the Highly Sensitive List Group E (HSL E), are covered under the program of progressive reduction/elimination of tariffs.

What are the timelines in the Agreement on Trade in Goods?

Under the TIG Agreement, parties commit to progressively reduce/eliminate tariffs on substantially all goods by:
• 01 January 2010 (with flexibility until 2012) for Korea and ASEAN-6;
• 01 January 2016 (with flexibility until 2018) for Viet Nam; and
• 01 January 2018 (with flexibility until 01 January 2020) for Cambodia, Lao PDR and Myanmar.

What is the modality for tariff reduction under the AKFTA?

a. Normal Track (NT):
(i) For Korea and ASEAN 6: All tariff lines are to be progressively eliminated by 2010 with limited flexibilities. Table 6.23 Tariff Modality for Korea and ASEAN-6 under AKFTA (AKFTA preferential rate, not later than 01 January 2006 / 2007 / 2008 / 2009 / 2010 by applied MFN tariff rate X): X > 20% – 20 / 13 / 10 / 5 / 0; 15% < X < 20% – 15 / 10 / 8 / 5 / 0; 10% < X < 15% – 10 / 8 / 5 / 3 / 0; 5% < X < 10% – 5 / 5 / 3 / 0 / 0; X < 5% – Standstill / 0.
(ii) For Viet Nam (Table 6.24): X > 60% – 60 (2006), 50 (2007), 40 (2008), 30 (2009), 20 (2011), 15 (2013), 10 (2015), 0 (2016); 40% < X < 60% – 45/40/35/25/20/15/10/0; 35% < X < 40% – 35/30/30/20/15/10/0-5/0; 30% < X < 35% – 30/30/25/20/15/10/0-5/0; 25% < X < 30% – 25/25/20/20/10/7/0-5/0; 20% < X < 25% – 20/20/15/15/10/7/0-5/0; 15% < X < 20% – 15/15/15/10/7/5/0-5/0; 10% < X < 15% – 10/10/10/8/5/5/0-5/0; 7% < X < 10% – 7/7/7/7/5/5/0-5/0; 5% < X < 7% – 5/5/5/5/5/0-5/0/0; X < 5% – Standstill (0 in 2015–2016).
(iii) For Cambodia, Lao PDR, and Myanmar (Table 6.25): similar modality ending at 0% in 2018 (Myanmar shall be allowed to maintain AKFTA preferential tariff rates at no more than 7.5% until 2010).
b. Sensitive Track (ST): (i) About 7% of all tariff lines and 7% of total import value for 2004 are included in the SL, and some 200 tariff lines, or 3% of all tariff lines and 3% of total import value, are categorized in the HSL. (ii) Table 6.26: Sensitive List – reduction to 20% by 01 January 2012; reduction to 0%-5% by 01 January 2016. Highly Sensitive List – Group A: reduction to not more than 50% by 01 January 2016; Group B: reduction by not less than 20% by 01 January 2016; Group C: reduction to not more than 50% by 01 January 2016; Group D: tariff lines subject to tariff rate quotas from entry into force; Group E: tariff lines exempted from concessions (maximum of 40 tariff lines at HS 6-digit level).

What is reciprocal tariff treatment under the AKFTA?

Reciprocal tariff treatment means determination of the preferential rate to be applied to an article placed in the ST of an exporting party (except those excluded from the concession – Group E) for which the same article is placed by the importing party in its NT.

The following conditions shall determine the reciprocal tariff rate to be applied under the AKFTA:
a. the tariff rate for a tariff line placed by an exporting Party in the ST, excluding Group E, must be at 10% or below and the exporting Party has given notification to that effect to the other Parties in order for that exporting Party to enjoy reciprocity;
b. the reciprocal tariff rate to be applied to a tariff line placed by an exporting Party in the ST shall be either the tariff rate of that exporting Party’s tariff line, or the NT tariff rate of the same tariff line of an importing Party from whom reciprocity is sought, whichever is higher;
c. notwithstanding sub-paragraph (b), the importing party can, on its own discretion, apply its NT tariff rate even if such rate is lower than the tariff rate of the exporting party; and
d. the reciprocal tariff rate to be applied to a tariff line placed by an exporting Party in the ST shall in no case exceed the applied MFN rate of the same tariff line of an importing Party from whom reciprocity is sought.

Table 6.27 illustrations (AKFTA rate in ST of exporting party with rate ≤10% / in NT of importing party / MFN rate of importing party → applicable): (10 / 5 / 20) – either 5% (importing party’s own discretion) or 10% (higher than importing party’s NT rate but not exceeding the MFN rate of 20%)*; (7 / 15 / 20) – 15% (NT rate of importing party); (7 / 10 / 10) – 10%; (10 / 5 / 7) – either 5% or 7% (MFN rate). *The Philippines applied option b.

What are the Rules of Origin in the AKFTA?

Products which are wholly obtained or produced in the exporting Party shall be deemed originating and eligible for preferential tariff treatment. The “General Rule” of RVC 40 and Change in Tariff Heading is applicable to all other goods except where there is a Product Specific Rule (PSR). The PSR becomes either the exclusive rule, or an alternative to the “General Rule”, or a combination with the “General Rule”, depending on the provisions of the Agreement.

Table 6.28 ROO under AKFTA: ROO Criteria – General Rule: RVC 40 or Change in Tariff Heading; Certificate of Origin (CO) Form: Form AK; Reciprocity Rule – Conditions: 1. The product to be imported is in the NT of the Philippines and in the ST of the exporting Party. 2. The ST rate of the exporting Party should be 10% and below. 3. The applicable rate is whichever is higher between the exporting Party’s ST rate and the Philippines’ NT rate. 4. The applicable rate should not be greater than the Philippines’ MFN rate.

What are the criteria for products to be eligible for tariff concession under the AKFTA?

• Product should be in the NT of both the exporting and importing Party, otherwise the product should comply with the criteria for Reciprocal Tariff Treatment;
• Product should be wholly obtained or produced entirely in the exporting Party, meet the RVC 40 or Change in Tariff Heading or Product Specific Rule (PSR), to be deemed originating; and
• Submission of Certificate of Origin Form AK

What Executive Orders were issued to implement Philippine tariff commitments under the AKFTA?

Table 6.29 EOs Issued to Implement the Philippines’ Commitments under AKFTA (EO No. – Commitment – Effectivity Date): EO 638 – Reciprocal Tariff treatment – 01 November 2007; EO 639 – Tariff Reduction Schedule for NT products – 02 November 2007; EO 812 – 90% Reduction to 0% for NT with flexibility until 2012 – 07 July 2009; EO 895 – Transfer of cochin from SL to NT – 15 September 2010; EO 52 – Compensation to Korea for delayed implementation of certain tariff commitments – 12 August 2011; EO 73 – Tariff Reduction Schedule for HSL products – 26 April 2012; EO 74 – Tariff Reduction Schedule for SL products and Accelerated Reduction for products transferred from HSL or SL to NT – 26 April 2012.

What is the frequency distribution of Philippine AKFTA rates?

Table 6.30 Frequency Distribution of Philippine Tariff Rates under AKFTA: 2017-2022 (number of AHTN 2017 tariff lines; unchanged 2017–2022): 0% – 9,533 (85.09%); 1% – 21; 3% – 17; 5% – 1,230 (10.98%); 12% – 73; 15% – 17; 16% – 6; 20% – 3; 24% – 8; 28% – 7; 32% – 43; 40% – 1; GE – 45 (0.40%); HSL E – 199 (1.78%); Grand Total 11,203. (GE & HSL E – excluded from any tariff concessions)

What is the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership?

The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is a proposed free trade agreement between the ten (10) AMSs and six (6) countries – Australia, China, India, Japan, South Korea, and New Zealand – with which ASEAN has existing free trade agreements.

What are the objectives of RCEP?

• To achieve a modern, comprehensive, high-quality and mutually beneficial economic partnership agreement establishing an open trade and investment environment in the region to facilitate the expansion of regional trade and investment and contribute to global economic growth and development
• To boost economic growth and equitable economic development, advance economic cooperation, and broaden and deepen integration in the region through the RCEP, which will build upon existing economic linkages

What are the Guiding Principles and Objectives in Negotiating RCEP?

• Scope - Broader and deeper engagement with significant improvements over existing ASEAN FTAs/CEPs with Dialogue Partners
• Process - to be accomplished in a sequential manner or single undertaking or through any other agreed modality
• Open accession - to include an open accession clause to enable participation of any of the ASEAN FTA partners if they are not ready to participate at the outset as well as any other external economic partners
• Transparency - signed agreements to be made public to ensure that stakeholders understand and take advantage of economic integration and cooperation
• Economic and Technical Cooperation - economic and technical cooperation to be an integral part of the agreement to support AMSs and maximize their benefits from the implementation of the agreement
• Facilitation - to include practical measures and cooperative efforts to facilitate trade and investment, including reduction of transaction costs for businesses recognizing that regulatory and administrative requirements and processes may constitute significant barriers to trade and investment
• Economic Integration - equitable economic development and strengthening economic cooperation between AMSs as well as between ASEAN and its partners
• Special and Differential Treatment - provide for special and differential treatment to AMSs, especially CLMV
• Consistency with the WTO Agreement
• Periodic review - subject to periodic review to ensure effective and beneficial implementation

What were the major events in RCEP?

• In November 2011, the ASEAN Framework for RCEP was adopted by the ASEAN Leaders in Bali, Indonesia.
• On 20 November 2012 at the 21st ASEAN Summit, the Leaders of ASEAN and ASEAN’s FTA partners adopted the Joint Declaration on the Launch of Negotiations for the RCEP in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. Leaders committed to commence negotiations in early 2013 to conclude by the end of 2015. The Guiding Principles and Objectives In Negotiating RCEP were adopted by the Economic Ministers in Siem Reap, Cambodia on 30 August 2012.
• The 1st Round of negotiations was held on 9-13 May 2013 in Brunei Darussalam. The Trade Negotiating Committee (TNC) agreed, among others, that the Working Groups (WGs) created must finalize their respective scoping papers consistent with the Guiding Principles and Objectives in Negotiating RCEP and to draft the principles for effective conduct of meetings.
• The highlights of the next Rounds of negotiations are summarized in Table 6.31 (2nd Round – 23-27 September 2013, Brisbane, Australia; 3rd – 20-24 January 2014, Kuala Lumpur; 4th – 31 March-04 April 2014, Nanning, China; 5th – 21-27 June 2014, Singapore; 6th – 01-05 December 2014, Greater Noida, India; 7th – 09-13 February 2015, Bangkok; 8th – 05-13 June 2015, Kyoto; 9th – 03-07 August 2015, Nay Pyi Taw; 10th – 12-16 October 2015, Busan; 11th – 15-19 February 2016, Bandar Seri Begawan; 12th – 17-29 April 2016, Perth; 13th – 12-18 June 2016, Auckland; 14th – 11-19 August 2016, Ho Chi Minh; 15th – 11-21 October 2016, Tianjin (Chapter on Economic and Technical Cooperation concluded); 16th – 02-10 December 2016, Tangerang (Chapter on SMEs concluded); 17th – 21 February-03 March 2017, Kobe; 18th – 02-12 May 2017, Manila; 19th – 24-28 July 2017, Hyderabad; 20th – 17-28 October 2017, Incheon; 21st – 02-09 February 2018, Yogyakarta; 22nd – 28 April-08 May 2018, Singapore; 23rd – 17-27 July 2018, Bangkok (Chapters on Customs Procedures and Trade Facilitation (CPTF) and Government Procurement concluded; total of concluded chapters to four); 24th – 18-27 October 2018, Auckland (Chapter on Dispute Settlement; total five); 25th – 19-28 February 2019, Bali; 26th – 22 June-03 July 2019, Melbourne (Telecommunications annex; 10 of 25 chapters concluded); 27th – 22-31 July 2019, Zhengzhou (Annexes on Financial Services and Professional Services concluded); 28th – 19-27 September 2019, Danang (of the 25 chapters and annexes, 19 concluded or technically concluded).)

ai.title: IV. ASEAN and Its Free Trade Area Partners
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ito ang mga FTA ng ASEAN sa mga partner na Australia-New Zealand, China, Hong Kong, India, Japan, at Korea, at ang RCEP na nasa negosasyon.

🔍 Breakdown
• AANZFTA: signed 27 Feb 2009; in force 01 Jan 2010; Form AANZ
• ACFTA: Framework Agreement 04 Nov 2002; TIG 29 Nov 2004; Form E
• AHKFTA: signed 12 Nov 2017; EO 102 (10 Jan 2020); Form AHK
• AIFTA: TIG in force 01 Jan 2010; Form AI
• AJCEPA: Form AJ; PH signed 02 April 2008, ratified 24 Dec 2008
• AKFTA: signed 29 Nov 2004; TIG 24 Aug 2006; Form AK
• RCEP: ASEAN + 6 partner

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'menu' ng preferential tariffs: bawat FTA ay may sariling iskedyul ng taripa, rules of origin, at certificate of origin form.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang importer na gagamit ng ACFTA preference ay kailangan ng Form E at dapat pasok ang produkto sa Normal Track o sumunod sa reciprocal tariff treatment.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Dito mo malalaman kung aling taripa ang tama sa isang produkto.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Normal Track (NT) at Sensitive Track (ST) sa maraming FTA
• Reciprocal tariff treatment: hindi awtomatiko
• General rule ng ROO: karaniwang RVC 40 o CTH

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang pares ng FTA at Certificate of Origin Form nila, at ang mga petsa ng pagsisimula at EO.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang Form AI?
Sagot: Certificate of Origin para sa ASEAN-India FTA (AIFTA).

title: I. Philippines – Japan Economic Partnership Agreement
subject: PART SEVEN – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: BILATERAL

sections.heading: I. Philippines – Japan Economic Partnership Agreement

paragraphs.text:
What is the Philippines-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement?

The Philippines-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (PJEPA) is the first bilateral Free Trade Agreement entered into by the Philippines. It was signed on 09 September 2006 in Helsinki, Finland, was ratified on 08 October 2008 pursuant to Senate Resolution No. 131, and was implemented on 11 December 2008.

The PJEPA is described as a “new age FTA” as it goes beyond tariff reduction and elimination on traded goods. Other provisions include: (i) movement of natural persons and services, (ii) investments and cooperation on areas such as technology transfer, (iii) human and resource development, (iv) small and medium enterprises development, (v) environment, and (vi) competition policy.

What are the objectives of the PJEPA?

• Liberalize and facilitate trade in goods and services between the Parties
• Facilitate the mutual recognition of the results of conformity assessment procedures for products or processes
• Increase investment opportunities and strengthen protection for investments and investment activities in the Parties
• Enhance protection of intellectual property and strengthen cooperation in the field thereof to promote trade and investment between the Parties
• Promote transparency in government procurement in the Parties
• Promote competition by addressing anti-competitive activities and cooperate in the field of competition
• Establish a framework for further bilateral cooperation and improvement of business environment
• Promote transparency in the implementation of laws and regulations respecting matters covered by the Agreement
• Create effective procedures for the implementation and operation of the Agreement and for the resolution of disputes

What is the product coverage of the PJEPA and its implementation period?

Except for rice and salt, all products falling under HS Chapters 1 to 97 at the HS 2002 nomenclature are covered.

Implementation period of the tariff commitments is ten (10) years from date of entry into force of the Agreement.

Table 7.1 Philippine Offer List under PJEPA (Category – Modality – Number of HS 2002 Tariff Lines – % to total): A – Immediate tariff elimination – 3,947 – 66.14; B4 – 4-years = 5 equal annual installments – 97 – 1.63; B4** – One single installment on the fourth year upon entry into force – 2 – 0.03; B5 – 5-years = 6 equal annual installments – 230 – 3.85; B5* – 5 years, 1 year grace period, 5 equal annual installments – 220 – 3.69; B5** – One single installment at the beginning of the 6th year – 14 – 0.23; B7 – 7-years, 8 equal annual installments – 2 – 0.03; B10 – 10 year = 11 equal annual installments – 1,077 – 18.05; B10* – 10 years, 1 year grace period, 10 equal annual installments – 154 – 2.58; B10** – 10 years, 5 years grace period, 6 equal annual installments – 103 – 1.73; R – Renegotiation – 24 – 0.40; S – Special tariff treatment – 92 – 1.54; X – Excluded from any commitment of preferential treatment or renegotiation – 6 – 0.10. Total 5,975 – 100.00.

What are the Rules of Origin under the PJEPA?

a. Criteria in determining if a product is originating:
• good is wholly obtained or produced entirely in the Party;
• good is produced entirely in the Party exclusively from originating materials of the Party; or
• good satisfies the Product Specific Rules (PSRs) set out in Annex 2 of the Agreement requiring that the materials used undergo a change in tariff classification or a specific manufacturing or processing operation, and all other applicable requirements of Chapter 3, when the good is produced entirely in the Party using non-originating materials.
b. The Qualifying Value Content must not be less than the percentage specified by the PSR for the good.

Table 7.2 ROO under PJEPA: ROO Criteria – General rule: No general rule. Each product has its own PSR; Certificate of Origin (CO) Form: Form JP; Reciprocity Rule: None.

What are the criteria that must be met for products to be eligible for concession under the PJEPA?

a. Product should be in the Inclusion List;
b. Product should be wholly produced or obtained in the exporting party, or meet the PSR, to be deemed originating; and
c. Submission of CO Form JP.

What EOs implement Philippine tariff commitments under the PJEPA?

• EO 767 issued on 07 November 2011 [as printed] and which took effect on 11 December 2008
• EO 905 issued on 29 June 2010 and which took effect on 01 July 2010
• EO 157 issued on 13 February 2014 and which took effect on 20 February 2014

When is the General Review of the Agreement undertaken and how often does the review take place?

The General Review of the Agreement and its implementation and operation commenced in 2011 and will take place every five (5) years thereafter, unless otherwise agreed by both Parties.

What is the frequency distribution of Philippine tariffs under PJEPA?

Table 7.3 Frequency Distribution of Philippine Tariffs under PJEPA: 2017-2022 (number of AHTN 2017 tariff lines; 2017 vs 2018–2022): 0% – 7,989 (69.79%) vs 10,812 (94.45%); 1% – 2,501 (21.85%) vs 0; 2% – 63; 3% – 136; 4% – 107; 5% – 11; 6% – 6; /e – 83 (0.73%); R (Renegotiation) – 83 (0.73%); S (Special Treatment) – 444 (3.88%); X (Exclusion List – excluded from any tariff concessions) – 25 (0.22%); Grand Total 11,448 (2017) / 11,447 (2018–2022). /e = 7% or the MFN applied rate at the time of importation, whichever is lower.

ai.title: I. Philippines – Japan Economic Partnership Agreement
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang PJEPA ang unang bilateral FTA ng Pilipinas, kasama ang Japan. Higit ito sa pagbabawas ng taripa dahil saklaw rin ang serbisyo, pamumuhunan, at kooperasyon.

🔍 Breakdown
• Nilagdaan: 09 September 2006 (Helsinki); ratified 08 October 2008 (Senate Res. No. 131); implemented 11 December 2008
• Saklaw: lahat ng produkto sa HS Ch. 1–97 (HS 2002) maliban sa bigas at asin
• Implementation period: 10 taon
• ROO: walang general rule; bawat produkto ay may sariling PSR; Form JP
• EO 767, 905, 157

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'bilateral deal' na mas malalim kaysa regular na FTA.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang importer ng produktong Hapon ay kailangan ng Form JP at dapat pasok sa PSR ng produkto.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Mahalaga ito dahil ang PJEPA ay may sariling rules of origin at tariff schedule (hiwalay sa AJCEPA).

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Walang reciprocity rule
• Review kada 5 taon mula 2011

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang pagkakaiba ng PJEPA (bilateral, Form JP, walang general rule) at AJCEPA (ASEAN-Japan, Form AJ, RVC 40/CTH).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Pareho ba ang PJEPA at AJCEPA?
Sagot: Hindi. Magkahiwalay na agreement na may magkaibang ROO at CO form.

title: II. Philippines – European Free Trade Association Free Trade Agreement
subject: PART SEVEN – TRADING ARRANGEMENTS: BILATERAL

sections.heading: II. Philippines – European Free Trade Association Free Trade Agreement

paragraphs.text:
What is the Philippines-European Free Trade Association Free Trade Agreement?

The Philippines – European Free Trade Association Free Trade Agreement (PH-EFTA FTA) is the second bilateral agreement the Philippines has entered into (after the PJEPA). The Agreement with the EFTA States (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland) was signed in Bern, Switzerland on 28 April 2016.

As a comprehensive agreement, the PH-EFTA FTA covers trade in goods (includes separate chapters for industrial goods, agricultural goods, fish and other marine products, rules of origin, trade facilitation, Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Measures and Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT)), trade in services, investment, competition, the protection of intellectual property rights, government procurement, trade and sustainable development, institutional provisions and dispute settlement.

What are the objectives of the PH-EFTA FTA?

• Achieve the liberalization of trade in goods
• Achieve the liberalization of trade in services
• Mutually enhance investment opportunities
• Prevent, eliminate or reduce unnecessary technical barriers to trade and to further the implementation of the WTO Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures and the WTO Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade;
• Promote competition in their economies, particularly as it relates to the economic relations between the Parties
• Achieve further liberalization on a mutual basis of the government procurement markets of the Parties
• Ensure adequate and effective protection of intellectual property rights, in accordance with international standards
• Develop international trade in such a way as to contribute to the objective of sustainable development and to ensure that this objective is integrated and reflected in the Parties’ trade relations
• To contribute to the harmonious development and expansion of world trade.

What were the milestones in the PH-EFTA FTA negotiations?

• In November 2013, the Philippines formally sat down with the EFTA States and announced its interest to undertake negotiations for an FTA.
• In 23 June 2014, in the Westman Islands, Iceland, the Philippines and the EFTA States signed a Joint Declaration on Cooperation (JDC) and established a Joint EFTA-Philippines Committee.
• A scoping paper was signed by the Parties prior to a negotiation round in Geneva, Switzerland on 24 November 2014.
• Five rounds of negotiations were conducted from March 2015 to February 2016.
• On 28 April 2016 in Bern, Switzerland, the Philippines signed a Free Trade Agreement with the EFTA States.

When is the entry into force of the Agreement?

The instrument of ratification for the PH-EFTA FTA was signed by President Rodrigo Duterte on 8 December 2017 and submitted to the Senate for its concurrence in accordance with the procedures under EO 459, s. 1998. Following the Philippine Senate’s concurrence on 05 March 2018, as per Senate Resolution No. 93, and the country’s submission of its Instrument of Ratification to Norway as Depositary on 22 March 2018, the PH-EFTA Free Trade Agreement entered into force on 01 June 2018. This is pursuant to paragraph 2, Article 14.5 of the Agreement which states that it shall enter into force on the first day of the third month following the date on which at least one EFTA State and the Philippines have deposited their instrument of ratification, acceptance or approval with the Depositary.

The implementing Executive Order (EO) No. 61 by the Philippines was signed on 02 August 2018 and was made effective immediately following its publication at the Manila Bulletin on 10 August 2018.

What is the product coverage of this FTA?

All products at the national level (8- digit Codes) falling under HS Chapters 1 to 97 are covered by the FTA for tariff elimination or reduction, except for certain excluded products including live animals, meat and meat offal, vegetables, tunas and tilapia for the Philippines.

What are the tariff commitments under the PH-EFTA FTA?

The EFTA States will abolish all customs duties on imports of industrial products originating in the Philippines, including fish and other marine products, upon entry into force of the Agreement.

On the other hand, the Philippines will gradually eliminate/reduce customs duties on industrial products, which include fish and other marine products, originating in an EFTA State. However, certain fisheries and petrochemical products are excluded from tariff concessions.

While market access on industrial and fishery products were negotiated with the Philippines by the EFTA Member States as a bloc, agricultural market access was negotiated bilaterally. The Philippines gained significant concessions on agricultural products particularly on the following: (1) those that are currently being exported to the EFTA States, such as desiccated coconut, prepared or preserved pineapples, tropical fruits and raw sugar; and (2) those with high potential export interest such as tropical fruit wine. Conversely, the Philippines granted the EFTA States greater market access (on a bilateral basis) on a number of agricultural goods, e.g., temperate fruits, mineral and aerated waters, food preparations, chocolate, cheese, and wine.

What are the Rules of Origin under this FTA?

There are Product Specific Rules (PSRs). The exporter does not need to secure a certificate of origin from the customs authorities. Instead, the exporter can issue an origin declaration stating that it has complied with the rules of origin under the Agreement.

What are the criteria for products to be eligible for concession under PH-EFTA?

a. the product should be in the Inclusion List;
b. the product should be wholly produced or obtained in the exporting party, or satisfies the Product Specific Rule (PSR), to be deemed originating; and
c. the exporter must provide an origin declaration.

What is the frequency distribution of Philippine Tariffs under the PH-EFTA FTA?

Tables 7.4 to 7.6 Philippine Schedule of Tariff Commitments on Products Originating from Switzerland/Liechtenstein, Norway and Iceland under the PH-EFTA FTA: 2018-2027 (number of tariff lines; Total 11,206 for Switzerland/Liechtenstein; 11,212 for Norway; 11,208 for Iceland). For Switzerland/Liechtenstein, lines at 0% grow from 8,869 in 2018 to 10,139 in 2027; the Exclusion List (X) is constant at 992 lines; for Norway, X is 1,267 lines (0% lines from 8,695 to 9,884); for Iceland, X is 1,180 lines (0% lines from 8,862 to 9,971). [Full tables: see PDF pp. 215–216]

ai.title: II. Philippines – European Free Trade Association Free Trade Agreement
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang PH-EFTA FTA ang pangalawang bilateral FTA ng Pilipinas, kasama ang Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, at Switzerland.

🔍 Breakdown
• Nilagdaan: 28 April 2016 (Bern)
• In force: 01 June 2018
• Implementing EO 61 (02 August 2018)
• Saklaw: Ch. 1–97 maliban sa ilang excluded products (live animals, meat, vegetables, tunas, tilapia para sa PH)
• ROO: PSR; origin declaration ng exporter (walang CO mula sa customs)

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Mas malawak ito kaysa sa tariff lang: kasama ang serbisyo, pamumuhunan, IP, procurement, at sustainable development.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang exporter mula Norway ay puwedeng mag-isyu mismo ng origin declaration, hindi na kailangan ng certificate mula sa customs.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Nagbubukas ito ng mga bagong market para sa coconut products, tropical fruits, at raw sugar.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Tatlong tariff schedules: Switzerland/Liechtenstein, Norway, Iceland
• Fisheries at petrochemical products ay may exclusion

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang kaibahan ng origin declaration (PH-EFTA) at Certificate of Origin (ibang FTA).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Kailangan ba ng CO sa PH-EFTA?
Sagot: Hindi. Origin declaration ng exporter ang gamit.

title: I. Rules of Origin
subject: PART EIGHT – RULES OF ORIGIN

paragraphs.text:
What are the types of ROO?

a. Non-preferential ROO - used to implement measures and instruments of commercial policy, such as quotas, anti-dumping, safeguards, subsidy, anti-circumvention, trade statistics, origin labeling, and marking
b. Preferential ROO - used to establish whether a product is qualified for preferential tariff treatment; they are an integral component of international trading arrangements, whether regional or bilateral, to ensure that only qualified goods are accorded preferential duties

What is meant by country of origin?

Country of origin refers to the country where a product is obtained, produced or manufactured.

Some products clearly originate in a given country. But in today’s world characterized by global production chains, other manufactured goods not only use materials originating from other countries but also undergo processing or assembly in multiple countries.

What are the three (3) major rules applied in substantial transformation?

a. Regional Value Content (RVC) Requirement. Value added can be expressed either as a minimum value-added content expressed as a percentage of total product cost, or a maximum allowable cost percentage assigned to the value of imported material including those of undetermined origin.
b. Change in Tariff Classification Criteria. This includes:
• Change in Chapter (CC) - implies that for origin to be conferred, the non-originating material used to produce a good should be classified outside the HS Chapter (2-digit level) where the final good whose origin is being determined is classified
• Change in Tariff Heading (CTH) - connotes that to obtain origin, the non-originating material used to produce a good should have been classified in a tariff heading (4-digit level) outside the heading where the good under consideration is classified
• Change in Tariff Subheading (CTSH) - suggests that to obtain origin, the non-originating material used for the good under consideration must come from a subheading (6-digit level) other than the subheading where the good in question is classified
• Change in Tariff Subheading Split (CTSHS) - same effect as change in tariff subheading except that an existing HS subheading is split into two or more tariff lines
c. Specific Process Rule. Some goods are required to meet special product-specific rules in the exporting FTA party. In many cases, these rules specify a process that must be undergone in order for a good to be considered originating.

ai.title: What are the three (3) major rules applied in substantial transformation?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Tatlong major rules ang ginagamit para malaman kung may substantial transformation: RVC, Change in Tariff Classification (CC, CTH, CTSH, CTSHS), at Specific Process Rule.

🔍 Breakdown
• RVC: porsyento ng value-added
• CC: iba ang Chapter (2-digit)
• CTH: iba ang heading (4-digit)
• CTSH: iba ang subheading (6-digit)
• CTSHS: parang CTSH pero ang HS subheading ay hinati sa dalawa o higit pang tariff lines
• Specific Process Rule: tiyak na proseso na dapat gawin

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Tatlong paraan para patunayan na 'lokal' o 'regional' ang produkto kahit imported ang ilang materyales.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung ang tela (Chapter 52) ay ginawang damit (Chapter 62), may Change in Chapter, kaya puwedeng mag-qualify.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Ito ang puso ng ROO sa lahat ng FTAs.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• May dalawang paraan ng pagkuwenta ng RVC: build-up at build-down

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Pagsunud-sunurin ang antas: CC (2-digit) > CTH (4-digit) > CTSH (6-digit).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Alin ang mas mahigpit, CC o CTH?
Sagot: Mas mahigpit ang CC dahil kailangang magbago ang buong Chapter.

🔗 Related Topics
Wholly obtained; substantial transformation; accumulation; de minimis

Give the meaning, a breakdown, a practical customs example, why it matters, key numbers and deadlines to remember, a board-exam tip, common confusions, and related CMTA sections, CAO/CMO issuances.

paragraphs.text:
What are the two (2) methods used in the determination of RVC?

a. Direct/Build-up Method. The sum of the value of originating materials, overhead cost and profit is divided by the free-on-board value of the finished product; for a good to be considered originating, a value equal to or higher than the RVC requirement must be obtained
b. Indirect/Build-down Method. The sum of the value of non-originating imported materials, parts and components including those of unknown origin is divided by the free-on-board value of the finished good; for a product to be considered as originating, the resulting value should be less than the value of “1 minus the RVC requirement”

ai.title: What are the two (2) methods used in the determination of RVC?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Dalawang paraan ng pagkuwenta ng RVC: direct (build-up) at indirect (build-down).

🔍 Breakdown
• Direct: (originating materials + overhead + profit) ÷ FOB value ≥ RVC requirement
• Indirect: (non-originating materials incl. unknown origin) ÷ FOB value < (1 − RVC requirement)

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Dalawang direksyon ng parehong tanong: gaano karami ang 'regional'?

📦 Halimbawa
Kung RVC 40%, sa indirect, ang non-originating ay dapat mas mababa sa 60%.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Madalas ginagamit ito sa mga problem solving.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• FOB value ng finished good ang denominator

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alalahanin: build-up = pataas ang originating; build-down = pababa ang non-originating.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang denominator?
Sagot: FOB value ng finished good.

🔗 Related Topics
ATIGA ROO; ACFTA; AANZFTA

Give the meaning, a breakdown, a practical customs example, why it matters, key numbers and deadlines to remember, a board-exam tip, common confusions, and related CMTA sections, CAO/CMO issuances.

paragraphs.text:
How does the “accumulation rule” apply in the determination of regional value content?

In ASEAN FTAs, goods produced in an FTA Party which comply with origin requirements and are subsequently used in another FTA Party as input or material to produce a finished good shall be considered as originating in the FTA Party where working or processing of the finished product has taken place. As a result, the use of originating goods as inputs or materials in the production of another good can be counted towards satisfying the finished product’s origin requirements.

In the determination of regional value content, what are considered indirect materials, accessories and spare parts, and packaging materials or containers? How are these treated?

• Indirect materials, e.g., fuel; tools, dies and moulds; lubricants, greases, compounding materials and other similar goods; gloves, glasses, footwear, clothing, safety equipment and supplies for any of these things; and catalysts and solvents, are inputs used in production, but do not form part of a good. These materials are considered originating regardless of origin.
• Accessories, spare parts and tools imported with originating goods are treated as originating regardless of their actual origin if (i) the accessories, spare parts and tools are not invoiced separately from the originating good that they are imported with and (ii) the quantities and value of the accessories, spare parts and tools is customary for the imported good.
• Packaging materials or containers. If goods are packaged for retail sale, and the packing material or container in which the goods are packed for retail sale is classified with the goods in accordance with HS General Interpretative Rule 5, then the packaging material or containers are not required to meet the change in tariff classification requirement of the product-specific rule that the originating good has to meet. However, the costs of these materials and containers would be added in case the RVC is applied.

What are the other rules that may be applied in determining the country of origin of a product?

a. Exception Rule. This rule provides exceptions to the Change in Tariff Classification Criteria (e.g., CC, CTH, or CTSH). For instance, under the PJEPA, the product specific rule for heading 48.16 (carbon paper, self-copy paper and other copying or transfer papers whether or not put up in boxes) is RVC (40) or CTH except from heading 48.09 (carbon paper, self-copy paper and other copying or transfer papers whether or not printed, in rolls or sheets).
b. Alternative Rule. Conferment of origin under two different circumstances, e.g., wholly obtained or change from youth to maturity (live horses).
c. Supplementary Rule. These are requirements, which could be in terms of production process or characteristics of the final product, which are imposed in addition to another rule in order to complete the conferment of origin for a particular good.
d. Residual Rule. This is to cover those goods to which the specific rules will not apply.

What does “de minimis” in ROO mean?

An FTA may incorporate a de minimis provision that allows a good to qualify as an originating good provided that the total value of all non-originating materials which do not satisfy the change in tariff classification requirement does not exceed a set percentage (usually ranging from 7% to 15%) of the free-on-board value of the final good.

What is a Certificate of Origin (CO)?

• Declaration of the exporter, certified by the issuing authority (BOC in the case of a Philippine exporter), that the exported product complies with the origin requirement as specified under a bilateral, regional, or multilateral trading arrangement
• In the same way that a passport is an evidence of the nationality of a person, the CO is an evidence of the economic nationality of a product that must be presented by Philippine importers to BOC for them to avail of preferential tariff rates
• There are two (2) kinds of COs:

Table 8.1 Kinds of Certificate of Origin: Non-Preferential Treatment – for general merchandise – White CO form. Preferential Treatment (FTA – CO Form): AANZFTA – Form AANZ; ACFTA – Form E; AHKFTA – Form AHK; AIFTA – Form AI; AJCEPA – Form AJ; AKFTA – Form AK; ATIGA – Form D; GSP – Form A; PJEPA – Form JP.

What are the implications of origin conferment to industry?

The benefits of qualifying for originating status include i) cheaper imported input costs; ii) greater price advantage on exports; and iii) wider access to foreign markets.

ai.title: I. Rules of Origin
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang Rules of Origin (ROO) ay mga alituntunin para malaman kung saan 'ipinanganak' o nagawa ang isang produkto, hindi kung saan ito galing ipinadala.

🔍 Breakdown
• Non-preferential vs preferential ROO
• Wholly obtained; substantial transformation
• Tatlong rules sa substantial transformation: RVC, Change in Tariff Classification (CC, CTH, CTSH, CTSHS), Specific Process Rule
• Direct/build-up at indirect/build-down method sa RVC
• Accumulation at de minimis

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'passport' ng produkto: patunay kung saan ito nagmula para makuha ang tamang taripa.

📦 Halimbawa
Kung ang T-shirt ay ginawa sa Pilipinas gamit ang imported na tela, titingnan kung nagbago ang tariff classification (CTH) o kung sapat ang RVC.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Ito ang batayan kung kwalipikado ang produkto para sa preferential tariff ng FTA.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Mga proseso na hindi nagbibigay ng origin (simpleng pag-pack, paghalo, paglagay ng label)
• De minimis: 7%–15% ng FOB value

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang CC, CTH, CTSH at ang dalawang paraan ng RVC.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Pareho ba ang country of origin at country of export?
Sagot: Hindi palagi. Origin ay kung saan ginawa o huling na-transform.

🔗 Related Topics
AHTN; HS; Certificate of Origin forms; FTAs

title: II. Harmonization of Rules of Origin
subject: PART EIGHT – RULES OF ORIGIN

sections.heading: II. Harmonization of Rules of Origin

paragraphs.text:
What is the WTO Agreement on Rules of Origin?

The WTO Agreement on ROO aims at harmonization of non-preferential rules of origin that are clear and predictable and are administered in a transparent, consistent, uniform, impartial and reasonable manner. It sets out a work program for the harmonization of rules of origin to be undertaken after the entry into force of the WTO, in conjunction with the WCO.

Why is there a need to harmonize the Rules of Origin?

At present, countries apply different ROOs which vary depending on considerations such as substantial transformation, value-added, and/or manufacturing and processing systems. The harmonization of these divergent rules, e.g., use of uniform criteria and standard interpretations, would be in conformity with the WTO advocacy of promoting trade.

Why is the Harmonized System used as a basis for the determination of the Rules of Origin?

As the internationally standardized and accepted coding system of classifying products, the HS is used as the basis for the determination of ROO. Its systematic grouping of goods into sections, chapters, headings and subheadings enables the determination of whether a good has undergone “substantial transformation” (e.g., change in tariff classification at the Chapter, heading or subheading level of non-originating materials used), one of the basic criteria in determining its origin.

Why was the WCO chosen to do the harmonization of ROOs?

The WCO, as author and drafter of the HS, has the familiarity on the features of the system used by most countries in the classification of goods.

What is the Technical Committee on Rules of Origin?

The Technical Committee on Rules of Origin (TCRO) was created under the auspices of the WCO and is open to all WTO Members. Its functions are: (i) to carry out harmonization work; and (ii) to deal with any matter concerning technical problems related to rules of origin. The TCRO meets once a year.

What is the representation of WTO Members in the Technical Committee on Rules of Origin?

Each WTO Member has the right to be represented in the TCRO by nominating one delegate and one or more alternates to be its representative. At the TCRO meetings, representatives may be assisted by advisers and the WTO Secretariat may be allowed to attend as an observer.

Members of the WCO which are not Members of the WTO may be represented at the TCRO meetings by one delegate and one or more alternates in an observer status.

What is the Committee on Rules of Origin?

The Committee on Rules of Origin (CRO) was established within the framework of the WTO and is open to all WTO Members. The CRO meets once a year to review the implementation and operation of the WTO Agreement on ROO.

What is the Harmonization Work Programme?

The Harmonization Work Programme (HWP) was officially launched on 20 July 1995 and was scheduled for completion by 20 July 1998. The program is conducted both by the WTO-CRO and WCO-TCRO in Geneva and Brussels, respectively. Harmonization of non-preferential ROO is intended to ensure that such rules do not themselves create unnecessary obstacles to trade.

What is the current status of the Harmonization Work Programme?

While substantial progress was made since the implementation of HWP, it could not be completed as scheduled due to the complexity of issues. In July 1998, the WTO General Council approved a decision whereby Members have committed themselves to make their best endeavors to complete the Programme by November 1999.

Negotiations came to a virtual halt in 2007, however, due to divergences on a number of “core policy issues” and have since lost momentum. As noted in the 2013 Report of the CRO to the Council for Trade in Goods, Members hold different views on the need to finalize the HWP.

Pending the continuation of the HWP, the CRO agreed to initiate a transparency exercise to exchange information about non-preferential ROO currently in place. Furthermore, the Committee has also reviewed the results of the transposition exercise conducted by the WTO Secretariat. All draft harmonized ROO have been transposed to the 2012 edition of the Harmonized System.

ai.title: II. Harmonization of Rules of Origin
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang harmonization ng ROO ay pagsisikap ng WTO at WCO na gawing pare-pareho at malinaw ang non-preferential rules of origin.

🔍 Breakdown
• Batayan ang HS
• Technical Committee on Rules of Origin (TCRO) ng WCO (isang beses kada taon)
• Committee on Rules of Origin (CRO) ng WTO
• Harmonization Work Programme (HWP): inilunsad 20 July 1995; dapat tapos sa 20 July 1998; huminto noong 2007

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang pagsulat ng 'iisang panuntunan' para sa lahat ng bansa kung paano malalaman ang pinagmulan ng produkto.

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag pare-pareho ang ROO, mas madali at predictable ang trade at hindi nagiging hadlang ang sari-saring patakaran.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Binabawasan nito ang unnecessary obstacles sa kalakalan.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• HWP: hindi natapos dahil sa core policy issues
• Lahat ng draft harmonized ROO ay na-transpose sa HS 2012

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang mga katawan (TCRO vs CRO) at ang status ng HWP.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Bakit HS ang batayan?
Sagot: Dahil ito ang standard na coding system kaya puwedeng gamitin ang tariff classification change bilang pamantayan.

🔗 Related Topics
WTO Agreement on ROO; WCO

title: I. Overview of Competition Policy and Law
subject: PART NINE – COMPETITION POLICY AND LAW

sections.heading: I. Overview of Competition Policy and Law

paragraphs.text:
What is Competition Law?

Competition law refers to the framework of rules and regulations designed to foster the competitive environment in a national economy. It consists of measures intended to promote a more competitive environment as well as legislation designed to prevent a reduction in competition.

What are the five (5) basic market structures in which the degree of competition affects prices, output, and profits?

a. Perfect competition - an ideal or extreme form of competition. It occurs when a market consists of many firms selling an identical product to many buyers. Any firm that wishes to do so can enter or leave the market.
b. Monopoly - a market with a sole supplier of a good, service or resource for which there is no close substitute. In addition, there are barriers to entry of new firms.
c. Natural monopoly - arises from natural barriers to entry (such as a unique source of supply) or from a situation in which one firm can supply the entire market at a lower price than two or more firms could offer.
d. Monopolistic competition – similar to perfect competition, but rather than firms producing identical products, there are many firms competing against each other by producing similar but slightly different products
e. Oligopoly - is characterized by a small number of firms where the quantity sold by any one firm is influenced by its choices in respect of strategic variables (such as prices, product design, research and development, advertising, and sales locations) and these choices are strongly influenced by other firms in the industry

What is market failure and its sources?

Market failure occurs when the market is unable to achieve an efficient and equitable allocation of resources.

The sources of the market failure are:
• Public goods – goods which if provided to one consumer are also freely available to all consumers
• Income distribution – the market will not necessarily ensure equitable distribution of incomes. This may motivate government to introduce policies/measures to redistribute wealth, e.g., income taxes and social security benefits.
• Monopoly – the operations of monopoly or natural monopoly often result in misuse of market power and inefficient allocation of resources, which reduce community welfare. For this reason, governments generally regulate monopolies and enforce laws preventing cartels. This type of market scenario is a major rationale for a comprehensive competition policy.
• Externalities – these arise when an activity confers a benefit (like the benefit of education or immunization) or imposes a cost (pollution) on a third party, without said costs or benefits being included in the market price of that activity
• Information asymmetries – in theory, buyers and sellers in a competitive market have complete knowledge about the characteristics and quality of a product or service. Information asymmetries between producers and consumers can lead to market failure and reduce community welfare.

What are competitive conduct rules?

Competitive Conduct Rules are government’s response to the absence of perfect competition in a market. The primary objective is to protect or enhance the competitive process in markets where said process is only partially operating. Typically, such rules prohibit arrangements that can be construed as anti-competitive.

What are examples of anti-competitive conduct?

• Price-fixing agreement – competitors agree to fix prices at a particular level; use of “recommended prices” which are less obvious, but which in reality involve the fixing of prices by agreement
• Market sharing agreement – agreement among competitors to share a market, e.g., a number of producers may choose to restrict their sales to certain geographic areas, thus developing local monopolies
• Exclusionary provision – agreement between competitors to limit dealings with a particular supplier or customer or a particular class of customer, e.g., boycotts. These actions are taken to prevent new firms from entering the market, or to force existing firms out of the market.
• Tie-in arrangements and third line forcing – when the supply of goods or services to a person is made conditional upon said person’s purchase of additional goods and services, either from the same supplier (tie-in arrangement) or from another specified supplier (third line forcing)
• Retail price maintenance – refers to action by suppliers, manufacturers or wholesalers specifying a minimum price below which goods or services may not be resold or advertised for resale

In addition, the ASEAN Regional Guidelines on Competition Policy have identified conduct that might restrict the freedom of action of the parties or cause the prevention, distortion, or restriction of competition:
• Bid-rigging – includes cover bidding to assist an undertaking in winning the tender. An essential feature of the tender system is that tenderers prepare and submit bids independently.
• Limiting or controlling production or investment – involves agreements which limit output or control production, by fixing levels or setting quotas, or agreements which deal with structural overcapacity or coordinate future investment plans
• Abuse of a dominant position – occurs where the dominant enterprise, either individually or together with other undertakings, exploits its dominant position in the relevant market or excludes competitors and harms the competition process. It is prudent to consider the actual or potential impact on competition of certain conducts of dominant enterprises, instead of automatically treating said conducts as abusive.
• Exploitative behavior towards consumers, customers and/or competitors – e.g., excessive, or unfair purchase prices or sales prices; tie-in arrangements
• Exclusionary behavior towards competitors – e.g., predatory pricing by a firm which involves deliberately incurring losses in the short-run through extremely low prices thus forcing one or more firms out of the market, with the view to charging higher prices in the long-run; margin squeeze
• Discriminatory behavior – e.g., applying dissimilar pricing or conditions to equivalent transactions and vice-versa
• Limiting production, markets, or technical development to the prejudice of consumers – e.g., restricting output or illegitimate refusal to supply; restricting access to/use of/development of a new technology

What are the potential solutions to the different types of anti-competitive conduct?

• Per se Prohibition – most direct form of anti-competitive measure that an authority can undertake; applies to activities which are detrimental to regular competitive behavior in a market (e.g., price fixing)
• Rule of Reason (Competition Test) – most widely-used test to determine whether or not a business activity reduces competition in the market; there are a wide variety of business practices that, while inhibiting competition, may not require total prohibition
• Authorization – a mechanism through which the public benefits from ostensibly anti-competitive conduct can be assessed as a counter-balancing consideration; includes direct intervention or inquiry by a government commission
• Notification – involves the approval of certain types of anti-competitive conduct upon the offender being granted immunity, conditional upon the consent of the market regulator

What are regulatory restrictions?

Regulatory restrictions are government’s own restrictions on competitive conduct, either through legislated regulation or direct ownership.

These restrictions can detract from overall competitiveness in the economy, in much the same way as market failure, in the sense that they detract from the regular workings of the market. Regulatory restrictions may entrench a smaller number of players in a less competitive environment. Consequences of these are higher prices, poorer quality goods, less consumer choices resulting from reduced competition, and a group of firms that have a diminished response to their market. In case of monopolies, competition in the market is prevented.

Regulatory restrictions in the Philippines include:
• regulatory barriers to market entry, including licensing and franchising agreements;
• government monopolies, including monopolies on public utilities such as electricity generation and supply, telephone services, and the shipping industry; and
• rural marketing boards.

What forms of regulation have a direct impact on competition?

a. Barriers to entry – these derive from: (i) economies of scale due to market share achieved by the incumbents; (ii) capital requirements (including investment in brand development through advertising and the like); (iii) cost savings accruing to existing firms from their experience and familiarity with the particular industry; (iv) monopoly access to key infrastructure; and (v) monopoly of key industry knowledge
b. Regulations which restrict competitive behavior such as price control and advertising restrictions

What is a natural monopoly?

The distinguishing feature of a natural monopoly is that a single facility can supply the entire market demand more efficiently than two or more smaller facilities.

Typically, natural monopolies have the following features: (1) large development and start-up costs; and (2) economies of scale, i.e., as output is increased, the average cost per unit output declines.

A natural monopoly is an outcome of the size of the market and the type of technology available to meet demand. It is not a market structure, rather a cost-minimizing method of production. There are two major implications:
• an industry may consist of more than one firm even though the existing technology would suggest that a single firm/monopoly is more economically efficient; and
• the existence of natural monopoly conditions in an industry may vary as demand varies and as the prevailing technology changes.

What is an essential facility?

Within the framework of competition policy, an essential facility is a major infrastructure which exhibits two characteristics:
• the facility is essential to the effective operation of an economic organization; and
• the facility exhibits natural monopoly characteristics, e.g., electricity grids, rail infrastructure, roads, port facilities, pipelines and telecommunications networks.

What are the main areas/concerns which competition policy and law need to address?

a. Preventing enterprises from entering into agreements which do not have any beneficial features, and which will restrict competition, either among themselves or between them and third parties
b. Controlling attempts by monopolists or dominant firms from abusing their market position and preventing new firms from entering the market
c. Ensuring that workable competition is maintained in oligopolistic industries
d. Monitoring mergers between independent enterprises, where the effect of the merger may result in market concentration and reduction in competition

ai.title: I. Overview of Competition Policy and Law
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang competition policy ay mga batas at patakaran para mapanatili ang patas na kompetisyon sa merkado. Ang competition law ay balangkas ng mga alituntunin laban sa pagbawas ng kompetisyon.

🔍 Breakdown
• Layunin: efficiency, itama ang market failure, kapakanan ng consumers, paglago, competitiveness
• 5 market structures: perfect competition, monopoly, natural monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly
• Sources ng market failure: public goods, income distribution, monopoly, externalities, information asymmetries
• Anti-competitive conduct: price-fixing, market sharing, bid-rigging, abuse of dominant position

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Gusto nitong pigilan ang iilang kompanya na kontrolin ang presyo at pahirapan ang consumers at maliliit na negosyo.

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag nagkasundo ang dalawang kompanya na itakda ang presyo ng produkto, price-fixing iyon at bawal sa competition law.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Pinapababa nito ang presyo at pinapaganda ang kalidad at pagpipilian ng consumers.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Per se prohibition vs. Rule of Reason
• Authorization at Notification bilang mga solusyon

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin ang 5 market structures, 5 sources ng market failure, at mga halimbawa ng anti-competitive conduct.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Pareho ba ang horizontal at vertical agreements?
Sagot: Hindi. Horizontal: magkapareho ang antas sa merkado; Vertical: magkaibang antas ng production chain.

🔗 Related Topics
RA 10667; PCC; ASEAN Competition Action Plan

title: II. Competition Policy and Law in ASEAN
subject: PART NINE – COMPETITION POLICY AND LAW

sections.heading: II. Competition Policy and Law in ASEAN

paragraphs.text:
What is the ASEAN Economic Community Blueprint?

Crafted and adopted by the ASEAN Leaders in Singapore during the 13th ASEAN Summit on November 20, 2007, the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) Blueprint serves as the master plan to establish the AEC by the year 2015.

In the AEC Blueprint, the AMSs committed to endeavor to introduce national competition policies by 2015, the rationale being to ensure a level playing field and develop a culture of fair business competition within the ASEAN region thereby attaining enhanced economic performance for the AMSs in the long term.

What is the ASEAN Experts Group on Competition?

The ASEAN Experts Group on Competition (AEGC) is a formal body established by the ASEAN Economic Ministers (AEM) in August 2007. Comprised of representatives from the competition authorities of all AMSs nominated by their respective Senior Economic Officials, the AEGC acts as a regional forum to discuss and coordinate competition policies with the goal of promoting a healthy and fair competitive environment in the ASEAN region. It also aims to promote a competition culture in ASEAN through regular exchange of information, networking and dialogue.

What are the benefits of cooperation in competition policy among the AMS?

• Promotes a culture of competition in the ASEAN region
• Facilitates co-operation or at least a high degree of consistency in the implementation of competition policy in the region
• Provides AMSs’ competition regulatory bodies with an avenue for maintaining regular contacts and addressing practical competition concerns
• Builds an effective legal framework to enforce competition policy against businesses that engage in cross-border business practices which restrict competition
• Improves the efficiency and effectiveness of national competition regulatory bodies through the sharing and exchange of non-confidential information, knowledge, and resources
• Facilitates the development of agreements on the basic elements of a common framework for national competition policy within the region

Who are the competition authorities/bodies in ASEAN?

Table 9.1 Competition Bodies/Authorities in ASEAN (AMS – Competition Authority – Website): Brunei Darussalam – The Competition Commission of Brunei Darussalam – www.ccbd.gov.bn; Cambodia – Ministry of Commerce – www.moc.gov.kh; Indonesia – Commission for the Supervision of Business Competition – http://eng.kppu.go.id; Lao PDR – Ministry of Industry and Commerce – http://www.moic.gov.la/?lang=en; Malaysia – Malaysia Competition Commission – http://www.mycc.gov.my; Myanmar – Myanmar Competition Commission, Ministry of Commerce – https://www.commerce.gov.mm/; Philippines – Philippine Competition Commission – www.phcc.gov.ph; Singapore – Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCCS) – www.cccs.gov.sg; Thailand – Office of Trade Competition Commission – otcc.or.th; Vietnam – Viet Nam Competition Authority – www.vca.gov.vn

ai.title: II. Competition Policy and Law in ASEAN
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang ASEAN ay may Experts Group on Competition (AEGC) at Competition Action Plan (ACAP) 2016–2025 para sa pagsulong ng patas na kompetisyon sa rehiyon.

🔍 Breakdown
• AEC Blueprint: national competition policies pagsapit ng 2015
• AEGC: itinatag August 2007 ng ASEAN Economic Ministers
• ACAP 2016–2025: 7 estratehikong hakbang
• Competition authority ng Pilipinas: Philippine Competition Commission

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Parang 'patas na laro' sa buong ASEAN: pare-pareho ang prinsipyo para pantay ang negosyo sa lahat ng bansa.

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag may cross-border cartel, ang kooperasyon ng mga competition authority ng AMSs ang tutulong sa pag-imbestiga.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Nakakatulong ito sa pagpapalakas ng regional integration.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• ACAP: 2016–2025 (10 taon)
• AEGC: regional forum para sa palitan ng impormasyon

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang AEGC, ACAP, at ang mga competition body ng ASEAN (hal. PCC para sa Pilipinas).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Anong ahensya ang competition authority ng Pilipinas sa ASEAN table?
Sagot: Philippine Competition Commission (www.phcc.gov.ph).
