title: III. Competition Policy and Law in the Philippines
subject: PART NINE – COMPETITION POLICY AND LAW

sections.heading: III. Competition Policy and Law in the Philippines

paragraphs.text:
What are the Philippines’ competition-related laws?

The Philippines has approximately 30 competition/anti-trust-related laws, leading examples of which include the following:
• 1987 Constitution – prohibits monopolization and combinations in restraint of trade (on rule of reason basis), but has no imposable sanctions for violation
• Revised Penal Code of the Philippines (Article 186) – describes monopolization and combinations in restraint of trade as acts punishable and describes penalties, including imprisonment and fines between Php200,000.00 and Php600,000.00; it is similar in nature to Section 2 of the US Sherman Act
• RA No. 3247 also known as an Act to Prohibit Monopolies and Combinations in Restraint of Trade – provides for treble damages for civil liabilities arising from anti-competitive behavior
• RA No. 165 (Patent Law) and RA 166 (Trademark Law) – describe the appropriate civil actions which can be resorted to and penalties imposable for breaches (Intellectual Property Office website: www.ipophil.gov.ph)
• PD No. 49 or Copyright Law – penalizes copyright infringement
• RA No. 386 or Civil Code of the Philippines – stipulates the collection of damages arising from unfair competition
• RA No. 7581 or The Price Act – protects consumers by stipulating price manipulation (hoarding, profiteering and cartels) as illegal for certain commodities in cases of emergency (DTI website: www.dti.gov.ph)
• RA No. 7394 or The Consumer Act of the Philippines – imposes penalties for behavior such as deceptive, unfair, and unconscionable sales practices in both goods and credit transactions (www.dti.gov.ph)
• Philippine Corporation Code – provides for rules and proceedings for approving mergers, consolidations and combinations for the Securities and Exchange Commission (Securities and Exchange Commission website: www.sec.gov.ph)
• EO No. 143, s. 1999 – reorganizes the Tariff Commission to strengthen its functions, including the conduct of advocacy campaign programs and capacity building for the development of competition policy and law in the Philippines and for the publication of certain competition policy studies and briefing materials; as formerly-designated Philippine representative to the AEGC, the Commission actively participated in competition policy and law regional fora to discuss and cooperate with AMSs as all endeavor to introduce, effectively implement, or develop competition policy and law in the ASEAN region by 2015
• EO No. 45, s. 2011 – designates the Office for Competition (OFC) of the Department of Justice (DOJ) as the Competition Authority (Department of Justice website: www.doj.gov.ph)

When is National Competition Day?

Proclamation No. 384 (s. 2012) signed on 18 May 2012 declares 05 December of every year as “National Competition Day.” On its first observance, the Commission provided assistance to the OFC in planning activities to mark the milestone event.

ai.title: What is the Philippine Competition Act (PCA)?
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang Philippine Competition Act (RA 10667) ang pangunahing batas sa kompetisyon at lumikha sa Philippine Competition Commission (PCC).

🔍 Breakdown
• Pinirmahan: 21 July 2015
• Ipinagbabawal: anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominant position, anti-competitive mergers at acquisitions
• PCC: independent quasi-judicial body
• Mga kapangyarihan: mag-imbestiga at humatol, mag-review ng mergers, mag-subpoena, mag-impose ng fines, mag-isyu ng cease and desist, divestiture orders at advisory opinions

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Ang PCC ay 'tagapagbantay' ng patas na kompetisyon sa negosyo.

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag may balak na merger na maaaring bumawas ng kompetisyon, puwedeng suriin ito ng PCC.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Nagbibigay ng legal na ngipin sa competition policy.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Ang criminal prosecution ay gawain ng OFC (Sec. 31)

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Kabisaduhin: 21 July 2015 at ang tatlong ipinagbabawal.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang PCC?
Sagot: Philippine Competition Commission.

PCA; OFC; AEGC

Were there changes in the functions of the OFC with the issuance of RA No. 10667?

Yes. Upon the creation of the PCC, EO 45, s. 2011 was amended and with modifications on the functions of the OCC [as printed].

In accordance with Section 31 of Chapter VI of the Philippine Competition Act, preliminary investigation and prosecution of all criminal offenses arising under said Act and other competition-related laws shall be undertaken by the OFC.

Are there competition-related provisions in the FTAs that the Philippines is a party to?

Yes. Competition policy chapters can be found in the following:
• Chapter 12 of the PJEPA
• Chapter 8, Article 53, paragraph (I) of the AJCEPA; and
• Chapter 14 of the AANZFTA.

title: I. E-Commerce and Digital Trade
subject: PART TEN – TRADE POLICY BRIEFERS

paragraphs.text:
Scope and Definitions

E-commerce is one of the components of the digital economy, as shown in Figure 10.1 (UNCTAD, 2019a, p. 6). It should be noted that there is no single standard definition for either e-commerce or digital trade. Various fora and institutions use their own working definition on the two concepts. For example, the Organization for Economic Co-operation (OECD) and UNCTAD define e-commerce as purchases and sales of products (for example, physical goods, digital products and services) and comprises of categories such as business-to-consumer (B2C), business-to-business (B2B), consumer-to-consumer (C2C) and business-to-government (B2G).

The World Trade Organization (WTO, 1998), on the other hand, defines e-commerce as the “production, distribution, marketing, sale or delivery of goods and services by electronic means” (1998). The World Customs Organization enumerates the following essential elements in the definition of e-commerce: a) online ordering, sale, communication and, if applicable, payment; b) cross-border transactions/shipments; c) physical (tangible) goods; and d) destined to consumer/buyer (commercial and non-commercial) (WCO, 2018, p. 8).

For purposes of collecting statistics, e-commerce is defined by the Philippine Statistics Authority “as the sale or purchase of goods and services, whether between businesses, households, individuals, governments, and other public or private organizations, conducted over computer-mediated networks. The goods and services are ordered over networks, but payment and ultimate delivery of the good or service may be conducted on or offline” (Serafica, R. and Albert, J. R., 2018).

The three main factors affecting the development of the e-marketplace are: (i) economic factors and conditions, (ii) legal and institutional environment, and (iii) social acceptance and awareness (Table 10.1). The benefits for an economy joining the e-commerce marketplace can be significant (Table 10.2). The macroeconomic benefits include boosting output and efficiency, increasing participation in regional and global value chains, and promoting inclusive growth, among others. (UNESCAP and ADB, 2018, p. 46).

Table 10.2 Economic Benefits and Costs of Using E-commerce – Benefits: boosts efficiency and has positive impact on gross domestic product; allows economies to increase participation in global value chain; increases labor productivity and supports job creation, entrepreneurship, innovation, and creativity; leads to energy savings and lower carbon emissions; potential to advance inclusive growth (developing economies, rural areas, women, etc.). Costs: requires social and physical capital investments; could lead to transfer pricing and erosion of tax revenue; potential to widen economic disparity; potential to distort competition.

World Trade and the Digital Economy

Deardorff (2017) describes the cross-border element of digital trade by defining digital trade as “commerce involving more than one country for which the product itself is digital and/or any of the following are accomplished at least in part by using the internet or a similar digital technology: advertising, ordering, delivering, payment or servicing.”

Digitally delivered trade has emerged due to factors such as reduction in transport and coordination costs, coupled with reduction in the cost of sharing information. This digital trade can be broken down into three dimensions: nature, type of flow, and the actors involved. The nature of digital trade can either be digitally or physically delivered. The type of flow depends on whether the item being traded is a good or a service and the actors involved can either be businesses, consumers, or governments (López González, J. and M. Jouanjean, 2017).

An estimated 1.3 billion people, or one quarter of the world’s population aged 15 years and older, shopped online in 2017 (Figure 10.2). Uptake in low-income economies is considerably lower, suggesting that it takes more than wireless connectivity for e-commerce to take off (Figure 10.3) (UNCTAD, 2019a).

Some economies have been successful at leveraging trade in ICT goods and services for value creation. This may lead to significant employment opportunities, add value to GDP and generate earnings in foreign exchange. However, apart from the Philippines, few countries have been successful at exporting both ICT goods and services, and some countries (e.g., Costa Rica and Finland) have offset significant declines in goods exports by increasing services exports. Other countries have seized opportunities for trade in so called ICT-enabled (or digitally delivered) services. Trade in ICT goods amounts to a substantially higher global value ($1.9 trillion in exports in 2017) than trade in ICT services ($568 billion in exports in 2018), but the latter have proved more resilient in the past decade. Trade in ICT goods is more concentrated geographically than it is in ICT services.

Figure 10.4 shows that East and South-East Asian economies dominate the share of ICT goods in total merchandise exports. In Hong Kong (China), ICT goods account for more than half of all merchandise exports, which are linked to re-exports from mainland China (UNCTAD, 2019a).

B2C E-Commerce Index

The UNCTAD B2C E-commerce Index measures an economy’s preparedness to support online shopping. The index consists of four indicators that are highly related to online shopping and for which there is wide country coverage. The extent to which people shop online in a country is correlated with the value of the index, with an adjusted R squared value of 0.8 (Figure 10.5).

A growing share of the world’s population is shopping online. In 2017, an estimated 1.3 billion people, or one quarter of the world’s population aged 15 years and older, shopped online (refer again to Figure 10.2). The Netherlands remains at the top of the B2C E-Commerce Index followed by Switzerland and Singapore (Table 10.3) (UNCTAD, 2019b).

Table 10.3 Top 10 economies in the UNCTAD B2C E-commerce Index 2019: 1 Netherlands (96.4); 2 Switzerland (95.5); 3 Singapore (95.1); 4 Finland (94.4); 5 United Kingdom (94.4); 6 Denmark (94.2); 7 Norway (93.4); 8 Ireland (93.3); 9 Germany (92.9); 10 Australia (91.8).

Among the nine (9) ASEAN countries (excluding Brunei Darussalam), the Philippines ranked six (6) in terms of index value. The movement of Philippines’ index value from 2015-2019 mirrors the trend of Indonesia (Figure 10.6).

Philippine E-Commerce Perspective

The primary law on e-commerce in the Philippines is Republic Act (RA) No. 8792 or the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000. It gives legal recognition to electronic forms of data messages, documents, signatures, transactions, storage of information. It provides penalties for access of data without consent, piracy, hacking, and other violation.

Consumers’ rights, privacy and data confidentiality under e-commerce are safeguarded through the Consumer Act of the Philippines (RA No.7394), Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA No. 10173), Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (RA No. 10175) and various other regulations issued by concerned government agencies (Annex C).

The Philippine E-Commerce Roadmap 2016-2020 and its update was developed by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI, 2016, n.d.) in coordination with relevant stakeholders. It presents the status of e-commerce adoption in the country and lays down the plans and programs necessary in strengthening e-commerce in the Philippines. The Roadmap identified opportunities for Philippines relating to e-commerce such as the fastest growing internet population in the world, youth population, online presence and mobile internet subscription.

A survey conducted by We are Social (2020) shows that there are 73 million internet users in the Philippines (67% of the population). Though majority of the internet use gravitate towards social media platforms, it is reported that e-commerce adoption in the Philippines (i.e., percentage of internet users aged 16 to 64 who say they bought something online via any device in the past month) is at 76%, a little above the world average of 74%.

In 2019, Philippine e-commerce consumers spent an approximate total of US$6.87 billion for travel (including accommodation), topping the amount spent in consumer e-commerce categories. This was followed by video games at US$741 million, electronics and physical media at US$258 million and by fashion and beauty at US$227 million.

UNESCAP and ADB (2018, pp. 60-61) identified four main actors that shape an economy’s e-commerce landscape, namely, national governments and international agencies, trade associations and industry bodies, businesses within the e-commerce ecosystem (e-commerce vendors, payment service providers, and logistics service providers, among others), and consumers and the public. A list on ways to develop and enrich the e-marketplace by each actor was compiled (Table 10.4) which can be used by the Philippines as a checklist towards further strengthening e-commerce in the country.

E-Commerce and the COVID-19 Pandemic

The enforcement of social distancing, lockdown and other measures in response to the COVID-19 pandemic has led consumers to ramp up online shopping, social media use, internet telephony and teleconferencing, and streaming of videos and films. This has resulted in spikes in business-to-consumers (B2C) sales and an increase in business-to-business (B2B) e-commerce. The increase in B2C sales is particularly evident in online sales of medical supplies, household essentials and food products.

E-commerce for goods and services trade has been adversely affected by the same factors that have caused disruption in supply and demand overall. Such disruptions have resulted in delivery delays or outright cancellation of orders. Several other e-commerce-related challenges including price gouging (i.e., increasing prices to unreasonably high levels), product safety concerns, deceptive practices, cybersecurity concerns, the need for increased bandwidth, and development-related concerns have arisen or been further amplified during this pandemic.

Governments have adopted new measures while the private sector has also responded by adopting measures to ensure that e-commerce can help alleviate some of the challenges faced in combatting the virus. These have included increasing network capacity, offering expanded data services at little or no cost, lowering or scrapping transaction costs on digital payments and mobile money transfers, improving delivery services and other logistics, using digital tools to enforce measures and disseminate information, promoting telehealth services, and leveraging ICT for surveillance.

The pandemic has highlighted the importance of digital technologies in general, but also differing vulnerabilities across the world. The resulting experiences and lessons from Covid-19 pandemic including its effects on electronic commerce are relevant to various discussions in the WTO, which could benefit from looking at greater international cooperation to facilitate the cross-border movement of goods and services, narrow the digital divide, and level the playing field for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) (WTO, 2020).

Effects on Philippines

The great potential and opportunities presented by digital trade should be taken advantage of by the Philippines. Serafica and Albert (2018) recommends the following: a) exploit the comparative advantage of the Philippines in digital trade; b) develop industry roadmaps and export strategies for digital products; c) improve Information Communications Technology (ICT) and e-commerce measurement and reporting; and d) address the policy gaps and regulatory constraints.

ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang e-commerce ay isa sa mga bahagi ng digital economy. Walang iisang pamantayang depinisyon, ngunit karaniwang tumutukoy sa pagbili at pagbebenta ng produkto at serbisyo sa pamamagitan ng electronic means.

🔍 Breakdown
• Pangunahing batas: RA 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000)
• Consumer rights: RA 7394; Data Privacy Act (RA 10173); Cybercrime Prevention Act (RA 10175)

• 73 milyong internet users sa PH (67% ng populasyon); 76% ng internet users 16–64 ang bumili online
• Tumaas ang B2C at B2B sales noong COVID-19

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Online shopping at digital na kalakalan: mas madaling bumili at magbenta nang hindi kailangang pumunta sa tindahan.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang pagbili ng laro o paglalakbay online ay bahagi ng digital trade. Sa 2019, US$6.87 bilyon ang gastos ng Pilipinong consumers sa travel.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Lumalaki ang papel nito sa kalakalan at policy-making ng bansa.

Alamin ang mga depinisyon (OECD/UNCTAD, WTO, WCO) at ang RA 8792.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students

title: II. Growing Global Protectionism
subject: PART TEN – TRADE POLICY BRIEFERS

paragraphs.text:
Background

Protectionism is on the rise globally. In international trade policy, protectionism refers to an economic policy of protecting domestic industries against foreign competition by means of tariffs, trade remedy measures, import quota, export subsidy, technical barriers, import- and export non-tariff measures.

The static arguments for protectionism consist of (1) existence of market failures (in the product or labor market); (2) infant-industry; (3) revenue/finance requirements; and (4) national security. In adopting the protectionist measures, most developing countries will argue mostly for revenue purposes and presence of an infant industry. Yet, the most important argument is for national security reasons which implies that government will protect industries or products that are deemed necessary for the country in cases of calamities and national emergency. Dynamic arguments for protectionism include potential spillovers of technology, marginal social benefits, and retaliation for other country’s protectionist measures.

By the beginning of the 21st century, we see a transition of the world trade regime from globalization and trade integration towards nationalism and protectionism. This is because Tariffs have fallen in the last three decades due to bilateralism, regionalism, and multilateralism. Hence, countries need to protect its national interests.

The Global Trade Alert Report for 2009-2020 points out that harmful measures have been steadily on the rise globally for the past 11 years. The highest number of interventions was recorded in 2018 with 2,204 harmful measures. It decreased by 41% (1,289) in 2019. To date, a total of 390 harmful measures has been recorded (Figure 10.7A).

ASEAN has contributed 895 harmful interventions, 27 of which came from the Philippines. Other FTA partners of the country contributed 5,657 harmful interventions, while the USA and EU added 2,089 and 2,902, respectively (Figure 10.7B). Philippine’s top trading partners severely affected by the protectionist measures include EU (83,787), USA (6,344), other FTA partners, (41,656), ASEAN (27,378), of which 3,298 harmful measures affected the Philippines (Figure 10.7C).

Clearly, the global rise in trade protectionism has also affected different sectors. The top sectors affected most often by protectionist measures of PH’s trading partners are metal based industries (products of iron and steel - 935, other fabricated metal products - 658, and basic iron and steel - 554), motor vehicles and parts industry (motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers - 559), and chemical industry (basic organic chemicals - 545) (Figure 10.7D).

Meanwhile, common harmful policy instruments used globally in imposing trade measures were accounted for by subsidies (7,431), export-related measures including export subsidies (3,772), tariff measures (2,429), contingent trade-protective measures (1,974), and trade-related investment measures (674), respectively (Figure 10.7E).

Falling Tariffs vs Increasing Non-Tariff Barriers and Other Non-Tariff Measures

Tariff is an import tax or a duty imposed on goods imported from abroad. According to the World Trade Organization (WTO) tariffs give a price advantage to locally produced goods over similar goods which are imported, and they raise revenues for the government. Non-Tariff Measures (NTMs) as defined by UNCTAD are policy measures other than ordinary customs tariffs that can potentially have an economic effect on international trade in goods, changing quantities traded, or prices or both. While tariffs are transparent and has widely been eliminated, NTMs are not easy to identify and said to be a major obstacle to trade.

a. PH Tariffs vs Global Tariffs
The Philippines’ average bound tariffs on agricultural products is at 35% which includes sensitive products such as sugar and rice. Among the ASEAN-6, the Philippines has the fourth highest average bound tariffs on agricultural products. For CLMV, Myanmar has the highest with 102.9%. For non-agricultural products, ASEAN-6 has higher bound tariffs than CLMV. For all products, Singapore has the lowest average bound tariffs in ASEAN (Figure 10.8A).

Other Philippine trading partners outside ASEAN have high average bound tariffs on agricultural products such as India and EFTA states (i.e., Iceland and Norway). For all other products, Norway and Japan have average bound rates below 5% while Hong Kong, China, being a free port, has none (Figure 10.8B).

Despite its high bound rates, Brunei Darussalam does not impose duties on imported agricultural products while Singapore’s average applied most-favored nation (MFN) tariffs is at 0.1%. The highest average applied MFN tariffs in ASEAN are imposed by Thailand (24%) and Viet Nam (16.5%) which are among the major producers of rice and other crops in the region. For non-agricultural products, CLMV have substantial rates while Singapore imposes duty-free on all imports. Overall, Cambodia, Thailand and Viet Nam are the most protectionist while Brunei Darussalam and Singapore are the most liberalized in the region in terms of tariff reduction and elimination (Figure 10.8C).

With Philippine’s FTA partners, South Korea imposes the highest applied MFN tariffs on agricultural products (57%) followed by Norway (44.9%), India (38.8%) and Switzerland (36.5%). Australia and New Zealand, on the other hand, imposes low MFN tariffs on agricultural products. For non-agricultural products, India has the highest applied MFN tariffs (13.6%) followed by China (8.8%). For all products, excluding Hong Kong, China, New Zealand and Australia are among the most liberalized FTA partners of the Philippines while India and South Korea are the most protectionist (Figure 10.8D).

b. PH NTMs vs World NTMs
The Philippines currently has a total of 1,031 measures in place wherein 196 are export-related measures such as accomplishment of export licenses for various commodities regulated and monitored by the Department of Agriculture (DA), the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), among others. Also, Philippines imposes 200 sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) measures mostly for agricultural products and 352 measures that are classified as technical barriers to trade (TBT) such as packaging requirements, standard compliance, mandatory inspection upon importation, etc. Other trade measures imposed by the Philippines are trade remedy measures, pre-shipment inspections, price control measures, quantity control measures, etc. (UNCTAD Trains Database).

In ASEAN, Thailand ranked first in terms of NTMs in place with 2,096 measures wherein 50% are TBTs. Cambodia, Lao PDR and Myanmar have less NTMs in place compared to other countries in the region. Singapore, which has almost no tariffs imposed on all its products, has a total of 589 NTMs in place which is among the lowest in the region. (Figure 10.9A).

Among the Philippine’s major trading partners outside ASEAN, China is the most stringent in terms of NTM imposition with a total of 5,684 measures. Majority (70%) of China’s NTMs are TBTs. India imposes more SPS measures among the Philippine’s FTA partners which is almost 40% of its NTMs in place. The EU and the EFTA state of Switzerland have the lowest NTMs in place among the list wherein majority are TBTs (Figure 10.9B).

c. Number of Trade Remedy Measures Taken by PH vs World
Trade remedy measures are trade policy tools that allow governments to take remedial action against imports which are causing material injury to a domestic industry.

The Philippines currently has two (2) anti-dumping measures imposed against imported clear and bronze float glass from China and wheat flour from Turkey. Having reached its fifth year of imposition of the anti-dumping duty on imported wheat flour from Turkey in 2020, the Philippine investigating authority (i.e., Tariff Commission) is currently conducting an expiry review for the said measure. In addition, the Philippines has two (2) safeguard measures in force on imported testliner board, and cement. In February 2020, the Philippines notified the WTO on the initiation of safeguard investigation on imported motor vehicles. The Philippines is the only ASEAN member country with special safeguards imposed on agricultural products, which is monitored by the DA.

In ASEAN, Thailand has the most number of anti-dumping measures currently in-force while Indonesia has the most number of safeguard measures imposed. ASEAN member states have no countervailing measures in-force (Table 10.5).

Table 10.5 Number of Trade Remedy Measures in Force in ASEAN (Anti-Dumping / Safeguards / Special Safeguards / Total): Indonesia 27 / 5 / 0 / 32; Malaysia 16 / 2 / 0 / 18; Philippines 2 / 2 / 11 / 15; Thailand 42 / 3 / 0 / 45; Viet Nam 7 / 4 / 0 / 11; TOTAL 94 / 17 / 11 / 112. Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Lao PDR and Myanmar have no trade remedy measures in-force.

Among the Philippine FTA partners, India has the most number of trade remedy measures in force wherein majority are anti-dumping measures. For safeguard measures, Australia has the highest number in force among the Philippines’ FTA partners. The EU and the US also have significant number of trade remedy measures in force especially anti-dumping measures and special safeguards (Table 10.6): Australia – AD 72, SG 11, total 83; China – 106, 4, CVD 1, total 111; EU – 119, 17, SSG 71, total 207; India – 263, 3, CVD 2, total 268; Japan – 7, SSG 173, total 180; South Korea – 39, SSG 75, total 114; Norway – SSG 2, total 2; New Zealand – 3, total 3; Switzerland – SSG 10, total 10; United States – 370, 120, CVD 2, SSG 496, total 988.

Impact of Increasing World Protectionism to Philippines

Rising protectionism could be a detriment to trade and negatively impact economic activities. Just recently, the International Monetary Fund warns that protectionism is increasing and poses a threat to global economic growth. While in some cases protectionist measures such as imposing higher tariffs, non-tariff barriers and other trade remedy measures are politically attractive in the short run, these can have large negative repercussions over the medium-term and in the long run.

Assuming a small-country case which does not affect world prices, an import tax or tariff increases the price of imported goods in the domestic market. Thus, protection is given to domestic industry through tariff, inducing local firm or industry to increase production. Tariff also implies higher manufacturing costs for those industries that rely heavily on imported raw materials and inputs to production. The import tax induces an increase in the domestic price of the good that makes the consumers worse-off as it reduces their purchasing power. Finally, global production supply chains may also be disrupted which will negatively impact on employment. Simply put, such an increase in worldwide protectionism would result in worldwide welfare losses. In terms of trade, small countries that do not influence world prices will stand to lose relative to large countries that can surely affect world prices.

In the same manner, should the Philippines breach its tariff commitments under the WTO, Free Trade Agreements, and other international trading arrangements, one possible form of retaliation is the removal of the Philippines from a Party’s list of GSP beneficiaries. Unless properly managed by the Philippine government, the identified breaches may lead to retaliation and/or requests for compensation from concerned Parties that will negate the revenue gains. Hence, the relevant provisions on international agreements with respect to consequences of this specific unilateral action by the Philippines should be carefully evaluated.

ai.title: II. Growing Global Protectionism
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang protectionism ay patakarang pang-ekonomiya na nagpoprotekta sa lokal na industriya laban sa dayuhang kompetisyon gamit ang taripa, trade remedy, quota, subsidy, at technical barriers.

🔍 Breakdown
• Mga pangunahing argumento: market failure, infant industry, revenue, national security
• Tumataas ang 'harmful interventions' mula 2009 (Global Trade Alert)
• Pinakamaraming ginagamit na instrumento: subsidies (7,431)
• Pinaka-apektadong sektor: iron at steel (935)

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Kapag lahat ay nagpoprotekta, bumababa ang kalakalan at lahat ay natatalo sa katagalan.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang taripa sa imported na bakal ay nagpapamahal sa mga industriyang gumagamit nito bilang input.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Nakakaapekto ito sa presyo, trabaho, at export ng Pilipinas.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• 3,298 harmful measures ang tumama sa Pilipinas mula sa trading partners
• Pilipinas: 1,031 NTMs; 196 export-related; 200 SPS; 352 TBT
• Panganib ng pagtanggal sa GSP kapag lumabag sa commitments

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang mga numero ng NTMs (1,031), trade remedy measures sa ASEAN (112), at mga implikasyon ng retaliation.

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang harmful intervention?
Sagot: Polisiyang nakakasama sa kalakalan na naitala ng Global Trade Alert.

🔗 Related Topics
WTO; UNCTAD; Global Trade Alert; WB

title: III. The United States and China Trade War
subject: PART TEN – TRADE POLICY BRIEFERS

sections.heading: III. The United States and China Trade War

paragraphs.text:
Background

The US-China Trade war is an ongoing economic conflict between the People’s Republic of China (China) and the United States of America (US). The US, through the issuance of Presidential Memorandum for the United States Trade Representative (USTR) issued on 14 August 2017 (Trump, 2017) has initiated a formal investigation under Section 301 of the United States Trade Act of 1974 on Chinese laws, policies, and practices related to intellectual property, innovation and technology that may have encouraged or required the transfer of American technology and intellectual property enterprises in China or that may otherwise negatively affect American economic interests. For the US, these laws, policies, practices, and actions may inhibit its exports, deprive US citizens of fair remuneration for their innovations, divert American jobs to workers in China, contribute to further trade deficit with China, and otherwise undermine American manufacturing, services, and innovation. In China, however, there is a perception that America is trying to curb its rise as a global economic power.

Through another memorandum dated 22 March 2018 (Trump, 2018), President Trump announced his decision on actions that US government will take in response to China’s supposed unfair trade practices covered under USTR Section 301. President Trump has instructed that appropriate response to China’s harmful acts, policies, and practices, and shall include separate actions on 1) tariff increase on a proposed list of products; 2) pursue dispute settlement in the WTO to address China’s discriminatory technology licensing practices; and 3) address concerns about investment in the United States directed or facilitated by China in industries or technologies deemed important to the United States (Congressional Research Service, 2019).

For instance, President Trump asked the US Trade Representative to level tariffs on $50 billion worth of Chinese imports following the investigation into intellectual property theft on 22 March 2018. The Chinese government retaliated by enacting its own tariffs on 128 products from the United States, including aluminum scraps, and pork products, as well as fruit, nut products, and steel piping. Over the following months, since the two countries have been embroiled in countless back-and-forth negotiations, a tit-for-tat tariff war (Figure 10.10), introduced foreign technology restrictions, fought several WTO cases, consequently leading US-China trade tensions to the brink of a full-blown trade war (BBC News, 2020).

A trade deal known as, “Economic and Trade Agreement between the United States of America and the People’s Republic of China”, was signed by the US and China in January 2020 and took effect on 14 February 2020. The agreement focuses on intellectual property rights, technology transfer, food and agricultural products, financial services, exchange rate matters and transparency, among others.

Figure 10.10 (How the US-China trade war has escalated): Jul 2018 – US $34bn / China $34bn; Aug 2018 – $16bn / $16bn; Sep 2018 – US $200bn at 10% / China $60bn at 10%; May 2019 – US $200bn at 25%; Jun 2019 – China $60bn at 25%; Sept 2019–Dec 2019 – US and China have threatened to impose new tariffs and increase existing ones.

Economic Significance of US and China to Philippines

a. China
Trade. China is a top-trading partner of the Philippines. From 2014 to 2018, China ranked 1st as source of imports of Philippine products with 19 percent share of total Philippine imports, while it ranked as the Philippines’ 3rd major export market with 12% share of total Philippine exports (PSA, 2020).

The Philippines, through its membership to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), has entered into a bilateral trade agreement with China called the ASEAN-China Free Trade Agreement (ACFTA). The ACFTA is a free trade agreement between the ASEAN Member States (AMS) including the Philippines, and China. The Agreement was signed by the Heads of Government / State of the AMS and China on 04 November 2002. The main objectives of the agreement include (1) to strengthen and enhance economic, trade and investment cooperation between the parties; (2) progressively liberalize and promote trade in goods and services; (3) explore new areas and develop appropriate measures for closer economic cooperation between the parties; and (4) facilitate the more effective economic integration of the newer ASEAN Member States and bridge the development gap among the parties. The ACFTA was fully implemented in 2018.

Investment. China is also one of the country’s top investors (Trade Policy Review Secretariat, 2018). The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported that during the fourth quarter of 2019, foreign direct investments (FDI) in the Philippines were mainly sourced from China amounted to ₱86.24 billion accounting for 77% of the total FDI in the country (PSA, 2020).

Remittances. China is the Philippines’ 38th source of remittances in 2019. Total value of remittances from China in the same year is US $33.45 million (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2020).

b. United States
Trade. Like China, US is also among the main trading partners of the Philippines. From 2014 to 2018, the US ranked as the country’s 3rd major import source with eight (8) percent share of total Philippine imports, while it ranked as the country’s 2nd major export with 15 percent share of total Philippine exports (PSA, 2020).

The Philippines does not have a bilateral trade agreement with the US. However, the Philippine authorities meet on a regular basis under the auspices of the 1989 bilateral Trade and Investment Framework Agreement (TIFA) to address outstanding bilateral economic issues and coordinate on bilateral, regional and multilateral issues (United States Trade Representative, n.d.).

Investment. The US is one of the largest foreign investors in the Philippines. The Philippine Trade Policy Review Secretariat Report in 2018 cited the US as the country’s 3rd largest investor accounting for 17% of total approved foreign direct investments (FDI) over the period between 2011 and 2016 (Trade Policy Review Secretariat, 2018).

Remittances. The US is the Philippines’ main source of the country’s remittances. In 2019, total remittances of overseas Filipino workers were recorded at US $ 11.3 billion (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2020).

Impact of the US - China trade war to the Philippines

Studies show that the current trade face-off between the US and China has resulted to a decline in the bilateral trade between the two countries and can lead to trade diversion (increased imports of countries not directly involved in the trade war) (International Trade Center, n.d.)

Since additional tariffs were imposed by both the US and China on each other’s traded goods, trade in goods with each other, and with the rest of the world was affected. Data show that all Chinese imports from and exports to the US decreased in value at the duration of the trade war (2018-2019). Same decreasing trend was seen in the US imports from and exports to China (Figures 10.11 and 10.12).

The existing trade war may also cause major traders from both the US and China to increase their trade with other economies to compensate revenue losses caused by the trade war; thus, resulting to trade diversion. A study made by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) shows that one consequence of the bilateral tariffs by both US and China will be an increase of each country’s imports from elsewhere. Trade diversion effects, however, do not necessarily happen, and generally are not complete, meaning that third countries are generally able to capture only part of the trade. Other countries may not have enough untapped supply capacity; exporters subject to tariffs may retain trade by reducing their prices; and trade frictions may make it very difficult to find other competitive suppliers because of high transportation costs given the inadequate trade infrastructures. In practice, various effects of tariffs are not mutually exclusive and often happen in concert: bilateral tariffs lead to higher prices for consumers, to lower profits for exporting firms, and are accompanied by trade diversion effects that will likely favor third countries (Nicita, 2019).

The current trade face-off between the US and China also has inevitable implications to the Philippines, most visibly in the recent trends of our foreign trade and their impact on the manufacturing sector, the dominant source of the country’s exports. The following explains the movement of the Philippine imports from and exports to China and the US from 2014 until the start of the imposition of tariffs in 2018.

a. Philippines Exports to China and the US (Figure 10.13) and Imports from China and the US (Figure 10.14) from 2014 to 2018
In the last five years, Philippine exports to China (valued at an average of US $ 7.11 billion) were evidently of smaller value than its exports to the US (with an average of US $ 8.75 billion). Note, however, that Philippine exports to China grew at a faster rate of 7% annually during the last three years compared to only 0.83 percent growth rate of Philippine exports to US. Philippine exports to US however remained stable in the same period. When trade war commenced in 2018, Philippine exports to the US grew at an 8% annual rate.

In terms of imports, the Philippines has sourced its goods doubly higher and faster from China than the US. Philippine imports from China were valued at US $15.58 billion on the average from 2014 to 2018. Trends indicate an upward one at 19 percent growth rate during the last three years. In contrast, imports of the Philippines from the US have been volatile since 2014, valued at an average of US $ 6.63 billion and grew at an 8% rate in the same period.

b. Top Philippine Imports and Exports to China (Tables 10.7 and 10.8) and the US (Tables 10.9 and 10.10) by HS Chapter from 2014 to 2018
Top Philippine imports from China (Table 10.7, in million USD; total US$77,877.21): HS 85 Electrical machinery and equipment – 15,717.26 (20.18%); HS 72 Iron and steel – 9,242.30 (11.87%); HS 84 Nuclear reactors, boilers, machinery – 8,768.23 (11.26%); HS 27 Mineral fuels – 7,319.66 (9.40%); HS 73 Articles of iron or steel – 3,466.94 (4.45%); HS 39 Plastics – 2,782.57 (3.57%); HS 87 Vehicles – 2,681.04 (3.44%); HS 69 Ceramic products – 1,887.09 (2.42%); HS 94 Furniture – 1,522.78 (1.96%); HS 29 Organic chemicals – 1,268.01 (1.63%). Top 20 chapters = 82.28% of total.
Top Philippine exports to China (Table 10.8; total US$35,570 million): HS 85 – 12,322 (34.64%); HS 84 – 8,394 (23.60%); HS 26 Ores, slag and ash – 4,374 (12.30%); HS 08 Edible fruit and nuts – 1,639 (4.61%); HS 27 – 1,525 (4.29%); HS 74 Copper – 1,429 (4.02%); HS 90 Optical, medical instruments – 1,119 (3.15%); HS 29 – 822 (2.31%). Top 20 = 96.61%.
Top Philippine imports from the US (Table 10.9; total US$33,138.60 million): HS 85 – 8,971.46 (27.07%); HS 23 Residues and waste from the food industries – 4,135.98 (12.48%); HS 10 Cereals – 3,328.92 (10.05%); HS 84 – 2,237.61 (6.75%); HS 88 Aircraft, spacecraft – 2,127.86 (6.42%); HS 04 Dairy produce – 1,071.08 (3.23%). Top 20 = 88.93%.
Top Philippine exports to the US (Table 10.10; total US$43,769 million): HS 85 – 16,454 (37.59%); HS 84 – 6,042 (13.81%); HS 15 Animal or vegetable fats and oils – 2,998 (6.85%); HS 61 Apparel (knitted) – 2,379 (5.44%); HS 90 – 2,020 (4.62%); HS 42 Articles of leather – 1,716 (3.92%); HS 62 Apparel (not knitted) – 1,704 (3.89%); HS 20 Preparations of vegetables, fruit – 1,331 (3.04%). Top 20 = 92.54%.

Top Philippine imports from and exports to China (Tables 10.7 and 10.8) are products from HS Chapter 85 classified as electrical machinery and equipment and parts thereof; sound recorders and reproducers, television image and sound recorders and reproducers and parts and accessories of such articles. Most-traded products by both the China and the US were from the Machinery sector which includes products used in the manufacturing.

With the rising trade conflict between the US and China, Philippine exports and imports of these products are likely to increase because of the trade diversion effects of the trade war. US and China trade with other countries might also increase. This would result to increased competition between third countries as regards to the traded products of China and the US to the rest of the world.

ai.title: III. The United States and China Trade War
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ang US-China trade war ay tuloy-tuloy na tunggalian sa kalakalan kung saan nagpapataw ng taripa ang dalawang bansa sa produkto ng isa't isa.

🔍 Breakdown
• Simula: 2017 imbestigasyon ng US sa ilalim ng Section 301 (IP, teknolohiya)
• 2018–2019: serye ng tariff retaliation
• Trade deal (Economic and Trade Agreement): nilagdaan January 2020; epektibo 14 February 2020
• Epekto sa Pilipinas: trade diversion, kompetisyon sa third markets

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Dalawang higante ang nagbabanggaan, at kahit hindi tayo kasali, nadadamay ang ating kalakalan.

📦 Halimbawa
Kapag mas mahal ang produkto ng China sa US, puwedeng lumipat ang US sa ibang supplier, tulad ng iba pang bansa sa Asya.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Mahalaga ito dahil parehong mahahalagang trading partner ng Pilipinas ang China at US.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• China: #1 source ng imports (19% share, 2014–2018); #3 export market (12%)
• US: #3 source ng imports (8%); #2 export market (15%)
• Pinakamalaking trade: Electrical machinery (HS Ch. 85)

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang timeline at ang posibleng epekto sa Pilipinas (trade diversion, competition).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Ano ang trade diversion?
Sagot: Paglipat ng imports sa ibang bansang hindi kasali sa trade war.

🔗 Related Topics
ACFTA; TIFA; WTO

title: IV. Trade Steps of Major Trading Partners
subject: PART TEN – TRADE POLICY BRIEFERS

sections.heading: IV. Trade Steps of Major Trading Partners

paragraphs.text:
Background

a. Lower tariffs attributed to increasing number of bilateral, regional, and multilateral arrangements
The Philippines has trading agreements with member economies of the WTO and APEC; nine (9) member states of ASEAN, and seven (7) countries that have bilateral free trade area (FTA) agreements with the ASEAN: Australia and New Zealand; China; Japan; Korea (Rep. of), India, Hong Kong; and with four (4) European Free Trade Area (EFTA) States (Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Iceland). Under these trade agreements, tariffs are progressively reduced and/or eliminated with the end goal of zero tariffs on substantially all goods by the agreed end dates (Table 10.11).

Table 10.11 Philippine Trade Agreements and Tariff Commitments (Date of Full Implementation – Elimination (zero duty) – Reduction 0%-5% / Non-zero – Exclusions): WTO – 2000 (developed), 2005 (developing) – Tariff bindings and average cut – exclusions for health and national security; ASEAN – 2015 – ~99% – ~1% – exclusions for health and national security; ASEAN-Korea – 2016 – 90% – 10% of total tariff lines and 10% of total trade value (2004 imports); ASEAN-China – 2018 – 90% – 400-500 6-digit HS lines, 10% of total 2001 imports; ASEAN-Japan – 2018 – 95%; APEC – 2020 – free and open trade within member economies; ASEAN-Australia/New Zealand – 2020 – 90%-100%; ASEAN-India – 2022 – 80% / 4% / 1% – exclusions 14%; ASEAN-Hong Kong – 2032 – 85% / 10% – exclusions 5%; Philippine-Japan – 2018 – 95%; Philippine-EFTA – 2027 – Agriculture: 14% (CHE/LIE), 36% (NOR), 72% (ICE), 17%-31% (PH) elimination; NAMA: EFTA 100% upon EIF, PH 92% upon EIF + 7% in 10 years; exclusions agriculture: 74% (CHE/LIE), 50% (NOR), 25% (ICE), 66%-82% (PH).

Under such agreements, the Philippines has reduced its tariffs by about 68% under the ASEAN India Free Trade Area (AIFTA) to 85% under the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) of the total tariff lines. On the other hand, it gained duty free access to over 90% of the tariff lines from ASEAN, Australia, New Zealand, and Japan and to more than 70% of imported goods from China, Korea, and India. Philippines has also begun eliminating/lowering tariffs on goods from EFTA States and Hong Kong since FTAs with these countries came in effect in 2018 and 2020, respectively.

It may be important to highlight that in ASEAN, which the Philippines is a member, the average Intra-ASEAN tariffs have been virtually eliminated across the 10 ASEAN Member States, from 3.11% in 2005 to just 0.20% in 2017. The average Intra-ASEAN tariffs for Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar and Viet Nam (CLMV), for which flexibilities were availed, significantly fell from 5.28% in 2005 to 0.46% in 2017, bringing them closer to the average rate for Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore and Thailand (ASEAN-6) at 0.03%.

b. Unfair trade practices by countries to protect themselves
The World Trade Organization allows imposition of measures against unfair trade practices by members. In Article 7-01, Chapter VII on the WTO Rights and Obligations provides that the Parties confirm their rights and obligations relating to the application of anti-dumping and countervailing duties under the WTO Agreement on Implementation of Article VI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of 1994 and the WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Duties.

In Article 2.1 of the Anti-Dumping Agreement, a product is to be considered as being dumped, i.e. introduced into the commerce of another country at less than its normal value, if the export price of the product exported from one country to another is less than the comparable price, in the ordinary course of trade, for the like product when destined for consumption in the exporting country.

From 1995 to June 2019, WTO records indicate a total of 5,883 anti-dumping initiations by 107 exporting countries, with China having the most total number of initiations at 23%, followed by Korea at 8%, and the US at 5%. Based on notification to the WTO from January 1995 to June 2019, 26% or 1,008 of the total 3,887 anti-dumping measures have been imposed on China and several countries. Meanwhile, 7% or a total of 283 anti-dumping measures have been imposed on Korea and 5% or a total of 189 anti-dumping measures against the US.

There are continued reports and allegations that the EU and US dumped their subsidized products on developing countries while concurrently keeping international price at low levels.

c. COVID-19 pandemic induced countries to increase tariffs & NTBs
Amidst the COVID-19 situation, 143 countries adopted trade measures and have notified the same to the WTO (Table 10.12). Of the total 151 restrictive measures affecting all countries, 116 such measures are still active until 2022, although some were imposed for an unknown period; 33 measures are already terminated, while two are under investigation. Three countries adopted tariff increases in petroleum products, pork and poultry, and other agricultural products. The restrictive non-tariff measures imposed include export prohibition on medicines; cereals, flour, sugar; other food products, medical supplies and other protective equipment; cigarettes and tobacco products, rice, fish products, beans, essential commodities, pharmaceutical products, fruits, wild animals and others for sanitary and phyto-sanitary (SPS) reasons; export licensing requirements on ventilators, medical supplies and equipment; quarantine requirements on all products; licensing permit requirements to export face masks, sanitizer, alcohol and disinfectant, medical and hospital products; import ban on medical supplies, non-essential goods, cement, second hand clothes, and petroleum products; export quotas on food products, wheat, meslin, barley; and certification requirement for testing kits.

Among the FTA partners of the Philippines, including ASEAN, Australia and New Zealand, India, Korea, Japan, and China, a total of 17 active restrictive measures were adopted including export prohibition on masks, drugs, medical supplies and equipment, and rice (12), licensing or permit requirements to export masks, medical supplies, rice (2), prohibition/restrictions of imports of wild animals and products (1), conformity assessments of medical supplies (2), and quarantine requirements, requirement to pass through specific port or customs (1).

Table 10.12 Trade Measures Adopted by Countries Amidst COVID-19 (as of 28 May 2020): Restrictive – 151 total; tariff increase 3; tariff elimination 0; tariff reduction 0; non-tariff measures 148. Liberalizing – 134 total; tariff increase 0; tariff elimination 4; tariff reduction 107; non-tariff measures 23.

Philippine Trade Strategy to FTA & Major Trade Partners

Philippine trade policy has not undergone major changes since 2005; the tariff remains as the main policy instrument. The Philippines grants at least MFN treatment to all WTO Members. It has preferential trading agreements with 15 partners: the other nine parties of ASEAN, and six countries that have negotiated agreements with ASEAN (Australia and New Zealand, India, China, Japan, and the Republic of Korea). An agreement between the Philippines and EFTA members has been signed and ratified. FTA negotiations with the European Union are ongoing.

a. Philippines and ASEAN
As a member of ASEAN, the Philippines is committed to deepening its economic integration among the members, including removing obstacles to trade and improving trade facilitation. The Philippines, both unilaterally and through the ASEAN, has continued to pursue a policy of negotiating regional trade agreements (RTAs) of varying scope with the focus on Asia-Pacific.

Hence, the Philippines continues to implement existing FTAs with ASEAN to maximize its benefits. It participates in ongoing reviews and upgrade initiatives under these FTAs to provide additional market access and generate more opportunities.

Recently, the Philippines signed the ASEAN-Hong Kong, China Free Trade Agreement and ASEAN-Hong Kong Investment Agreement. These two Agreements are part of the region’s continuous efforts in expanding external economic relations to foster greater trade opportunities for the ASEAN Economic Community. This will ensure more opportunities for ASEAN products by providing greater market access for their products and sustained flow of foreign direct investments. Further, these agreements would provide job opportunities for people and enhance collaboration among businesses, particularly MSMEs. The FTA is ASEAN’s sixth free trade agreement with external partners, after ASEAN-China FTA (ACFTA), ASEAN-Korea FTA (AKFTA), ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership (AJCEPA), ASEAN-India FTA (AIFTA) and ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand FTA (ANZFTA). It covers trade in goods, rules of origin, non-tariff measures, customs procedures and trade facilitation, trade remedies, technical barriers to trade, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, trade in services, intellectual property rights, and economic and technical cooperation.

b. Philippines and the European Region
In 2016, the Philippines ranked as the 39th EU trading partner. Philippines’ share of total EU imports and exports was 0.4%. By mid-2017, the EU became the second largest export market for Philippine-made products accounting for 15% of total Philippine exports behind Japan (17%) and ahead of US (15%) and China (11%). Philippine exports include preparations of meat, aircraft, spacecraft, and parts thereof, Animal or vegetable fats & oils, optical, medical or surgical instruments, Machinery and mechanical appliances, electrical machinery. With regard to Philippine imports, the EU is the 4th largest supplier to the Philippines. Products exported by EU to the Philippines includes meat; optical, medical, or surgical instruments; pharmaceutical products; aircraft, spacecraft, and parts thereof; machinery and mechanical appliances; electrical machinery and equipment. Latest available statistics indicate EU’s share to total Philippine exports and imports are at 13% and 8%, respectively.

The Philippines has adopted a parallel three-pronged strategy to increase the country’s presence in the European region. Two of these strategies capture the country’s interest in the EU through the inclusion of the Philippines in the list of beneficiaries under the EU Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) - Plus and the ongoing negotiations for an FTA. To have a wider reach in the region, the Philippines, as its third strategy, has also negotiated an FTA with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA).

The exploratory FTA scoping meetings between the Philippines and the EU started in 2013. It includes discussions on the objectives and key principles of the FTA negotiations. The launch of the FTA negotiations was announced by both sides on 11 December 2015. Two rounds of negotiations have been held. The areas covered so far are: trade in goods (text and market access); sanitary and phytosanitary measures; rules of origin; customs and trade facilitation; services; investments; intellectual property rights; government procurement; trade and sustainable development; and legal and institutional issues (LII).

The Philippines’ inclusion in the EU’s GSP Plus provides duty free entry to the EU for some of the most important Philippine exports, including processed fruit and foodstuffs, coconut oil, footwear, fish and textiles. This will likewise result in attracting new industrial investments in sectors where relatively high tariffs are slashed to zero under GSP Plus scheme. The GSP Plus scheme includes established Philippine exports that are labor intensive such as pineapple juice (currently 28.5%); garments (currently 5%-9%); preserved fruits (currently 6%-9%); tuna (currently 20.5%); fruit, jams, and jellies (currently 20.5%); and footwear (currently 11.9%). The GSP Plus preferences cover over 6,200 tariff lines. It gave the Philippines the required attractiveness as a destination for new agricultural and manufacturing facilities for products that will now enjoy duty free access to the EU, aside from producing more jobs for Filipinos, especially those in the rural areas.

The Philippines also signed a bilateral FTA with the European Free Trade Association on 28 April 2016.

c. Philippines and the United States
The Philippines is a major trading and investment partners of the US, with bilateral trade in goods and services in 2017 totaling an estimated $29.6 billion, with a $6.7 billion deficit in favor of the Philippines. The United States is one of the largest foreign investors in the Philippines, and is the Philippines’ third-largest trading partner, with over $27 billion in goods and services traded. Philippine exports to the US: semiconductor devices and computer peripherals, automobile parts, electric machinery, textiles and garments, wheat and animal feeds, coconut oil, and information technology/business process outsourcing services. Philippines imports from the US are agriculture goods, machinery, cereals, raw and semi-processed materials for the manufacture of semiconductors, electronics, and transport equipment. At present, the Philippines enjoys US GSP schemes.

New Trade Measures taken by above countries

Philippine major trade partners continue to uphold their commitment under the WTO. These trade partners have participated in new developments (i.e. Trade Facilitation Agreement) and reforms in the WTO. They also joined the increasing number of RTAs and FTAs.

With the COVID-19 situation, most of Philippine trade partners implemented trade measures (Annex D). For instance, India has implemented a total of 13 trade measures while the EU and United States implemented 9 and 6 measures, respectively. On the other hand, China implemented a total of three measures. Most of these trade measures cover importation of medical supplies and other essential goods in response to the pandemic. The Philippines has also implemented similar measures as a response to the pandemic situation.

Moreover, same Philippine trade partners have also issued joined statements on WTO proposals relating to COVID-19 (Table 10.13: WTO Member Proposals on COVID-19, dated 20 March 2020 to 29 May 2020 – joint ministerial statements, e.g., “Responding to the COVID-19 pandemic with open and predictable trade in agricultural and food products”; “Statement on COVID-19 and the multilateral trading system by Ministers responsible for WTO”; ASEAN Declaration; APEC Ministers statement; G20 Trade and Investment Ministerial Statement; LDC group statements). [Full member lists: see PDF pp. 279–280]

Impact on Philippines or PH Response

Except for Japan, the Philippines has trade deficits in most of its FTA partner countries. Hence, the Philippines should continue to pursue trade cooperation strategies through the lowering of tariffs; and improving trade facilitation measures that promote seamless value chains. Emphasis must be given to the support and further development of MSMEs.

The Philippines can build on the gains of existing FTAs and maximize their utilization. It must also take advantage of the opportunities from the GSP schemes of the EU (GSP+) and the United States (GSP) and may consider pursuing an FTA with the latter.

The Philippines can also explore strengthening economic relations with non-traditional trading partners.

ai.title: IV. Trade Steps of Major Trading Partners
ai.content:
📖 Kahulugan
Ipinapakita ng bahaging ito ang trade agreements at tariff commitments ng Pilipinas, ang mga hakbang ng major trading partners laban sa unfair trade, at ang mga naging trade measures sa panahon ng COVID-19.

🔍 Breakdown
• Pilipinas: may FTA sa ASEAN at 6 na partner + EFTA
• Intra-ASEAN average tariff: bumaba mula 3.11% (2005) tungong 0.20% (2017)
• 143 bansa ang nag-adopt ng COVID-19 trade measures; 151 restrictive at 134 liberalizing
• EU: GSP+ para sa Pilipinas; US: GSP

💡 Simpleng Paliwanag
Pinagsama-sama rito ang kung sino ang kasosyo natin sa kalakalan, ano ang kasunduan, at ano ang ginagawa ng mga bansa para protektahan ang sarili.

📦 Halimbawa
Ang export ng pineapple juice sa EU ay may duty-free access sa ilalim ng GSP+, kaya mas mura ito doon.

⭐ Bakit Mahalaga Ito?
Tumutulong ito sa pagpaplano ng trade strategy ng Pilipinas.

⚠️ Dapat Tandaan
• Maraming trade deficit ng PH sa FTA partners maliban sa Japan
• Mungkahi: palakasin ang FTA utilization at tuklasin ang non-traditional partners

🎯 Board Exam Tip
Alamin ang buod ng Table 10.11 at ang mga numero ng COVID-19 trade measures (151 restrictive; 134 liberalizing).

❓ Madalas Malito ang Students
Tanong: Anong EU scheme ang nagbibigay ng duty-free sa Pilipinas?
Sagot: GSP Plus.

🔗 Related Topics
